Since Java 9, module rules can block this. - Reflection is slower than a direct call. It does access checks, boxes the arguments (wraps primitives into objects), and is not inlined at first. So frameworks speed things up by: - caching metadata; - using MethodHandle s (a faster way to call methods dynamically); - generating bytecode or proxies at runtime (CGLIB, ByteBuddy); - or doing the work at compile time with annotation processors (Lombok, MapStruct). How does it work? At startup, Spring does roughly this: 1. Scans the classpath for classes. 2. Reads @Component / @Service on them through reflection. 3. Finds their constructors. 4. Works out the dependencies each one needs. 5. Creates the beans (instantiates them). 6. Wraps some of them in proxies (for things like transactions). Jackson works similarly. It uses reflection over getters, fields and record components to turn objects into JSON. Example This example defines a @Masked annotation. A small reflection method reads every field. If a field has @Masked , it prints instead of the value. When would I use it? - Mostly you are a user of annotation-driven frameworks: Spring, JPA, validation, Jackson, JUnit. - Write your own annotations for cross-cutting concerns — things needed in many places, like timing, auditing or masking ( @Timed , @Audited , @Masked ). Something must process them: an aspect or a validator. - Reflection inside business code is rarely justified. What can go wrong? - Annotations do nothing on their own. Something must process them. A custom @Timed with no aspect behind it is just a comment. - Reflection breaks encapsulation and refactoring safety. Method names live in strings, so renaming a method won't update them. It also fails with the module system or GraalVM native images unless you configure it. - Performance. Reflective calls in hot paths, without caching, are slow. Interview questions Q1. What is annotation retention? It defines how long an annotation lives: SOURCE (only for the compiler), CLASS (in the bytecode, but not at runtime), or RUNTIME (available through reflection, which frameworks need). Q2. How does Spring use reflection? It scans classes, reads their annotations, finds constructors and fields, creates and injects beans, and builds proxies. It caches this metadata for performance. Q3. What are the downsides of reflection? Slower calls, broken encapsulation, loss of compile-time safety, and problems with the module system and native images.

t: 2.1 The collections hierarchy and choosing the right one
x: Why? In simple words: Java gives you a few standard "containers" for groups of data. Each one is good at some jobs and bad at others. Pick the one that matches how you will read and write the data. Every program keeps groups of things: orders, users, IDs. If you pick the wrong structure, two bad things can happen: - A fast operation becomes slow. For example, an O(1) lookup (constant time — same speed for any size) turns into O(n) (time grows with the number of items). - You waste memory. The Collections Framework gives you a small set of interfaces: List , Set , Queue , Deque and Map . Each interface has several implementations that you can swap. So you write your code against the interface. Then you pick the implementation based on your access pattern — how you will add, find and remove items. What is happening internally? Here is the family tree of the main types: Under the hood, almost every class uses one of only four memory layouts: 1. A contiguous array — items sit side by side in one block of memory. 2. Linked nodes — each item is in its own small object that points to the next one. 3. A hash table — the key is turned into a number that picks a slot. 4. A balanced tree — items are kept sorted in a tree that never gets too tall. If you know which layout sits under a class, you can work out its speed for each operation. You do not need to memorise tables. How does it work? Choose by asking yourself a few simple questions: - Do I need the items kept in order? - Must every item be unique? - Do I look things up by a key? - Do I need sorted order, or ranges like "between X and Y"? - Do I need the smallest or largest item quickly? - Will many threads use it at the same time? Then match your answer to this table. ("Amortised O(1)" means usually instant, sometimes slow, but fast on average.) Requirement Pick Layout Key operations --- --- --- --- Indexed list, append ArrayList Array get O(1), add O(1) amortised Stack or queue ArrayDeque Circular array push/pop/offer/poll O(1) Key → value, fast HashMap Hash table get/put O(1) average Key → value in insertion/access order LinkedHashMap Hash table + linked list O(1) + ordered iteration Sorted keys, floor/ceiling/ranges TreeMap Red-black tree O(log n) Unique elements HashSet / TreeSet Same as maps O(1) / O(log n) Repeatedly take min/max PriorityQueue Binary heap offer/poll O(log n), peek O(1) Enum keys or flags EnumMap / EnumSet Array / bit vector O(1), tiny memory Shared across threads ConcurrentHashMap , CopyOnWriteArrayList , BlockingQueue Chapter 4 Coming from C ? Here is the mapping: - List<T → ArrayList - Dictionary → HashMap - SortedDictionary → TreeMap - Queue / Stack → ArrayDeque - PriorityQueue<T,P → PriorityQueue<T with a Comparator - ConcurrentDictionary → ConcurrentHashMap Example Declare the variable with the interface type. Create the object with the implementation class. When would I use it? On every task. In an interview, say your choice and the reason in one sentence. For example: "I'll use a TreeMap, because I need the nearest earlier timestamp ( floorKey ) in O(log n)." What can go wrong? - Using legacy classes. Vector , Stack and Hashtable lock (synchronise) on every single call, so they are slow. Use ArrayList , ArrayDeque , and HashMap or ConcurrentHashMap instead. - Choosing LinkedList "because inserts are O(1)". This is usually wrong in practice (see 2.3). - Using a List for "is it present?" checks inside a loop. list.contains is O(n) — it checks items one by one. Inside a loop, the whole thing becomes O(n²). Use a HashSet instead. Interview questions Q1. Which collection would you use for X? Decide by how the data will be accessed: random access by index → ArrayList; lookup by key → HashMap; sorted order or ranges → TreeMap; take the min or max again and again → PriorityQueue; first-in-first-out (FIFO) or last-in-first-out (LIFO) → ArrayDeque. Q2. Why is Map not part of the Collection interface? A map holds key-value pairs and works through keys. It does not fit the Collection contract, which is about single elements added with add(E) . Instead, a map gives you collection views of itself: keySet , values and entrySet .

Why? In simple words: An ArrayList is a normal array that grows by itself. When it is full, Java makes a bigger array and copies everything across. Arrays are the fastest structure when you read by index. But an array has a fixed size. ArrayList is a growable array. You get array speed, plus good locality (items sit close together in memory, so the CPU reads them fast). And it resizes itself automatically. What is happening internally? Inside, there are just two fields: size is how many items you have stored. Capacity is the length of the backing array — how many items fit before it must grow. Key facts: - new ArrayList< () starts with a shared empty array. The first add creates the real array with capacity 10 . - When the array is full, grow() makes a new array 1.5× the old capacity ( old + (old 1) ). It copies everything with Arrays.copyOf , which is a fast native memory copy. - The array holds references (pointers) to your objects, side by side. So looping over it is friendly to the CPU cache. The objects themselves live elsewhere on the heap. - A counter called modCount goes up on every structural change (add or remove). Iterators use it to detect changes and fail fast (see 2.10). Think of a tiffin box with 10 compartments. When all are full, you buy a box with 15 compartments and move the food across. How does it work? - get(i) : check that i is in range, then return elementData[i] → O(1) . - add(e) : if size == capacity , grow first (an O(n) copy). Then store at position size and increase size . Growth is rare and the array grows by a multiple each time. So across n adds, the total copying is only O(n). That makes each add amortised O(1) — usually instant, occasionally slow, fast on average. - add(i, e) / remove(i) : System.arraycopy shifts all items after i right or left → O(n − i) . - remove(Object) : search item by item using equals , then shift → O(n). - contains / indexOf : check item by item → O(n). Why is the average add O(1)? Start at 10 and grow ×1.5 each time. The copies are 10 + 15 + 22 + … and this total stays below 3n. Spread over n adds, each add costs O(1) on average. Example When would I use it? It is the default list for almost everything: query results, DTO lists, DSA arrays when you don't know the size up front, building responses. It is best at two things: adding at the end, and looping over items. What can go wrong? - remove(int) vs remove(Object) confusion with a List<Integer . remove(5) removes the item at index 5, not the value 5. - Removing items one by one from the front, in a loop, is O(n²). Each removal shifts every item after it. Use removeIf , loop from the back, or use an ArrayDeque . - subList is a view, not a copy. If you then add to or remove from the parent list, using the view throws ConcurrentModificationException . - Not thread-safe. If two threads add at the same time, items can get lost. You may also see ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException during a resize. - Huge lists of boxed numbers waste memory. Each Integer is a full object. For millions of numbers, prefer int[] or a primitive collection library. Interview questions Q1. How does ArrayList grow? When the array is full, it creates a new array 1.5× larger and copies the elements over. Because it grows by a multiple each time (geometric growth), adding at the end is amortised O(1). Q2. What is the default capacity? 10. It is created lazily, only on the first add. Q3. Time complexity of get, add, add(index), remove(index)? O(1), amortised O(1), O(n), O(n).

Why? In simple words: A LinkedList is a chain of small boxes, each holding one item and pointing to the box before and after it. Adding or removing in the middle is cheap only if you are already standing at that spot. In a doubly linked list, each element knows its previous and next neighbour. So you can insert or remove an element in O(1), without shifting anything. But there is a condition: you must already hold a reference to the neighbour (for example, an iterator's current position). LinkedList implements both List and Deque (a double-ended queue — you can add or remove at both ends). What is happening internally? Every element needs its own Node object. A node has an object header (~12 bytes) plus 3 references. That is roughly 24–32 bytes per element , on top of the element itself. These nodes are scattered across the heap. So the CPU cannot read them in one smooth run. This is called poor cache locality , and it makes the list slow to walk through. Think of a treasure hunt. Each clue tells you where the next clue is. To reach clue 50, you must visit all 49 before it. How does it work? - addFirst / addLast / removeFirst / removeLast : change a few pointers → O(1) . - get(i) : walk from whichever end is closer → O(n) . - add(i, e) : O(n) to walk to the position, then O(1) to relink. - ListIterator.add/remove at the iterator's current position: O(1), because you are already there. Example When would I use it? Rarely. Even for queues and stacks, ArrayDeque is faster and uses less memory. Real uses are few: - You hold iterators and keep inserting or removing in the middle all the time. - You need a list that is also a deque, and you need to store null . In DSA, you usually write your own node class instead (LRU cache, LeetCode ListNode ). You don't use LinkedList there. What can go wrong? - Calling get(i) inside a loop. Each get walks the list, so the loop takes quadratic time — O(n²). - Memory. It uses 3–5× more memory than an ArrayList with the same elements. - It loses in practice. In benchmarks, ArrayList usually beats LinkedList even for middle inserts on lists of moderate size. Why? System.arraycopy moves contiguous memory extremely fast. Following pointers, on the other hand, keeps missing the CPU cache. Interview questions Q1. ArrayList vs LinkedList? ArrayList is a contiguous array: O(1) random access, amortised O(1) append, cache-friendly, and low memory. LinkedList is a chain of nodes: O(1) insert/remove at the ends or at a position you already hold, but O(n) access by index and high memory use. Choose ArrayList by default. Q2. When is LinkedList actually better? When you insert or remove often at an iterator position inside a large list, or when you need a Deque that allows nulls. In other cases, ArrayDeque or ArrayList wins.

Why? In simple words: A HashMap is a set of numbered boxes. From the key itself, Java calculates which box the value goes in — so to find it again, it jumps straight to that box instead of searching everywhere. You often need to find something by a key, fast. For example: find a user by ID, count how many times each word appears, or look up a product by SKU. If you keep the data in a list, you must check items one by one. With a million items, that can be a million checks. This is O(n) — the work grows with the size of the data. A hash table avoids this. It uses the key to calculate where the value should be stored. Finding it later means doing the same calculation and going straight there. So a lookup takes about the same time whether you have 10 items or 10 million. This is called O(1) on average. Think of a railway parcel office with 16 numbered racks. The clerk does a small sum on your receipt number to pick a rack. When you come back, he does the same sum and walks straight to the right rack. What is happening internally? The main fields: A few terms: - Bucket — one slot in the table array. - Capacity — the number of buckets (the array length). - Load factor — how full the table may get before it grows. Default 0.75, meaning 75% full. - Threshold — the size at which the table grows: capacity × load factor. For the default, 16 × 0.75 = 12. Here is what the table can look like: A collision is when two different keys land in the same bucket. They are then kept in a small linked list (a chain ) in that bucket. Key constants: - TREEIFY THRESHOLD = 8 — a chain this long may turn into a tree. - UNTREEIFY THRESHOLD = 6 — a tree this small turns back into a chain. - MIN TREEIFY CAPACITY = 64 — the table needs at least this many buckets before any tree is made. How does it work? put(key, value) in steps: 1. Hash spreading. Java computes h = key.hashCode(); hash = h ^ (h 16) . This mixes (XORs) the top 16 bits into the bottom 16 bits. Why? Only the low bits are used to choose the bucket. Without mixing, keys whose hashCodes differ only in the high bits would all land in the same bucket. 2. Index. Java computes i = (n - 1) & hash . Here n is always a power of two, so n - 1 is all ones in binary (16 → 1111 ). So this & is a fast way to do hash % n . 3. Empty bucket? If table[i] is empty, put a new Node there. Done. 4. Look for the same key. Otherwise, walk through the bucket. If a node has the same hash and key.equals() is true , replace its value and return the old value. 5. Add a new node. If no node matched, append the new node at the end of the chain. (Java 8+ adds at the tail; Java 7 added at the head.) 6. Chain too long? If the chain length reaches 8 : - If the table has at least 64 buckets, convert this bucket into a red-black tree (a self-balancing sorted tree). Now the worst case in this bucket is O(log n). - Otherwise, resize the table instead. In a small table, too few buckets is the more likely reason for collisions. 7. Too full? If ++size threshold , resize the table. get(key) in steps: 1. Compute the same hash and the same index. 2. Check the first node in that bucket. 3. If it is not a match, walk the list or search the tree. 4. At each node, compare the hash first (cheap). Call equals only if the hashes match. Resize in steps: 1. Make a new table with double the capacity. 2. For each node, check just one bit : (hash & oldCap) . 3. If that bit is 0 , the node stays at index i . 4. If that bit is 1 , the node moves to i + oldCap . No hash is recomputed. Each old chain simply splits into a "low" chain and a "high" chain, and the order inside each chain is kept. Why 0.75 and 8? - 0.75 is a balance. A lower value wastes many empty buckets. A higher value makes chains longer. - With a decent hash function, chain lengths follow roughly a Poisson distribution (a standard pattern for random events). At this load the average chain length is about 0.5. - So the chance of one chain reaching 8 is about 0.00000006 — practically never. - That means treeification is a safety net. It protects against bad hashCodes or deliberate collision attacks. It is not the normal path. Example When would I use it? All the time: - Caches and lookups by ID. - Counting and grouping. - Memoisation in DSA — saving answers you already computed ( Map<String, Integer memo ). - Removing duplicates. - Two-sum style problems, where you look up the "complement" you need. - Adjacency lists for sparse graphs (graphs with few edges). What can go wrong? - Bad or mutable keys. If a key class has no proper hashCode / equals , or you change a key after putting it in (1.12), the entry can no longer be found. - All keys colliding. For example, a hashCode that returns a constant. Then every key lands in one bucket, and lookups slow down to O(n). After treeification it is O(log n), but the tree works well only if the keys are Comparable . - Iteration order is not stable. It can change after a resize, or between Java versions. Never depend on it. Use LinkedHashMap or TreeMap when order matters. - Not thread-safe. Two threads calling put together can lose updates and corrupt the size. In Java 7, a concurrent resize could even create a loop in a chain, so get ran forever. Use ConcurrentHashMap (4.9). - Memory. Each entry is a Node object (~32–48 bytes), plus the key and value objects. A map of a million Long → Long takes about 80+ MB. - Double lookups. Looping over keySet() and calling get(k) for each key does two lookups per key. Loop over entrySet() instead. Interview questions Q1. Explain HashMap internals. It is an array of buckets whose length is always a power of two. The key's hashCode is spread ( h ^ h 16 ) and masked to get an index. Keys that collide form a linked list in the bucket; that list becomes a red-black tree when a chain reaches 8 and the table has 64+ buckets. A lookup compares the hash first, then equals . When size goes above capacity × 0.75, the table doubles, and each node either stays at i or moves to i + oldCap , decided by one bit. Q2. Why is HashMap O(1) and when isn't it? A good hash spreads keys evenly, so each bucket holds about one entry; a lookup is just index arithmetic plus one or two comparisons. It gets slow when many keys collide because of a poor hashCode — O(n) per bucket, or O(log n) once the bucket becomes a tree. Q3. Why must the capacity be a power of two? So that (n-1) & hash can replace the slower modulo ( % ), and so that a resize can split each bucket by checking a single bit. Q4. What changed in Java 8? Long chains are turned into trees (treeification); new nodes are added at the tail instead of the head, which fixed Java 7's infinite loop during concurrent resize; and the hash spreading was simplified. Q5. Can HashMap have a null key? Yes, one. Its hash is treated as 0, so it is stored in bucket 0. Values can be null too. ConcurrentHashMap allows neither null keys nor null values. Q6. What happens when two keys have the same hashCode? Both go into the same bucket, and equals tells them apart. Both are stored and found correctly — it just costs one extra comparison.

t: 2.5 LinkedHashMap and building an LRU cache
x: Why? In simple words: A LinkedHashMap is a HashMap that also remembers order. It can remember the order you added keys, or the order you last used them — and the second one gives you an LRU cache almost for free. HashMap gives no promise about order. Sometimes you need fast lookup and a predictable order. Two common cases: - Insertion order — the order in which keys were first added. Useful to keep JSON fields in order, or to get the same output every run. - Access order — the order in which keys were last used. Useful to throw out the least recently used entry. This is an LRU cache (Least Recently Used). What is happening internally? LinkedHashMap extends HashMap . Each entry gets two extra pointers, before and after . These pointers join all entries into one doubly linked list . The map also keeps head and tail pointers to the two ends of that list. When accessOrder = true : - Every get or put of an existing key moves that entry to the tail . The tail is the "most recently used" end. - After each insertion, the map calls removeEldestEntry(head) . If your method returns true, the head is removed. The head is the least recently used entry. Think of a stack of newspapers on a table. Whenever you read one, you put it back on top. When the table is full, you throw away the one at the bottom — the one nobody has touched for longest. How does it work? 1. get(k) : a normal hash lookup, O(1). Then the node is unlinked and relinked at the tail, also O(1). 2. put(k, v) for a new key: the entry goes into its bucket and is appended at the tail. Then removeEldestEntry is asked whether to remove the head. 3. Iteration walks the linked list. So it costs O(size). A plain HashMap must scan every bucket, which costs O(capacity + size). Example When would I use it? - Small caches inside one process (per request or per instance). - When output must always come in the same order. - When you need LRU behaviour quickly. In LeetCode 146 (LRU Cache), interviewers usually want the manual HashMap + doubly linked list version (10.3). Mention this one as the production shortcut. For real production caches, use Caffeine — it has better hit rates, handles concurrency, and supports TTL (time-to-live, i.e. entries expire after a set time). What can go wrong? - Not thread-safe. In access-order mode, even get changes the structure (it moves the entry). So two threads that only read can still corrupt it. Guard it with a lock, or use Caffeine. - ConcurrentModificationException with access order. If you call get while looping over the map, it throws. This is because get counts as a structural change in this mode. - No TTL. It cannot expire entries by time. It also cannot evict by weight (for example, by how many bytes an entry uses). Interview questions Q1. How does LinkedHashMap maintain order? A doubly linked list runs through all the entries. It keeps insertion order by default, or access order when accessOrder is true. Q2. How do you build an LRU cache in Java quickly? Extend LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true , and override removeEldestEntry to return size() capacity . Q3. Is that LRU cache thread-safe? No — even reads change the order. Synchronise access to it, or use Caffeine or ConcurrentLinkedHashMap -style libraries.

Why? In simple words: A TreeMap keeps its keys sorted all the time. So it can answer "what is just before or just after this key?" and "give me everything between A and B" quickly. A hash map cannot answer questions about order. For example: - "What was the price at 14:05?" — that is, the latest price change at or before that time. - "Give me all orders between two timestamps." - "What is the smallest key greater than x?" - "Give me the top or bottom N." A sorted structure answers all of these in O(log n) — the work grows very slowly, roughly with the number of times you can halve n. What is happening internally? TreeMap is a red-black tree . That is a binary search tree (smaller keys go left, larger keys go right) that balances itself. It follows four rules: 1. Every node is red or black. 2. The root is black. 3. A red node has only black children. 4. Every path from the root down to a leaf has the same number of black nodes. Because of these rules, the tree's height stays at most 2·log₂(n+1). So search, insert and delete are O(log n) , guaranteed — even in the worst case. After an insert or a delete, the tree may break the rules for a moment. It fixes them with rotations (small re-arrangements of a few nodes) and by recolouring nodes. Insert needs at most 2 rotations; delete needs at most 3. How are keys ordered? By the key's compareTo method (if the key is Comparable ), or by a Comparator you pass in. equals is not used at all. TreeSet is simply a TreeMap where every value is the same dummy object. Think of a dictionary book. Words are always in alphabetical order. So you can open it in the middle and quickly narrow down to the word — or to the word just before it. How does it work? Example: floorKey(25) — find the largest key that is ≤ 25, using the tree above. 1. Start at the root, 20. Since 20 ≤ 25, remember 20 as a possible answer and go right. 2. Now at 30. Since 30 25, go left. 3. There is nothing on the left. Stop. 4. The answer is the last remembered key: 20. Each step throws away about half of the remaining tree. So the search is O(log n). Example When would I use it? - Time-series lookups : rates, prices or configs that were effective at a given time. - Calendar and booking conflicts : find the neighbouring bookings of a new interval. - Leaderboards where you loop in rank order. - Range queries : everything between A and B. - DSA problems that need a sorted multiset (a sorted collection that allows duplicates): sliding window median, "contains nearby almost duplicate", "my calendar". What can go wrong? - Comparator inconsistent with equals. If two different keys compare as 0, TreeMap treats them as the same key . One silently overwrites the other. - null keys throw NPE (NullPointerException), because null cannot be compared. The only exception is a comparator that handles null. - Slower than HashMap for plain lookups. It is O(log n) and must follow pointers down the tree. So use it only when you need order. - headMap / subMap are views. Changing them changes the original map too. Interview questions Q1. TreeMap vs HashMap? TreeMap keeps keys sorted, is O(log n), has navigation methods (floor, ceiling, ranges), needs Comparable keys or a Comparator, and allows no null keys. HashMap has no order, is O(1) on average, and uses hashCode/equals. Q2. What data structure backs TreeMap? A red-black tree — a self-balancing binary search tree (BST) with height ≤ 2·log₂(n+1). So every operation is O(log n) even in the worst case. Q3. How would you find the latest price effective at a given time? Store the price changes in a TreeMap keyed by effective time, and call floorEntry(time) .

Why? In simple words: A set is a bag that never holds the same thing twice. Use it to ask "have I already seen this?" in one quick step. You use a set to: - Answer "have I seen this before?" in O(1). - Remove duplicates. - Do set operations like union (everything in either) and intersection (only what is in both), without writing nested loops. What is happening internally? A HashSet is really a HashMap . Your elements are the keys. Every value is the same shared dummy object. So everything in 2.4 applies here too, including the hashCode/equals rules. The other sets follow the same idea: - LinkedHashSet uses a LinkedHashMap inside, so it keeps insertion order. - TreeSet uses a TreeMap inside, so it keeps elements sorted. - EnumSet is different. It stores one bit per enum constant inside a long (or a long[] if there are more than 64 constants). So checking membership is a single bit operation — extremely fast and tiny in memory. Think of a guest register at a wedding gate. Before writing a name, the guard checks whether it is already there. If it is, he does not write it again. How does it work? add(e) returns false if e was already in the set. So "detect a duplicate while adding" takes just one line. For set algebra, use the bulk methods: - retainAll — intersection (keep only common items). - addAll — union (add everything). - removeAll — difference (remove the other set's items). Example When would I use it? - Removing duplicates. - "Visited" sets in BFS/DFS (graph searches). - Membership checks inside loops. - Set algebra across lists of IDs. - "First unique element" problems (use LinkedHashSet, since it keeps order). - Flags (use EnumSet). What can go wrong? The same problems as HashMap keys: a missing hashCode / equals , or elements that change after being added. Also, retainAll with a List as the argument is O(n·m). For each of your n elements, it searches the m-item list one by one. Pass a Set instead. Interview questions Q1. How does HashSet work internally? It wraps a HashMap. Elements are stored as keys with one constant dummy value. Uniqueness comes from how the map treats keys — the same key cannot be stored twice. Q2. HashSet vs TreeSet vs LinkedHashSet? HashSet: no order, O(1). TreeSet: sorted, O(log n). LinkedHashSet: insertion order, O(1).

t: 2.8 ArrayDeque — your stack and your queue
x: Why? In simple words: ArrayDeque is one class that works as both a stack and a queue. It is an array whose ends wrap around in a circle, so adding or removing at either end is instant. Stacks and queues need O(1) operations at their ends: - Stacks (last in, first out): DFS, undo, matching brackets, monotonic stack. - Queues (first in, first out): BFS, task buffers, sliding windows. The older options are poor. Stack is a legacy class and locks (synchronises) on every call. LinkedList creates a new node object for every element. ArrayDeque is a circular array that does both jobs faster. What is happening internally? Here is how it works inside: - Two indices, head and tail , mark the two ends. - They move using modular arithmetic. When an index passes the end of the array, it wraps back to the start. - When the array fills up, it doubles in size and "unwraps" the items into the new array in order. - Every operation at either end is O(1) amortised (usually instant; occasionally a resize, but fast on average). No node objects are created per element. - null elements are not allowed . Inside, null means "empty slot". Also, poll returns null to tell you the deque is empty. Think of a round table in a canteen with numbered seats. People join at one end and leave from the other. When you reach the last seat number, you simply continue from seat 1. How does it work? Use as Methods --- --- Stack (LIFO, at the head) push , pop , peek Queue (FIFO) offer (tail), poll (head), peek Deque (both ends) offerFirst/Last , pollFirst/Last , peekFirst/Last The methods come in two families: - add / remove / element throw an exception when they fail. - offer / poll / peek return a special value instead (false or null). Prefer the second family in DSA loops. Example When would I use it? - Every stack and queue in DSA: BFS, DFS, monotonic stack, sliding-window deque. - Task buffers in single-threaded code. - Undo history. If several threads share the queue, use a BlockingQueue instead (4.14). What can go wrong? - push and offer add to different ends. push adds to the head , but offer adds to the tail . If you mix them on the same deque, the order becomes confusing. - Adding null throws NPE. - Not thread-safe. Interview questions Q1. Why prefer ArrayDeque over Stack and LinkedList? Stack is old, synchronised code that extends Vector. LinkedList creates a node object for every element. ArrayDeque is a cache-friendly circular array with O(1) amortised operations at both ends. Q2. Why can't ArrayDeque hold null? Inside, null is used to mark empty slots. Also, poll / peek return null to say "the deque is empty".

Why? In simple words: A PriorityQueue always keeps the smallest item at the front. You can peek at it instantly and take it out quickly, without sorting everything. Many problems keep asking for "the smallest (or largest) item so far". For example: - The next job by deadline. - The K most frequent elements. - The nearest unvisited node in Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm. - Merging K sorted lists. Sorting everything for each question costs O(n log n) every time. A heap is much cheaper. It gives you the minimum in O(1) and removes it in O(log n). Think of a hospital emergency ward. The most serious patient is always seen next. But the waiting patients are not kept in a perfectly sorted line. What is happening internally? PriorityQueue is a binary min-heap stored in an array. A binary min-heap is a complete binary tree (every level is full except maybe the last, which fills from the left). Its one rule: every parent is ≤ its children. Only the root is guaranteed to be the minimum. Siblings are not ordered between themselves. So looping over a PriorityQueue does not give you sorted order. How does it work? - offer(x) : put x at the end of the array. Then sift up : while x is smaller than its parent, swap them. This is O(log n). - poll() : take the root. Move the last element into the root's place. Then sift down : while it is larger than its smaller child, swap with that child. This is O(log n). - peek() : just read the root → O(1). - remove(Object) and contains : O(n), because they search item by item. - Building from a collection ( new PriorityQueue< (list) ): this "heapifies" all items at once in O(n). Trace of offer(0) into [1,3,2,7,4,5] : 1. Append 0 at index 6. Its parent is at index 2, with value 2. 2. 0 < 2, so swap. Now 0 is at index 2. Its parent is at index 0, with value 1. 3. 0 < 1, so swap. Now 0 is at the root. 4. The result is [0,3,1,7,4,5,2] , with 0 at the root. Example When would I use it? - Top-K problems. - K-way merges (merging K sorted lists). - Dijkstra and Prim (graph algorithms). - Scheduling by time or priority (timer wheels, cron schedulers). - Running medians (using two heaps). - Event simulation. What can go wrong? - Expecting sorted iteration or a sorted toString() . You won't get it. To get sorted output, call poll again and again. - Changing an element's priority field after adding it. The heap does not notice, so its order breaks. Remove the element and add it again instead. (In Dijkstra, the usual trick is to add a new entry and skip the old, stale ones when you poll them.) - Comparator overflow. Writing a[0] - b[0] can overflow with large values and give the wrong sign. Use Integer.compare . - Not thread-safe. Across threads, use PriorityBlockingQueue . Interview questions Q1. How is PriorityQueue implemented? As an array-based binary min-heap. offer and poll are O(log n) using sift-up and sift-down, and peek is O(1). Q2. Why use a min-heap of size k to find the k largest elements? The root is the smallest of the current top k. Each new element either replaces the root in O(log k) or is thrown away. So the total time is O(n log k), and memory is only O(k). Q3. Is PriorityQueue iteration sorted? No. Only the head is guaranteed to be the minimum.

Why? In simple words: If you change a list while you are looping over it, things go wrong. Normal Java collections notice this and throw an error at once; concurrent collections instead let you loop safely over a stable picture of the data. Changing a collection while looping over it causes trouble. The loop can skip elements, see some twice, or read half-updated data. Java's standard collections fail fast . They throw an exception immediately, instead of quietly giving you wrong results. Concurrent collections make a different choice. They let you loop safely, either over a snapshot (a frozen copy) or over a weakly consistent view (the live data, which may or may not show recent changes). Think of a teacher taking attendance from a register. If someone tears out a page in the middle, she stops and complains at once. She does not quietly mark the wrong students. What is happening internally? - Non-concurrent collections keep a counter, int modCount . It goes up on every structural change — an add or a remove. ( set does not count, because it doesn't change the size.) - When an iterator is created, it saves a copy: expectedModCount = modCount . - On each next() , the iterator checks that both numbers still match. If they don't, it throws ConcurrentModificationException (CME). - The iterator's own remove() updates both counters. So removing through the iterator is allowed. - Fail-safe / weakly consistent iterators work differently: - CopyOnWriteArrayList loops over the array snapshot taken when the iterator was created. Later writes are not seen. - ConcurrentHashMap iterators walk the live buckets (bins). They may or may not see changes made at the same time, but they never throw. How does it work? The enhanced for loop is just a shortcut for an iterator. So for (x : list) list.remove(x) changes the list behind the iterator's back. The next call to next() then throws. Example When would I use it? To filter a collection in place, use removeIf , iterator.remove() , replaceAll , or "collect first, then remove". When other threads change the collection while you loop, use a concurrent collection. What can go wrong? - Treating CME as a thread-safety tool. It is only best-effort detection — it may not fire every time. And it is not only about threads: single-threaded code can trigger it too. - Using CopyOnWriteArrayList for data that changes often. Every write copies the whole array (O(n)). Use it only for data that is read much more than written, such as listener lists. Interview questions Q1. What is ConcurrentModificationException and when is it thrown? A fail-fast iterator throws it when the collection was structurally changed after the iterator was created, by anything other than the iterator itself. It detects this using modCount . Q2. Fail-fast vs fail-safe iterators? Fail-fast iterators throw CME when the collection is changed during the loop (ArrayList, HashMap). Fail-safe or weakly consistent iterators work on a snapshot, or put up with changes, without throwing (CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap). Q3. How do you remove elements while iterating? Use Iterator.remove() or Collection.removeIf , or collect the items to remove first and remove them after the loop.

Why? In simple words: An immutable collection cannot be changed after it is made, so nobody can break your data by mistake. Java also gives you ready-made helpers in Collections and Arrays , and its sort methods — you use these daily, so know their traps. If your class returns its internal list as-is, callers can change it and corrupt your object. Immutable collections fix this: nobody can change them. They are also thread-safe by nature, because there is nothing to change. The Collections and Arrays utility classes, and the JDK's sort methods, are used constantly. They have a few sharp edges worth knowing. Think of a printed railway timetable versus a whiteboard. Anyone can scribble on the whiteboard. The printed copy stays the same, no matter who reads it. What is happening internally? Two words matter in this table: - A view is a window onto another collection. If the original changes, the view shows the change. - A copy has its own data. Later changes to the original do not affect it. Factory Mutability Nulls Notes --- --- --- --- List.of(...) , Set.of , Map.of (Java 9) Immutable Rejected (NPE) Small, specially built classes; Set.of / Map.of reject duplicates; the iteration order of Set.of / Map.of is deliberately left unspecified List.copyOf(c) (Java 10) Immutable copy Rejected Independent of the source Collections.unmodifiableList(l) Read-only view Allowed Changes to l show through Arrays.asList(arr) Fixed size, backed by the array Allowed set works (it writes into the array), add / remove throw stream.toList() (Java 16) Unmodifiable Allowed Sorting : - Arrays.sort(int[]) (primitives) uses dual-pivot quicksort . It is O(n log n) on average. It is not stable — stable means equal items keep their original order. For primitives this doesn't matter, because two equal numbers look exactly the same. - Arrays.sort(Object[]) , List.sort and Collections.sort use TimSort . It is a stable mix of merge sort and insertion sort. It spots runs of data that are already sorted and reuses them. It is O(n log n) in the worst case, and O(n) on input that is already sorted. How does it work? Immutability is enforced simply: every method that would change the collection throws UnsupportedOperationException . A view passes every read through to the collection it wraps. A copy owns its own data. Example When would I use it? - From getters, return List.copyOf(...) or an unmodifiable view. - Use List.of / Map.of for constants and test data. - Use the immutable factories for DTOs and records. - Use the Arrays utilities all the time in DSA. What can go wrong? - List.of with a null element throws NPE. This surprises code that used to use Arrays.asList , which allows nulls. - Arrays.asList(...).add() throws UnsupportedOperationException , because the list has a fixed size. - Map.of iteration order changes between runs. Don't rely on it in tests. - Sorting a huge boxed Integer[] is much slower than sorting an int[] . Interview questions Q1. Collections.unmodifiableList vs List.copyOf ? The first is a read-only view: the original list can still change, and the changes show through the view. The second is an independent immutable copy. Q2. What sorting algorithms does Java use? Dual-pivot quicksort for arrays of primitives, and TimSort (which is stable) for objects and lists. Q3. What is the gotcha with Arrays.asList ? The list has a fixed size and is backed by the array, so add/remove don't work. And if you pass a primitive array, you get a list with one element: the array itself.

Why? In simple words: A lambda is a small piece of code that you pass around like a value. You hand it to a method, and the method runs it when it needs to. Sometimes you need to pass behaviour to a method. For example: a comparator for sorting, a callback, or a filter rule. Before Java 8, the only way was an anonymous inner class — a class with no name, written inline. That meant five lines of boilerplate for one line of real logic. Each one also created an extra .class file. Lambdas fix this. You can pass behaviour as a short value, like o - o.amount() 100 . This is what made streams, CompletableFuture and Spring's functional configuration practical to use. If you know C , a Java lambda is like a C lambda assigned to a Func or Action delegate. What is happening internally? Functional interface. This is an interface with exactly one abstract method. Default methods and static methods don't count. - A lambda is an implementation of that one method. - The target type — the variable or parameter type the lambda is assigned to — decides which interface it becomes. Lambdas are not anonymous inner classes. The compiler does something smarter: 1. It moves the lambda body into a private hidden method. The compiler creates this method itself, so it is called a synthetic method (for example lambda$main$0 ). 2. At the place where the lambda is created, it writes an invokedynamic instruction. This instruction means "work out what to do the first time this line runs". 3. The first time the line runs, the JVM calls a helper called the LambdaMetafactory bootstrap method . 4. The LambdaMetafactory generates a tiny class at runtime. This class implements the interface and simply calls the synthetic method. 5. The JVM then links that call site permanently. Later runs skip the setup. Capturing vs non-capturing. - A non-capturing lambda uses no outside variables. It is created once and reused as a singleton (one shared object). - A capturing lambda uses outside variables. Each time, it creates a small object that holds the captured values. The JVM's escape analysis (a check that sees the object never leaves the method) can often remove even this allocation. Effectively final. A local variable used inside a lambda must be effectively final . This means you never change it after you assign it. The reason: the lambda gets a copy of the value, not the variable itself. How does it work? Java gives you ready-made functional interfaces in java.util.function . Learn the shape of each one — what goes in and what comes out. Interface Method Shape C equivalent --- --- --- --- Function<T,R apply T → R Func<T,R BiFunction<T,U,R apply (T,U) → R Func<T,U,R Supplier<T get () → T Func<T Consumer<T accept T → void Action<T Predicate<T test T → boolean Predicate<T UnaryOperator<T / BinaryOperator<T apply T → T / (T,T) → T Runnable / Callable<V run / call () → void / () → V (may throw) Action / Func<V There are also primitive versions, like IntPredicate , IntFunction , ToLongFunction and IntBinaryOperator . They work on int or long directly. So Java does not need to box each number (wrap it in an Integer or Long object). This matters in hot paths — code that runs millions of times. Method references. When a lambda only calls one existing method, you can write a shorter form called a method reference : Kind Reference Equivalent lambda --- --- --- Static Integer::parseInt s - Integer.parseInt(s) Bound instance System.out::println x - System.out.println(x) Unbound instance String::toUpperCase s - s.toUpperCase() Constructor ArrayList::new () - new ArrayList< () "Bound" means the object is already fixed ( System.out ). "Unbound" means the object comes in as the lambda's argument. Example The example below shows three things: - Composition: joining small predicates and functions with and , negate , compose and andThen . - Your own functional interface: marked with @FunctionalInterface . - Effectively final: what happens if you change a captured variable. Remember the order: f.compose(g) runs g first, then f . f.andThen(g) runs f first, then g . When would I use it? - Comparators for sorting. - Stream operations. - Callbacks, such as CompletableFuture.thenApply . - Strategy objects that are really just one function — pricing rules, validators. - Spring beans of type Function or Supplier . - Event handlers. What can go wrong? - Changing a local counter inside a lambda. It won't compile. People then hack around it with int[] count = {0} or an AtomicInteger . This is usually a sign you should use a stream reduction instead, like count() or sum() . - Checked exceptions. Function cannot throw checked exceptions. So a lambda that does I/O must wrap the exception (for example in UncheckedIOException ). Or you write your own functional interface that declares throws . - Long multi-line lambdas. They are hard to read. Stack traces also show ugly names like lambda$process$7 . Move the logic into a named method and use a method reference. - this means something different. Inside a lambda, this is the enclosing object (the class the lambda is written in). Inside an anonymous class, this is the anonymous object itself. Interview questions Q1. What is a functional interface? It is an interface with exactly one abstract method. You can use it as the target of a lambda or a method reference. The @FunctionalInterface annotation makes the compiler check this rule. Q2. How are lambdas implemented — are they anonymous classes? No. The compiler moves the body into a private synthetic method. The lambda object is created through invokedynamic and LambdaMetafactory the first time that line runs. Non-capturing lambdas are cached and reused as singletons. Q3. Why must captured variables be effectively final? The lambda captures a copy of the value, not the variable. If you could change the variable later, the copy would be out of date. It would also invite data races when the lambda runs on another thread. Q4. Function vs Supplier vs Consumer vs Predicate? Function takes T and returns R (T→R). Supplier takes nothing and returns T (()→T). Consumer takes T and returns nothing (T→void). Predicate takes T and returns a boolean (T→boolean).

Why? In simple words: A stream is a factory conveyor belt for your data. You describe the stations — filter, transform, collect — and each item travels down the belt one at a time. A normal loop mixes two things: - What you want — filter, transform, add up. - How to loop — indexes, temporary lists, running totals. Streams let you write only the what . You describe the data transformation as a pipeline. This gives you code that: - is easier to read, - joins together cleanly, - can stop early ( short-circuit ) when it has enough, - can run in parallel if needed. C developers: streams are Java's version of LINQ. What is happening internally? A stream pipeline always has this shape: source → zero or more intermediate operations → one terminal operation . Laziness. An intermediate operation ( filter , map , …) does not run anything . It only returns a new pipeline stage, linked to the previous one. Nothing happens until you call the terminal operation. This is called lazy evaluation . One element at a time. When the terminal operation runs: 1. Java joins all the stages into one chain of small objects called Sinks . 2. The source's Spliterator (the object that walks over the source data) pushes elements into this chain one at a time . 3. Element 1 goes through filter → map → collect. Then element 2 does the same. And so on. 4. So no temporary collection is created between stages. Stateless vs stateful operations. - Stateless operations ( filter , map , flatMap , peek ) look at each element on its own. - Stateful operations ( sorted , distinct , and limit in parallel) must remember or hold back elements. - sorted is a barrier . It must collect every element before it can pass even one forward. Short-circuiting. Some operations ( limit , findFirst , anyMatch , takeWhile ) stop pulling from the source as soon as they have their answer. This is why a stream can even work on an infinite source like Stream.iterate . One use only. You can consume a stream only once . Using it again throws IllegalStateException . The diagram shows each element flowing down the whole pipe before the next one starts: How does it work? Intermediate (lazy) Terminal (triggers execution) --- --- filter , map , mapToInt/Long/Obj , flatMap , distinct , sorted , peek , limit , skip , takeWhile , dropWhile , boxed forEach , collect , toList , reduce , count , min , max , sum , average , anyMatch/allMatch/noneMatch , findFirst/findAny , toArray map vs flatMap : - map turns each element into exactly one element. If your function returns a list, you get a Stream<List<X — a stream of lists. - flatMap turns each element into a stream . Then it flattens all those streams into one Stream<X . - Think of tiffin boxes. map gives you a row of tiffin boxes. flatMap opens every box and puts all the food on one plate. reduce : It combines all elements into one value. You give it a starting value (the identity ) and a combining function. The function must be associative — grouping must not change the answer, like (a+b)+c == a+(b+c) . Example: reduce(0, Integer::sum) . Example Look at the "laziness proof". findFirst gets its answer at "bb" . So "ccc" and "dddd" are never even read. When would I use it? Use streams for business data transformation: - filtering, - mapping entities to DTOs, - grouping and adding up results, - building lookup maps from lists, - generating reports, - validating collections. In DSA problems, a simple for loop is usually clearer and faster. What can go wrong? - Side effects in lambdas. For example forEach(x - externalList.add(x)) , or changing shared state inside map . These break in parallel and hide what you mean. Use collectors instead. - Using peek for real logic. peek is meant for debugging. It may not run at all if the terminal operation can skip elements. - Reusing a stream , or storing a Stream in a field. - Performance. For small collections inside hot loops, streams add extra object creation and extra method calls. Measure with a profiler before you "optimise" in either direction. - Debugging. Stack traces through stream internals are long. Keep pipelines short and move logic into named methods. - Checked exceptions inside lambdas must be wrapped. Interview questions Q1. What is lazy evaluation in streams? Intermediate operations only build the pipeline; nothing runs until a terminal operation is called. Then each element flows through all the stages, one element at a time. This allows short-circuiting and avoids temporary collections between stages. Q2. Intermediate vs terminal operations? Intermediate operations return a stream and are lazy. Terminal operations produce a result or a side effect, and they start the execution. Q3. map vs flatMap? map is one-to-one: one element in, one element out. flatMap maps each element to a stream and then flattens all those streams into one stream. Q4. Can you reuse a stream? No. After a terminal operation the stream is consumed, and using it again throws IllegalStateException . Create a new stream from the source instead.

Why? In simple words: A collector is the last station on the stream's belt. It decides what box the items land in — a list, a set, a map, a count or a joined string. Most real stream code ends with collecting the results. For example: - a list, - a map by ID, - a count per status, - a total per outlet, - a comma-separated string. Collectors gives you these patterns ready-made. The official name is mutable reduction : you build up a result by adding into a changeable container. Because Collectors does this for you, you don't hand-write accumulation loops. What is happening internally? A Collector<T, A, R is just four functions working together: 1. supplier — creates an empty mutable container of type A (for example a new ArrayList ). 2. accumulator — adds one element into that container. 3. combiner — merges two containers into one. This is used in parallel streams, where each thread fills its own container. 4. finisher — converts the container A into the final result R . How groupingBy(classifier, downstream) works: 1. It keeps a Map<K, A — one container per key. 2. For each element, it calculates the key using the classifier. 3. It gets that key's container, or creates it if it is new. 4. It adds the element into that container using the downstream collector. The downstream collector can itself be another groupingBy . You can nest them as deep as you like. Think of a school teacher sorting answer sheets into piles by section. The classifier is "which section?". The downstream collector is what she does with each pile — count it, total the marks, or just keep the sheets. How does it work? A few notes on the list above: - toMap with a merge function (the third argument) tells Java what to do when two elements have the same key. - teeing (Java 12) sends every element to two collectors at once, then combines their two results. Example Ten exercises to do in Week 3. Four of them are answered above. Do all ten by hand: 1. Words longer than 3 letters, uppercased, distinct, sorted. 2. Second-highest salary. 3. Highest-paid employee per department. 4. Character frequencies. 5. First non-repeating character. 6. Partition numbers into even and odd. 7. Flatten a List<List<Integer and sum it. 8. Orders → total per customer. 9. Duplicates in a list. 10. Names per department, joined with commas, sorted. When would I use it? - Building lookup maps from database results: toMap(Entity::getId, identity()) . - Dashboard numbers: counts and sums per status, per tenant. - CSV export: joining . - Splitting records into valid and invalid: partitioningBy . What can go wrong? - toMap throws on bad input. Duplicate keys throw IllegalStateException . Null values throw NullPointerException (NPE). So give a merge function and avoid nulls. - groupingBy order is random. It returns a HashMap , so key order is not fixed. Pass TreeMap::new (sorted keys) or LinkedHashMap::new (insertion order) when order matters. - The seen.add trick is wrong in parallel streams. It is a stateful lambda — it changes shared state, and a plain HashSet is not thread-safe. - Grouping huge datasets in memory. When the data is large, do the aggregation in the database with GROUP BY instead. Interview questions Q1. Why does Collectors.toMap throw? There are two cases. Duplicate keys without a merge function throw IllegalStateException . Null values throw an NPE. Q2. How do you count elements per category? Use groupingBy(classifier, counting()) . Q3. groupingBy vs partitioningBy? partitioningBy always splits into exactly two groups, true and false , using a predicate. groupingBy creates as many groups as there are distinct keys.

Why? In simple words: A parallel stream splits your data into pieces and gives each piece to a different CPU core. It is like opening more billing counters when the queue is long. On a machine with many cores, a big CPU-heavy job can be split across those cores. parallelStream() does this for you. You don't write any thread code yourself. What is happening internally? 1. Splitting. The source's Spliterator keeps cutting the data into smaller chunks. This works well for arrays and ArrayList . It works badly for LinkedList and I/O sources, because they can't be cut in the middle cheaply. 2. Running. Each chunk becomes a task on the common ForkJoinPool . This is one thread pool shared by the whole JVM. It has (cores − 1) worker threads, plus the thread that called the stream. 3. Work stealing. When a thread finishes its own tasks, it takes ("steals") tasks from the queue of a busy thread. So no core sits idle. 4. Merging. The partial results are combined using the collector's combiner. How does it work? Splitting and merging have a cost. A parallel stream is faster only when all of these are true: - There is a lot of data — roughly 10,000+ elements. - The work per element is CPU-heavy . - The source is easy to split . - There is no shared mutable state (no shared variable that threads change). - The operations are associative — grouping the work differently gives the same answer. Example When would I use it? Rarely in server code. It fits: - offline batch calculations, - CPU-heavy transformations over big in-memory arrays, - one-off data processing jobs. For I/O fan-out — calling many services or URLs at once — use your own executor with CompletableFuture , or virtual threads (Chapter 4). What can go wrong? - The common pool is shared by the whole JVM. This includes CompletableFuture s that were not given an executor. So one blocking task in it can stall unrelated code elsewhere. - Order-dependent operations lose most of the benefit. For example findFirst , forEachOrdered and limit . They force threads to wait for each other. - Thread-unsafe collectors or lambdas corrupt the results. - Busy servers don't gain anything. Every request already uses a thread. So parallel streams just add fighting for CPU ( contention ) without adding speed. Interview questions Q1. How do parallel streams work? A Spliterator splits the source into chunks. Each chunk runs as a ForkJoin task on the common pool, and idle threads use work stealing to pick up extra tasks. Finally the partial results are combined. Q2. When are parallel streams a bad idea? With small data; with I/O or other blocking work; with shared mutable state; with order-dependent operations; with sources that split poorly; and inside servers, where the common pool is shared by everything.

Why? In simple words: Optional is a box that may be empty. The method's return type tells the caller "check the box first", so nobody forgets. When a method returns null , you can't see that in its signature. Every caller must remember to check for null. Someone forgets, and you get a NullPointerException . Optional<T puts "this may be missing" right in the return type . The caller can't ignore it. They must decide what to do when the value is absent. C developers: this is similar in spirit to nullable reference types ( User? ), but as a real wrapper object. What is happening internally? Optional is a small final wrapper class. It holds either one value or nothing. Optional.empty() is one shared object (a singleton). It is a value-based class . This means its identity has no meaning. So never use synchronized on it, and never compare two Optionals with == . Use equals instead. How does it work? The most important pair to remember: - orElse(def) — the default is calculated every time (eagerly), even when a value is present. - orElseGet(() - def) — the default is calculated only when the box is empty (lazily). Example When would I use it? Use it as the return type of a lookup that may find nothing. For example findById or findFirstActiveScheme . Don't use it for: - fields, - method parameters, - collections. Return an empty collection instead of Optional<List<T . What can go wrong? - Calling opt.get() without checking. This just swaps the NPE for a NoSuchElementException . Use orElseThrow() so the intent is clear. - orElse(expensiveCall()) . The expensive call runs every time, even when the value is present. Use orElseGet . - Optional fields. Optional isn't Serializable . It also adds one extra heap object per field. - Returning null from a method declared to return Optional . This defeats the whole purpose. Interview questions Q1. Why use Optional? To make "value may be absent" visible in the API signature. It forces callers to handle the empty case, so you get fewer NullPointerExceptions. Q2. orElse vs orElseGet? orElse evaluates its argument eagerly, even when a value is present. orElseGet calls the supplier only when the Optional is empty. Q3. Where shouldn't you use Optional? In fields, method parameters and collections, and in performance-critical inner loops.

Why? In simple words: The old Date and Calendar classes were buggy and confusing. java.time gives you clean, safe types — one for each idea of time — so date bugs become much rarer. The old classes, java.util.Date and Calendar , had many problems: - Mutable. Anyone holding a shared date object could change it by accident. - Not thread-safe. SimpleDateFormat gives wrong results when many threads use it at once. - Months start from zero. January is 0, which causes off-by-one bugs. - Mixed concepts. They mix an exact moment in time with a calendar date. Our platform runs in 32+ countries. There, a date bug means wrong expiry dates, wrong reports and missed schedules. java.time (Java 8) fixes all of these problems. What is happening internally? Every class in java.time is immutable and thread-safe . A "change" like plusDays(1) never edits the object. It returns a new object instead. Each type models one clear idea: Type Represents Example use --- --- --- Instant A point on the UTC timeline (seconds + nanos since epoch) Event timestamps, DB audit columns, logs LocalDate / LocalTime / LocalDateTime Wall-clock values with no zone Birthdays, business dates, "store opens at 09:00" ZonedDateTime / OffsetDateTime Date-time with a zone / offset Scheduling in Asia/Kolkata, API payloads ZoneId A region with DST rules ( Asia/Kolkata , Europe/London ) Conversions Duration / Period Time-based amount (hours, seconds) / date-based (days, months) Timeouts / validity periods DateTimeFormatter Thread-safe formatting/parsing APIs, reports Clock Source of "now" — injectable Testable time A few terms from the table: - Epoch — the fixed starting point, 1 January 1970 UTC. - Wall-clock value — what a clock on the wall shows, with no idea which country it is in. - DST (Daylight Saving Time) — some countries move clocks one hour forward in summer and back in winter. How does it work? Follow one simple rule: 1. Store and calculate in UTC , using Instant . 2. Convert to a time zone only at the edges — in the UI, in reports, or for a user's schedule. For amounts of time, pick the right type: - Use Period for calendar maths. Adding 1 month to 31 Jan gives 28 Feb (or 29 Feb in a leap year). - Use Duration for exact elapsed time, like "2 seconds". Example The Clock trick matters for tests. If code calls now() directly, the answer changes every second. If you pass in a Clock , a test can give a fixed time. So the test gives the same result every run — it is deterministic . When would I use it? Everywhere time appears: - expiry of points and coupons, - scheduling jobs in a tenant's time zone, - audit timestamps, - report periods, - SLAs and timeouts. What can go wrong? - Using LocalDateTime for event timestamps. It has no zone. So the same value means different moments on servers in different countries. Use Instant . - Calling LocalDate.now() with the server's default zone. A server running in UTC will think "today" is still yesterday until 05:30 IST. - DST. In zones with DST, some local times don't exist, and some happen twice. India has no DST, but European tenants do. - Mixing with old JDBC code that uses Date / Timestamp . Convert at the boundary, for example Timestamp.from(instant) . Interview questions Q1. Why is java.time better than Date/Calendar? It is immutable and thread-safe. It keeps exact instants separate from local and zoned values. Its API is clear, and its formatter is thread-safe. Q2. Instant vs LocalDateTime? Instant is one exact moment on the UTC timeline. LocalDateTime is a wall-clock value with no zone, so it can mean different moments in different places. Q3. How do you make time-dependent code testable? Inject a Clock and call now(clock) . In tests, pass Clock.fixed(...) so time does not move.

Why? In simple words: A record is a class whose only job is to carry data. You write one line, and Java writes the constructor, getters, equals , hashCode and toString for you. Classes that only carry data are everywhere: DTOs, events, value objects, composite keys. Each one needed: - a constructor, - getters, - equals , - hashCode , - toString . That is about 50 lines of boilerplate, and it is easy to get wrong (1.12). Records (Java 16) generate all of it from a one-line declaration. They are also immutable by design — the values can't change after creation. C developers: this is the same idea as a C record . What is happening internally? When you write record Money(long paise, String currency) {} , the compiler turns it into a final class extends java.lang.Record with: - a private final field for each component, - a canonical constructor — the one constructor that takes all components, - accessor methods named exactly after the components ( paise() , not getPaise() ), - equals , hashCode and toString that use all components. These are built through invokedynamic and the ObjectMethods helper. What records can do: - implement interfaces, - have static fields and static methods, - have extra instance methods. What records cannot do: - extend another class (they already extend Record ), - declare extra instance fields. How does it work? You can add a compact constructor . It has no parameter list. It runs before the fields are assigned. So you use it to check inputs (validation) or to clean them up (normalisation), for example converting "inr" to "INR" . Example Note OrderPlaced . A record's fields are final, but a List inside it can still be changed by whoever holds it. That is what "shallowly immutable" means. List.copyOf makes a read-only copy, so the record is truly safe. When would I use it? - API request and response DTOs. - Kafka event payloads. - Value objects (like Money ). - Composite map keys — a key made of two or more values. - Query projections — Spring Data supports records as projections. - Configuration properties — @ConfigurationProperties records. - Returning more than one value from a method. What can go wrong? - JPA entities can't be records. Hibernate needs a no-arg constructor, mutable state, and the ability to create proxies (subclasses). Use records only for DTOs and projections. - Mutable components leak. A List or array inside a record can still be changed, unless you copy it in the compact constructor. Arrays have another problem: the generated equals compares them by reference, not by contents. - Every component is part of equals . This includes ones you may not want, like timestamps. So choose components with care. - Changing a record's components breaks its JSON. Its serialised form changes, which is a breaking change for clients. Interview questions Q1. What does a record generate? Private final fields, a canonical constructor, accessor methods, and equals / hashCode / toString that use all components. Q2. Records vs Lombok @Data ? Records are part of the language, they are immutable, and they need no annotation processing. @Data generates mutable getters and setters, and it needs the Lombok library. Use records for DTOs and value objects. Q3. Can a JPA entity be a record? No. JPA needs a no-arg constructor, mutable fields, and classes it can subclass to create proxies.

Why? In simple words: A sealed type says "these are the only possible kinds, no others". Then when you switch over it, the compiler can check you handled every kind — and shouts if you forget one. Some domains have a closed set of variants. For example, a payment result is Success, Declined or Pending — nothing else. With a normal open interface, the compiler can't know all the variants. So it can't check that your switch handles every case. When someone adds a new variant, it silently falls into default , and the bug ships. Two features fix this: - Sealed types make the hierarchy closed. The compiler knows the full list of subtypes. - Pattern matching lets you check a type and pull out its data in one step. So the compiler can verify the switch is exhaustive — it covers every case. Together they give Java algebraic data types — a type that is "exactly one of these fixed shapes". Think of a railway ticket status: Confirmed, RAC or Waitlisted. There is no fourth option. A sealed type lets you say that in code. What is happening internally? Sealed declaration. - sealed interface PaymentResult permits Success, Declined, Pending stores the allowed subclasses in the class file, in the PermittedSubclasses attribute. - The JVM refuses to load any other subclass. - Each permitted subclass must itself be final , sealed or non-sealed . Pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16). if (o instanceof Order ord) checks the type and creates the variable ord in one go. No cast is needed. Pattern matching for switch and record patterns (Java 21). - case Declined(String reason) when … does three things at once: 1. checks the type, 2. deconstructs the record — pulls its fields out into variables, 3. applies a guard — the extra when condition. - Pattern switches compile to invokedynamic with SwitchBootstraps.typeSwitch . - Because the hierarchy is sealed, the compiler knows all the cases. So no default is needed. - If you add a new variant, every switch that doesn't handle it becomes a compile error . How does it work? 1. Declare the sealed hierarchy. Records make ideal leaves (the final concrete types). 2. Switch over the base type, with one case per variant. 3. Later, add a new variant. Every switch that doesn't cover it now fails to compile, until you handle it. Example When would I use it? - Results and errors: Result = Ok Err . - Domain events: OrderEvent = Placed Paid Shipped Cancelled . - State machines. - Command types in a CQRS handler (CQRS = keeping write commands separate from read queries). - Parsed syntax-tree (AST) nodes. The rules engine in 11.12 uses a sealed Condition . What can go wrong? - Adding default to a sealed switch. It silently switches off the exhaustiveness check. A new variant will then fall into default without any compile error. - Placement rules across modules or packages. Permitted subclasses must be in the same module. If you are not using modules (the unnamed module ), they must be in the same package. - Case order matters. Guards ( when ) are checked from top to bottom. Put specific cases before general ones. Otherwise the compiler reports a dominated pattern — a case that can never be reached. Interview questions Q1. What are sealed classes for? To restrict which classes can extend a type. This makes the hierarchy closed and known to the compiler, so pattern-matching switches can be checked for exhaustiveness. Q2. What does pattern matching for switch add? It allows type patterns, record deconstruction and guards ( when ) in case labels. The compiler also checks exhaustiveness over sealed types. Q3. How does this compare to the Visitor pattern? It reaches the same goal — one operation per variant — without the boilerplate of double dispatch (the accept / visit back-and-forth calls). A new operation is just a new method with a switch.

t: 3.9 Switch expressions, var and text blocks
x: Why? In simple words: Three small features that make everyday code shorter and safer: a switch that returns a value and never falls through, var to skip repeating long types, and """ for clean multi-line strings. Each feature removes a common bug or a lot of noise: - Old switch statements fell through to the next case when you forgot a break . They also couldn't return a value. - Long generic types made variable declarations hard to read. - Multi-line SQL or JSON strings needed + and \n everywhere. What is happening internally? Switch expressions (Java 14). - case X - arms never fall through. - The whole switch yields a value — you can assign it to a variable. - Inside a block arm { ... } , use yield to return the value. - The compiler checks exhaustiveness for enums and sealed types. var (Java 10). - The compiler works out the type of a local variable from its right-hand side. This is type inference , and it happens at compile time. - The variable still has one fixed type. This is not dynamic typing like JavaScript. - It only works for local variables that have an initial value. It doesn't work for fields, parameters or return types. - C developers: it is the same as C var . Text blocks (Java 15). - A """ literal can span many lines. - The compiler removes the common indentation and makes line endings consistent. - The result is an ordinary String . How does it work? Example See the code above. In interviews: - write switch expressions for state machines and enum mappings, - write text blocks for SQL inside @Query annotations. When would I use it? - Switch expressions — for any mapping over an enum or a sealed type. - var — when the type is obvious from the right-hand side, like var list = new ArrayList<Order () . - Text blocks — for SQL, JSON test fixtures (sample data for tests) and templates. What can go wrong? - var x = getThing(); hides the type when it isn't obvious. This hurts readability. - var list = new ArrayList< (); infers ArrayList<Object , because there is nothing to infer the element type from. - Text block whitespace. Trailing spaces at line ends are removed unless you escape them with \s . A closing """ on its own line adds a final newline. Interview questions Q1. Is var dynamic typing? No. The type is inferred once, at compile time, and then it is fixed. var only removes the repeated type name from the declaration. Q2. What does yield do? It returns a value from a block-style arm ( { ... } ) of a switch expression.

t: 3.10 What else is new in Java 21
x: - Virtual threads — very light threads managed by the JVM, not the OS. They let you run a huge number of blocking I/O tasks at once (full section: 4.12). - Sequenced collections — new interfaces SequencedCollection and SequencedMap . They give the same methods everywhere: getFirst() , getLast() , reversed() , firstEntry() , pollLastEntry() . They work on lists, deques, LinkedHashMap and TreeMap . - Record patterns and pattern-matching switch — now final (no longer preview) in 21 (3.8). - Generational ZGC — the low-pause garbage collector, now with separate young and old generations (5.5). - Mention-only previews (features you can try but which may still change): - structured concurrency — start a group of tasks together and treat them as one unit; - scoped values — an immutable replacement for ThreadLocal ; - unnamed variables — final in Java 22. - String templates were previewed and then withdrawn. So don't mention them as a feature. Interview questions Q1. What are the headline features of Java 21? Virtual threads; record patterns and pattern matching for switch (now final); sequenced collections; and generational ZGC. There are also previews of structured concurrency and scoped values.

Why? In simple words: A thread is one worker inside your program. With many workers, one can wait for the database while another uses the CPU, so nothing sits idle. A server handles thousands of requests. Most of the time, each request is just waiting — for the database, the network or the disk. If one thread did all the work one after another, the CPU would sit idle during every wait. Threads let independent pieces of work run at the same time. This is called concurrency . With threads you get three benefits: - Waits overlap, so total time drops. - All CPU cores get used. - The system stays responsive. Think of a bank with one counter versus five counters. With five counters, while one clerk waits for a printout, the others keep serving customers. What is happening internally? - A process is a running program. It owns memory: the heap (where objects live) and the code. - Threads live inside a process. All threads share the same heap. But each thread has its own stack (its method calls and local variables) and its own program counter (which line it is on). - A Java platform thread is a thin wrapper around an OS thread . The OS scheduler decides which thread runs on which core. It also pauses threads and switches between them using small time slices. This is called preemption . - Creating a platform thread is not free. It reserves stack memory (default ~512 KB–1 MB). It also costs tens of microseconds. So you can have thousands of them, not millions. - Switching from one thread to another is called a context switch . The CPU saves and restores registers and stack pointers. It also spoils the CPU caches (the CPU's small, fast memory). Each switch typically costs a few microseconds. RUNNABLE means "running or ready to run". Java does not separate these two. One surprise: a thread that is blocked reading from a socket also shows as RUNNABLE in thread dumps. So RUNNABLE does not always mean "using CPU". How does it work? 1. new Thread(task) creates the object. The state is NEW. No OS thread exists yet. 2. start() makes the JVM create the OS thread. That thread calls run() . The state becomes RUNNABLE. 3. The thread may block on a lock (BLOCKED), wait for a condition (WAITING), or sleep (TIMED WAITING). After that it returns to RUNNABLE. 4. When run() returns or throws, the state becomes TERMINATED. A thread can't be restarted. Interruption is the polite way to ask a thread to stop. The thread must cooperate. Here is how it works: 1. Another thread calls t.interrupt() . This only sets a flag on t . 2. If t is inside a blocking method ( sleep , wait , join , BlockingQueue.take ), that method notices the flag. It throws InterruptedException and clears the flag. 3. If t is running normal non-blocking code, nothing happens by itself. The code must check Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() regularly. Example When would I use it? In application code, you should almost never create raw threads. Instead, submit tasks to an executor (4.3) or use virtual threads (4.12). But you must understand the lifecycle for two jobs: - Reading thread dumps. A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread and its state. Many threads BLOCKED on one lock means contention — too many threads fighting for one lock.
