In simple words: The garbage collector starts from a few fixed starting points, follows every reference it can reach, and treats everything it could not reach as rubbish — while your app keeps running and changing things. In C, you manage memory by hand with malloc and free . That causes three classic bugs: - use-after-free — using memory that was already freed, which crashes or corrupts data; - double free — freeing the same memory twice; - leaks — forgetting to free memory. Java frees memory automatically. But the collector has a hard job. It must decide safely which objects are dead. And it must do this while the application keeps changing references. What is happening internally? Reachability, not reference counting. An object is live if you can reach it by following references from GC roots . GC roots are the fixed starting points: - local variables and operands on thread stacks, - static fields, - JNI references (references held by native code), - live threads, - objects used as synchronisation monitors (locks). Everything that cannot be reached is garbage. This includes cycles — objects pointing to each other but not reachable from any root. Reference counting (counting how many references point to an object) cannot free such cycles, because each object in the cycle still has a count above zero. Reachability handles them correctly. Core algorithms: - Mark : start from the roots, walk all references, and mark every reachable object. - Sweep : free the memory of unmarked objects in place. This leaves gaps, called fragmentation . - Compact : slide live objects together and update all references to them. No fragmentation, but extra work. - Copy/evacuate : copy live objects into an empty area, then treat the old area as empty. Cost depends on the amount of live data. Used for the young gen and for G1 regions. Stop-the-world (STW) pause. Some GC phases need all application threads to be stopped. Threads can only stop at safepoints . A safepoint is a place where the JVM knows exactly what the thread's state is — for example a method return or the jump back to the start of a loop. Modern collectors do most of their work concurrently , meaning while the application keeps running. To do this safely they use barriers . A barrier is a small piece of code the JIT inserts wherever your code reads or writes a reference. It lets the GC track changes made during concurrent marking. Tri-colour marking. During marking, each object has one of three colours: - White : not seen yet. - Grey : seen, but its children (the objects it points to) are not scanned yet. - Black : fully scanned. During concurrent marking, the app could move a reference to a white object into a black object. The GC will never rescan the black object, so it would miss the white one and wrongly free it. Write barriers prevent this by telling the GC about such changes. How does it work? Here A, B and C are reachable from a root, so they are marked and kept. D and E point to each other, but nothing from the roots reaches them. So they stay unmarked and are freed, even though each one references the other. Example When would I use it? - To reason about leaks. The question "which path from a GC root keeps this object alive?" is exactly what heap-dump tools answer. - To reason about latency, because of STW pauses. - To explain why calling System.gc() is pointless. It is only a hint to the JVM — and a harmful one, because it can trigger an expensive full GC. What can go wrong? - Long STW pauses. These come from a large live set (lots of live data to process) or from full GCs. - Time-to-safepoint delays. A GC pause must wait until every thread reaches a safepoint. A long counted loop with no safepoint check inside can make everyone wait for that one thread. - Finalizers (deprecated). A finalizer can bring an object back to life ("resurrect" it) and delays the freeing of its memory. Interview questions Q1. How does the JVM decide an object is garbage? If it cannot be reached from any GC root — thread stacks, static fields, JNI references, active threads — it is garbage. Unreachable cycles are collected too. Q2. What is a stop-the-world pause and a safepoint? A stop-the-world pause is a phase where all application threads are halted so the GC can work safely. Threads stop at safepoints, which are points where the JVM knows the exact state of their stacks. Q3. Mark-sweep vs mark-compact vs copying? Mark-sweep frees dead objects in place, which leaves fragmentation. Mark-compact moves live objects together, so there are no gaps. Copying evacuates live objects to a fresh area; its cost is proportional to the amount of live data.

t: 5.5 The garbage collectors: Serial, Parallel, G1, ZGC
x: Why? In simple words: Different apps want different things from the GC — maximum work done, shortest pauses, or least memory used. No collector wins on all three, so Java gives you several to choose from. Each type of application cares about something different: - A batch job wants maximum throughput — the most total work done per hour. Pauses don't matter much. - A trading or ordering API wants low latency — short pauses, so no request waits long. - A small container wants a low footprint — little memory and CPU used by the GC itself. No single collector is best at all three. So the JVM offers several. What is happening internally? Collector Flag How it works Pauses Best for --- --- --- --- --- Serial -XX:+UseSerialGC One thread. Stops the app and does mark-copy for young gen and mark-compact for old gen Long Tiny heaps, 1-CPU containers Parallel -XX:+UseParallelGC Same as Serial, but uses many threads Long but efficient Batch jobs, max throughput G1 (default since Java 9) -XX:+UseG1GC Splits the heap into ~2048 equal regions (1–32 MB each). Young collections evacuate the young regions. Concurrent marking finds old regions that are mostly garbage. Mixed collections then evacuate the regions with the most garbage first ("Garbage First"), staying within a pause-time target ( MaxGCPauseMillis , default 200 ms). Huge objects get humongous regions. Typically 10–200 ms General-purpose services, 2–32+ GB heaps ZGC -XX:+UseZGC (+ -XX:+ZGenerational on 21; generational by default from 23) Does almost everything while the app runs, including compaction . It uses coloured pointers (extra metadata bits inside each reference) and load barriers (checks on every reference read), so objects can be moved while the app runs. If the app reads an outdated reference, it is fixed on the spot < 1 ms , no matter how big the heap is Latency-sensitive APIs, very large heaps Shenandoah -XX:+UseShenandoahGC Compacts while the app runs, using forwarding pointers (built by Red Hat) < 10 ms Similar to ZGC CMS removed in Java 14 Concurrent mark-sweep with no compaction → fragmentation Legacy only How does it work? A G1 cycle, step by step: 1. Young pauses happen all the time, cleaning the young regions. 2. When heap usage crosses a threshold, concurrent marking starts and runs alongside the app. This threshold is called IHOP (Initiating Heap Occupancy Percent), about 45%. 3. Short remark and cleanup pauses finish the marking. 4. A series of mixed pauses follows. Each one evacuates the young regions plus the old regions with the most garbage. 5. The cycle repeats. A full GC compacts the entire heap in one long pause. G1 does this only as a last resort, when evacuation can't keep up with the app. This is the multi-second pause you see in incidents. ZGC's trade-off: It gives up some throughput and CPU — for the barrier checks and its concurrent GC threads. In return, pauses stay below a millisecond even with heaps of hundreds of GB. Example When would I use it? - Keep G1 unless measurements show GC pauses breaking your SLO (service level objective — your latency promise). Then try ZGC. - Use Parallel for offline batch jobs that need maximum throughput. - Tune heap size and allocation rate first. Only then touch collector flags. What can go wrong? - MaxGCPauseMillis set too low. G1 then does less work per pause. It falls behind the app and ends up triggering full GCs — the opposite of what you wanted. - Humongous allocations. In G1, an object of at least half a region (huge arrays or Strings) gets its own humongous region. Many of these fragment the heap. - ZGC without enough headroom. ZGC needs extra free heap. If the app allocates faster than the concurrent collector can free memory, application threads are forced to wait. This is called an allocation stall . Interview questions Q1. G1 vs ZGC? G1 is region-based. It evacuates mostly during stop-the-world pauses and aims for a pause target of tens of milliseconds, giving a good balance with throughput. ZGC compacts concurrently using load barriers. Its pauses stay under a millisecond regardless of heap size, but it costs some throughput and CPU. Q2. Why is G1 called "Garbage First"? After concurrent marking, it evacuates first the old regions that contain the most garbage. This gets back the most space for each pause. Q3. Which collector for a batch job vs a low-latency API? Parallel for batch throughput. G1 by default for services. ZGC when pause times threaten the latency SLO.

t: 5.6 Strong, soft, weak and phantom references
x: Why? In simple words: Sometimes you want to point to an object but still let the GC throw it away. Special reference types let you say "keep this only while someone else needs it" or "tell me when it is gone". Normally, if you hold a reference to an object, the object stays alive. But sometimes you want to refer to an object without keeping it alive . For example: - a cache that should give memory back when memory is short; - extra data attached to objects, which should disappear together with them; - cleanup work that should run when an object is collected. What is happening internally? Type Cleared by GC when Typical use --- --- --- Strong (normal) Never, while it is reachable Everything SoftReference Memory is running low (before an OOM) Memory-sensitive caches (rare now, because behaviour is unpredictable) WeakReference At the next GC, if only weak references point to it WeakHashMap keys, listener registries, canonicalising maps (maps that keep one shared copy per value) PhantomReference After the object has been finalised; get() always returns null Cleanup after the object is gone, via ReferenceQueue / Cleaner (for off-heap resources) When the GC clears a reference, it can put it on a ReferenceQueue . Your code reads that queue to learn that the object is gone. How does it work? WeakHashMap holds its keys through weak references. Once nothing else points to a key, the GC clears it. The entry then disappears during the next operation on the map. There is a classic gotcha. The values are held strongly. So if a value references its own key, the key stays reachable through the value. The entry is never removed. Example The Cleaner here is only a safety net. The preferred way is to call close() yourself (for example with try-with-resources). When would I use it? Rarely in business code. You mostly need to recognise these in interviews and in library code. For caches, use Caffeine with size and time limits instead of soft references. What can go wrong? - Soft-reference caches cause GC thrashing (the GC runs again and again) and unpredictable latency. - WeakHashMap entries never cleared , because their values reference their keys. - Relying on GC timing for cleanup. You don't know when the GC will run. Always provide an explicit close() . Interview questions Q1. Weak vs soft references? A weak reference is cleared at the next GC once the object is reachable only through weak references. A soft reference is cleared only when memory is under pressure. Q2. How does WeakHashMap work? It holds keys through weak references. When a key is no longer reachable from anywhere else, the GC clears it and the map removes that entry.

t: 5.7 Memory leaks in a garbage-collected language
x: Why? In simple words: The GC only frees objects nobody points to. If your code keeps pointing to objects it will never use again — like a register where entries are added but never struck off — memory keeps filling up. That is a leak, even in Java. "Java has a GC, so it can't leak" is a classic wrong answer. A Java leak is an object that is still reachable but no longer needed . The GC cannot know you won't use it again. It only knows something still points to it. How a leak shows up, in order: 1. The heap grows slowly. 2. GCs become longer and more frequent. 3. Latency spikes appear. 4. Finally, OutOfMemoryError . What is happening internally? Some long-lived root holds a reference graph that keeps growing. The root can be a static field, a singleton bean, a long-lived thread or a cache. On every GC, the collector marks all of it as live. It copies or keeps it, and can never free it. The usual suspects : 1. Unbounded caches and static collections : for example, a static Map<String, Result CACHE that only ever grows. 2. Listeners and callbacks that are registered but never removed. 3. ThreadLocals in pooled threads that are never removed. Pool threads live forever, so their ThreadLocal values do too (4.15). 4. Inner classes and lambdas that capture a large outer object and are stored long-term (1.17). 5. Mutable map keys whose hash changed after insertion. The map can't find the entry any more, so it can never be removed (1.12). 6. Unclosed resources : streams, result sets, HTTP responses. These also use up connection pools and file descriptors. 7. Unbounded queues in executors that keep growing under overload (4.3). 8. ClassLoader leaks on redeploy, which fill Metaspace (5.1). 9. Session or per-tenant maps with no expiry. How does it work? The signature in monitoring is the "sawtooth" heap graph. The heap rises as objects are created, then drops at each GC. Look at the floor — the heap level right after each GC. - In a healthy app, the floor stays flat. - In a leak, the floor rises steadily over hours or days. Along with this, old-gen GCs become frequent, and the percentage of time spent in GC goes up. Example Why the first version leaks: every request has a new, unique ID. So every request adds a new entry, and nothing ever removes one. The fix limits both the size (50,000 entries) and the age (10 minutes) of entries. When would I use it? Every time you add a static or long-lived collection, ask two questions: 1. What limits its size? 2. What removes entries? In incident reviews, use the investigation flow in 5.9. What can go wrong? - Restarting pods "fixes" the symptom. It hides the leak until the next traffic peak. - Increasing -Xmx only delays the OOM. The leak is still there. Interview questions Q1. Can Java have memory leaks? Yes. A leak is an object that stays reachable but is no longer needed. Common causes: unbounded caches, static collections, listeners and ThreadLocals that are never removed, lambdas or inner classes holding outer references, and unclosed resources. Q2. How do you recognise a leak from metrics? Heap usage right after GC rises steadily over time. GC frequency and duration grow. Eventually you get an OOM. A restart resets it, but only for a while.

t: 5.8 Diagnosing high CPU, hangs and slow requests
x: Why? In simple words: When production is slow or stuck, you don't guess. You take snapshots of what every thread is doing, find the busy or stuck ones, and follow the evidence. Production problems rarely tell you what is wrong. You see "CPU at 100%", "requests hanging" or "p99 doubled". To handle these, you need a repeatable approach driven by evidence. Interviewers ask "walk me through debugging this" to check exactly that: do you have a method? What is happening internally? Two main tools: - A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread: its state (running, blocked, waiting) and its stack trace (which methods it is inside right now). - A CPU profile samples which methods are running, many times over a period, and adds up where the time goes. Combine them with OS tools. Together they tell you which thread is busy and what it is doing. How does it work? High CPU : 1. Run top -H -p <pid . This shows CPU use per thread. Note the thread IDs (TIDs) using the most CPU. 2. Convert the TID to hex: printf '%x\n' 12345 → 3039 . Thread dumps show IDs in hex. 3. Run jcmd <pid Thread.print dump.txt . Search for nid=0x3039 . That thread's stack shows the hot code. 4. Take 3 dumps 5–10 s apart. If you see the same stack every time, you have confirmed it. 5. Check the common culprits: - GC threads — if these are the busy ones, the real problem is memory; go to memory analysis (5.9) instead; - an infinite loop; - regex catastrophic backtracking (a badly written regex that tries millions of combinations); - huge JSON serialisation or deserialisation; - a HashMap infinite loop after unsafe use from many threads (old Java versions); - busy spin loops (a loop that keeps checking a condition without sleeping). 6. For a full picture, use async-profiler flame graphs, or JFR ( jcmd <pid JFR.start duration=60s filename=cpu.jfr ) and open the recording in JDK Mission Control. Hangs and slow requests : 1. Take thread dumps again. Look for these patterns: - Many threads BLOCKED and "waiting to lock" the same monitor → lock contention (threads queueing for one lock). - Threads WAITING in HikariPool.getConnection → the DB connection pool is exhausted . Causes are slow queries or leaked connections. - Threads RUNNABLE in SocketInputStream.read for minutes → a downstream call with no read timeout . The thread waits forever for a reply. - A section saying "Found one Java-level deadlock" → a deadlock (4.13). 2. Match what you see with APM traces and metrics: pool usage, GC pauses, downstream latency. Think of a railway reservation hall where the queue has stopped moving. You don't guess — you walk up and see what each counter clerk is doing. A thread dump is that walk. Example When would I use it? - On-call incidents. - Performance tuning. - Telling an interview story with a concrete diagnosis. Your ~30 s → ~10 s API improvement can be told this way: measure, find the bottleneck, fix it, verify the result. What can go wrong? - Trusting a single dump. One snapshot can mislead. Take several. - Heavy instrumenting profilers in production. They add code to every method and change how the app behaves. Prefer sampling profilers such as JFR or async-profiler. - Fixing symptoms instead of causes. Bigger pools or more pods without finding the real cause just move the problem. Interview questions Q1. CPU is at 100% on a Java service. What do you do? Find the hot threads with top -H . Convert their TIDs to hex and match them to the nid in thread dumps taken a few seconds apart. Read their stacks. Check whether the busy threads are GC threads, which would point to a memory problem. Profile with JFR or async-profiler. Then fix the hot code path. Q2. Requests are hanging. How do you investigate? Take thread dumps to see what the threads are waiting on — locks, connection pools, sockets without timeouts, or deadlocks. Then correlate that with traces and pool metrics.

t: 5.9 Diagnosing memory problems: GC logs, heap dumps, JFR
x: Why? In simple words: Memory problems are the most common JVM incidents. You must switch on evidence collection in advance, because when the process dies, the evidence dies with it — and then you need a clear method to read that evidence. Leaks, GC thrashing and OOMs are the most common JVM incidents. To handle them you need two things: 1. The right artefacts (logs, dumps, recordings), captured before the process dies. 2. A method for reading them. What is happening internally? The four sources of evidence: - GC logs record every collection: its type, its cause, heap size before and after, and the pause time. - Class histogram : for each class, how many live objects exist and how many bytes they use. It is cheap and needs no full dump. - Heap dump ( .hprof file): a copy of every object and every reference in the heap. Analysis tools compute two key things from it: - The dominator tree : for each object, how much memory would be freed if that object disappeared. This is its retained size . - The path to GC roots : the chain of references that keeps an object alive. - JFR (Java Flight Recorder): a recording that runs all the time with low overhead (~1%). It captures allocations, GC, locks, I/O and CPU samples. How does it work? Note: a heap dump pauses the app and writes a file as big as the heap. Check disk space first, and remember it contains user data (PII — personally identifiable information). Investigation flow: 1. Which OOM is it? Heap, Metaspace, direct buffers or native threads. Each type has a different cause (5.2). 2. Read the GC logs. Is heap-after-GC rising over time? That is a leak. Or is it just high under load? That means the heap is too small, or there was a traffic spike. 3. Take two class histograms some time apart. Which classes keep growing? 4. Open the heap dump in Eclipse MAT. Run the "Leak Suspects" report. Then open the dominator tree. Follow the path to GC roots of the biggest retainers. Find the code that owns that root. 5. Fix it, then verify using the same metrics. Example Say this: "p99 latency of the reward API jumped from 300 ms to 4 s every few minutes. GC logs showed full GCs of about 3 s, and old gen never dropped below 85%. I took two class histograms ten minutes apart, and RuleResult objects were growing. The heap dump's dominator tree pointed to a static ConcurrentHashMap keyed by request ID, with no eviction. We replaced it with a Caffeine cache limited by size and TTL. Old gen settled around 40%, p99 went back under 300 ms, and we added an alert for old-gen-after-GC above 70%." Build your own version of this from a real incident you handled. When would I use it? - For any OOM or memory alert. - Proactively before launches: run a load test and check the heap. What can go wrong? - Heap dumps contain customer data (PII). Handle and store them securely. - Dumping a big heap hurts. A 16 GB heap dump pauses the service for a long time and needs a lot of disk. So first remove that instance from the load balancer, then take the dump. - No HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError flag. Then the evidence dies with the process. Interview questions Q1. How do you investigate an OutOfMemoryError? First identify the OOM type. Check the GC logs for the heap-after-GC trend. Compare class histograms taken some time apart. Analyse the heap dump's dominator tree and the paths to GC roots. Fix the reference that is holding the memory. Then verify with metrics. Q2. What is retained size? The memory that would be freed if an object were collected. It includes the object itself and everything that is reachable only through it. Q3. What is JFR? Java Flight Recorder. It is a built-in event recorder with low overhead. It captures CPU samples, allocations, GC, locks and I/O, and you analyse the recording in JDK Mission Control. It is safe to run in production.

Why? In simple words: Java first runs your code slowly, by interpreting it, while watching what it actually does. Then it compiles only the busy parts into fast machine code, tuned to how your app really behaves. There are two simple options, and both have problems: - Interpreting bytecode (running it instruction by instruction) is slow — 10–50× slower than native machine code. - Compiling everything ahead of time loses runtime information. For example: which branches are actually taken, and which subclass actually shows up at a call. The JIT (just-in-time compiler) takes a middle path: - It compiles only hot code (code that runs a lot). - It uses live profiling data collected while the app runs. - So it can make optimistic optimisations that a normal ahead-of-time compiler cannot safely make. What is happening internally? Tiered compilation. Code moves up through levels: - Level 0: the interpreter. - Level 3: the C1 compiler, with profiling. It compiles quickly and collects statistics. - Level 4: the C2 compiler, with full optimisation. It compiles slowly but produces very fast code. - (Levels 1–2 are C1 variants.) Key C2 optimisations: - Inlining : copying the body of a small, hot method directly into its caller. This removes the cost of the call. More importantly, it enables every other optimisation. It is the most important one. - Devirtualisation : An interface or virtual call normally needs a lookup to find the right implementation. If profiling sees only one implementation at a call site ( monomorphic ), the JIT calls it directly and can inline it. If it sees two types ( bimorphic ), it adds a quick type check. With more types ( megamorphic ), it falls back to a normal vtable call (a table lookup). - Escape analysis : If an object never leaves the method, it is scalar-replaced — its fields become local variables and no allocation happens. Any locks on it are removed too ( lock elision ). - Loop optimisations : unrolling (doing several iterations per loop pass), range-check elimination (removing repeated array-bounds checks), and vectorisation (SIMD — one CPU instruction working on several values at once). - Dead-code elimination (removing code that can never run) and constant folding (calculating constant expressions at compile time). Deoptimisation. The JIT's optimisations rely on assumptions. Sometimes an assumption becomes false — for example, a new subclass gets loaded, or a branch that was never taken is suddenly hit. Then: 1. The JVM throws away that compiled code at a safepoint. 2. Execution goes back to the interpreter. 3. Later, the JIT may compile it again with the new information. On-stack replacement (OSR). Suppose a method is still interpreted but is stuck in a very long loop. The JVM can switch that running loop to compiled code in the middle, without waiting for the method to be called again. How does it work? In steps: 1. Call counts or loop iterations cross a threshold. C1 compiles the method, with profiling counters. 2. The profile shows the hot path, the receiver types and how often each branch is taken. C2 compiles optimised code for exactly those cases. 3. The assumptions are protected by cheap checks called guards . 4. If a guard fails → deoptimise → back to the interpreter → recompile later. Example When would I use it? - Explaining warm-up , and how to design benchmarks correctly. - Explaining why hot paths should be small, monomorphic methods. - Explaining that final and sealed classes help readability — the JIT does not need them for speed, because profiling already tells it the real types. - Discussing startup options: CDS archives (pre-loaded class data), CRaC (restoring a saved, warmed-up JVM), and GraalVM native image for fast-starting CLIs and serverless functions. What can go wrong? - Benchmarks without warm-up. You end up measuring the interpreter, not the real performance. - Megamorphic call sites in hot loops. For example, many different lambda implementations called through one interface. The JIT can't inline them. - A full code cache. The JIT stops compiling, and new hot code stays slow. - Deoptimisation storms. Repeated deoptimise-and-recompile cycles cause latency jitter. Interview questions Q1. What does the JIT do? It profiles running code and compiles hot methods into optimised native code, first with C1 and then C2. It uses inlining, devirtualisation, escape analysis and loop optimisations. If its assumptions break, it deoptimises. Q2. Why do Java services need warm-up? Code starts in the interpreter. The JIT needs profiling data and time to compile the hot paths. Caches and connection pools also need time to fill up. Q3. What is escape analysis? A JIT analysis that proves an object does not escape its method or thread. This allows the JIT to skip the allocation entirely (scalar replacement) and to remove locks on it (lock elision).

t: 5.11 The JVM in containers and the flags that matter
x: Why? In simple words: Inside a container, the JVM must size itself from the container's limits, not the whole machine's. A handful of flags control this, and getting them wrong causes OOM kills and slow, throttled services. Your services run in Kubernetes on Azure. Imagine a JVM that ignores container limits. It looks at the host machine's RAM and CPUs instead. It then sizes its heap and thread pools for that much bigger machine. The results are OOM kills and CPU throttling (the container being slowed down for using more CPU than allowed). Knowing a handful of flags lets you configure services sensibly and explain incidents. What is happening internally? Since Java 10 (also backported to 8u191), the JVM reads cgroup limits. Cgroups are the Linux feature that enforces a container's CPU and memory limits. This means: - availableProcessors() returns the container's CPU limit, rounded up. - The default maximum heap is a percentage of the container's memory. The default is 25%, which is too low for most services. - The CPU count also decides the number of GC threads, the size of the common ForkJoinPool, and the size of many library thread pools. How does it work? Example Take a Kubernetes pod with limits.memory: 2Gi and limits.cpu: 2 : - MaxRAMPercentage=70 → about 1.4 GiB of heap. - G1 runs with 2 parallel GC threads. - Tomcat has max 200 threads, which reserve about 200 MB for stacks. - A readiness probe points at /actuator/health/readiness . So traffic arrives only after the app has warmed up. When would I use it? - Writing Dockerfiles and Helm values. - Sizing pods. - Investigating OOMKilled restarts (exit code 137) and CPU throttling. What can go wrong? - -Xmx equal to the container limit. Non-heap memory pushes the process over the limit → OOMKilled. - A very low CPU limit (e.g., 500m, meaning half a CPU). The JVM thinks it has only 1 CPU. So it picks Serial GC and tiny thread pools. - Requests and limits set far apart. This causes noisy, unpredictable throttling. - No volume for heap dumps. The dump has nowhere to go, so the evidence is lost. Interview questions Q1. How does the JVM behave in containers? It is container-aware. It reads the cgroup CPU and memory limits and uses them to size the heap, the GC threads and thread pools. You should set MaxRAMPercentage to about 70–75%, to leave room for non-heap memory. Q2. A pod keeps restarting with exit code 137 but no Java OOM in the logs. Why? The kernel OOM-killed it. The total process memory — heap plus metaspace, threads and direct buffers — went over the container limit. Fix it by lowering the heap percentage or raising the limit, and check native memory usage with NMT (Native Memory Tracking).

t: 6.1 What Spring and Spring Boot solve
x: Why? In simple words: Spring builds all your objects and connects them to each other, so you don't write new everywhere. Spring Boot does the remaining setup for you, so a working web service needs almost no configuration. A real backend has hundreds of objects that depend on each other: - Controllers need services. - Services need repositories, clients, caches and config. - Repositories need a DataSource (the object that gives out database connections). You could create and connect all of them by hand with new . But that causes three problems: 1. The code becomes rigid. Each class hard-codes which implementation it uses. 2. The code is hard to test. You can't swap in a fake object for a test. 3. The same plumbing repeats everywhere. Transactions, security checks and logging get copy-pasted into many methods. Spring fixes this. It creates these objects and connects them for you. It can also add shared behaviour (like transactions) around them. Behaviour that many classes need is called cross-cutting behaviour. Spring Boot removes the setup that is still left. It gives you: - sensible defaults, - infrastructure that configures itself automatically, - a web server built into your app, - and a single JAR file that you can run directly. What is happening internally? - Spring Framework = an IoC container ( ApplicationContext ) + modules built on top of it. The container is the object that creates and holds all your objects. The modules include Web MVC, Data/JDBC/ORM integration, transactions, AOP, events, Security (a separate project), and more. - Spring Boot adds these things on top: - Starters : ready-made bundles of dependencies. For example, spring-boot-starter-web brings Spring MVC, Jackson (for JSON), embedded Tomcat and validation hooks — all in one line. - Auto-configuration : configuration classes guarded by @Conditional checks. They create beans (DataSource, ObjectMapper, transaction manager…) only when two things are true: the needed classes and properties are present, and you haven't defined your own bean (6.9). A bean is simply an object that Spring creates and manages. - Externalised configuration : settings live outside the code — in application.yml , profiles and environment variables (6.8). - An embedded server : Tomcat runs inside your app. So you don't deploy your app onto a separate server; the app carries its own server. - Executable fat JAR : one JAR that holds your classes, all dependency JARs nested inside, and a special launcher class loader that can read the nested JARs. - Actuator : ready-made endpoints for health, metrics and info (8.9). Here is how the ideas map from ASP.NET Core, which you already know: ASP.NET Core you know Spring Boot --- --- Program.cs , WebApplication.CreateBuilder @SpringBootApplication + SpringApplication.run builder.Services.AddScoped<IFoo, Foo () @Service class Foo implements IFoo (found by component scan) or a @Bean method Singleton / Scoped / Transient singleton (default) / request / prototype Middleware Servlet filters, HandlerInterceptor s, AOP [ApiController] @RestController appsettings.json + IOptions<T application.yml + @ConfigurationProperties ASPNETCORE ENVIRONMENT spring.profiles.active EF Core Spring Data JPA + Hibernate IHostedService @Scheduled , ApplicationRunner , SmartLifecycle Health checks Actuator /actuator/health How does it work? When you run the JAR, these steps happen in order: In plain words: 1. JarLauncher sets up a class loader. It can read your classes and every library JAR nested inside the fat JAR. 2. Your main() method calls SpringApplication.run . 3. Spring creates the ApplicationContext (the container). 4. It scans your packages for components and applies auto-configuration. 5. It creates all the beans, connects them, and wraps some of them in proxies (wrapper objects — see 6.7). 6. It starts the embedded Tomcat server on port 8080. The app is now ready. Example The parent POM imports the Spring Boot BOM (Bill of Materials). A BOM is a list that fixes compatible versions of hundreds of libraries. Because of it, your starters need no version numbers — Boot has already chosen versions that work together. When would I use it? For any Java backend service. It is the default stack at most Indian product companies (Flipkart, PhonePe, Swiggy, Walmart Global Tech). It is also widely used at FAANG for internal services. What can go wrong? - "Magic" you don't understand. A bean you never defined behaves in an unexpected way. Learn to read the auto-configuration report, which tells you what Boot set up and why (6.9). - Pulling in starters you don't need. This gives you a larger JAR, slower startup and surprise auto-configuration. For example, adding spring-boot-starter-data-jpa makes the app fail to start if there is no DataSource configured. - Overriding managed dependency versions by hand. If you change versions that the BOM picked, you can break compatibility between libraries. Interview questions Q1. Spring vs Spring Boot? Spring is the IoC container plus its family of modules. Boot is an opinionated layer on top of it — it makes default choices for you. It adds starters, auto-configuration, externalised config, an embedded server, executable JARs and Actuator, so an app needs almost no setup. Q2. What does @SpringBootApplication do? It combines three annotations: @Configuration , @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan . The component scan starts from the annotated class's package and goes downward into its sub-packages. Q3. What is a starter? It is a dependency bundle that brings everything needed for one capability (web, JPA, security), with versions that work together. Having it on the classpath also triggers the matching auto-configuration.

t: 6.2 Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection
x: Why? In simple words: A class should not build the things it needs. It should just ask for them, and someone else (the Spring container) hands them over. This makes the class easy to test and easy to change. Suppose RedemptionService creates its own dependencies: - new PostgresLedgerRepository() - new TwilioSmsClient() Now it is welded to those exact implementations. Two problems follow: 1. You can't unit test it without a real database and a real SMS account. 2. Switching to another SMS vendor means editing your business code. Inversion of Control (IoC) flips this. The class only declares what it needs. An outside container creates those dependencies and hands them in. This handing-in is called Dependency Injection (DI). Think of a restaurant kitchen. The chef does not go to the market for vegetables. He writes what he needs on a list, and the supplier delivers it. If the supplier changes, the chef's recipes don't change. What is happening internally? The ApplicationContext works in two phases. 1. Phase 1 — Bean definitions (the recipes). - Spring collects a recipe for each bean. A recipe says: which class, which scope, which constructor arguments, which dependencies, and which init/destroy methods. - Recipes come from component scanning, @Bean methods and auto-configuration. - Each recipe is stored as a BeanDefinition object in a registry. - No real objects exist yet. 2. Phase 2 — Instantiation (cooking the recipes). For each singleton that is not marked lazy, Spring: 1. works out the dependency graph (who needs whom), 2. creates the dependencies first, 3. calls the constructor with them, 4. injects fields and setters, 5. runs lifecycle callbacks, 6. applies post-processors (these may wrap the bean in a proxy), 7. stores the result in the singleton cache (a ConcurrentHashMap<String, Object ). Spring finds a dependency by type first. If several beans match that type, it narrows the choice by qualifier or by name (6.4). In the diagram, nothing can be created before the things it needs. So the EntityManager comes first and the controller comes last. How does it work? There are three ways to inject a dependency: 1. Constructor injection — use this by default. 2. Field injection — avoid it. The dependencies are hidden, the field can't be final , and tests need reflection to set it. 3. Setter injection — use it only for optional dependencies. Why constructor injection wins: - Dependencies are explicit. You can see them all in the constructor signature. - Fields are final . So they are immutable (can't change), and other threads always see them correctly set. This is called safe publication . - The object is never half-built. It can't exist without its dependencies. - Unit tests are simple. You just call new RedemptionService(fakeLedger, fakeNotifier) . - It warns you about bad design. If the constructor has too many parameters, the class is clearly doing too much. Example This test needs no Spring at all. You pass in fake objects by hand. This is the real payoff of DI. When would I use it? For every service, repository, client and component. Program to interfaces (also called ports ) for anything you might swap or fake in tests: - external clients, - notification channels, - clocks, - ID generators. What can go wrong? - Circular dependencies. A needs B, and B needs A. - With constructor injection, Spring can't create either one first. So startup fails with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException . - Since Boot 2.6, circular references are blocked by default, even with field injection. - The fix is to change the design. Extract the shared logic into a third bean, or use events. - Putting @Lazy on one parameter is a last resort. It injects a proxy (a stand-in object) instead of the real bean. - Calling new yourself on a Spring-managed class. The object you get has no injection, no proxies and no @Transactional . Spring never touched it. - Static access to beans. For example, a static holder that keeps the ApplicationContext. This hides the dependencies again, which is exactly what DI was meant to fix. Interview questions Q1. What are IoC and DI? IoC means the container, not your code, controls creating objects and connecting them. DI means dependencies are given to the object through the constructor, a setter or a field, instead of the object creating them itself. This gives loose coupling, easy testing and one central place for configuration. Q2. Why prefer constructor injection? Dependencies are explicit and immutable, objects are never partly initialised, unit tests are easy without Spring, and circular dependencies fail early at startup. Q3. How does Spring resolve which bean to inject? First by type. If several beans match, it uses @Primary , then @Qualifier , then the parameter name matching a bean name. If none of these decides it, startup fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException . Q4. How do you fix a circular dependency? Refactor the design: move the shared responsibility into a new bean, or reverse one dependency using an interface or events. Only as a last resort, use @Lazy injection.

Why? In simple words: You must tell Spring which objects to create. For your own classes, put an annotation on the class. For classes you can't edit, write a small method that builds the object and mark it @Bean . The container needs to know two things: which classes to manage, and how to build them. - Your own classes: an annotation on the class is enough. - Third-party classes you can't annotate (an ObjectMapper , an ExecutorService , an SDK client), or objects that need some building logic: you write a factory method — a method whose job is to create and return the object. What is happening internally? - Component scanning walks through the packages under your @SpringBootApplication class. - It reads the class files with a library called ASM. So it does not need to load every class into memory. - For each class marked with @Component , or with an annotation built on @Component (a stereotype ), it registers a bean definition. Annotation Meaning --- --- @Component A general managed component @Service Business logic (just a label; no extra behaviour) @Repository Data access; Spring also converts database exceptions into its own DataAccessException family @Controller / @RestController Web handler; @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody @Configuration A class that holds @Bean factory methods - @Configuration classes are wrapped in a CGLIB proxy. CGLIB is a library that creates a subclass of your class at runtime. - Because of this proxy, when one @Bean method calls another @Bean method in the same class, the call goes through the proxy. - The proxy returns the existing singleton instead of creating a new object. - "Lite mode": @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false) . There is no proxy, so startup is a bit faster. - But now the methods are plain Java calls. Calling one @Bean method from another creates a new instance each time. - So in lite mode, take other beans as method parameters instead of calling their methods. How does it work? Three patterns are shown here: 1. Clock is a third-party type, so you create it with a @Bean method. 2. The thread pool uses destroyMethod = "shutdown" . So Spring calls shutdown() on it when the app stops. 3. PartnerClient needs other beans. It receives them as method parameters, and Spring fills them in. Example With the default full @Configuration , both places get the same B . In lite mode you silently get two B objects. That can mean two caches or two connection pools — bugs that are hard to spot. When would I use it? - Stereotype annotations for your own classes. - @Bean for third-party objects, clients that need configuration, thread pools, and variants that depend on a condition or a profile. - Group your infrastructure beans into a few @Configuration classes, one per concern. For example: PersistenceConfig , KafkaConfig , SecurityConfig . What can go wrong? - A class outside the scanned packages is silently ignored. If it sits above the main class's package, scanning never sees it. You get NoSuchBeanDefinitionException . - final @Configuration classes or final @Bean methods can't be proxied by CGLIB. CGLIB works by subclassing and overriding, and final blocks both. - Two beans of the same type defined in different places (yours plus an auto-configured one). - Usually yours wins, because the auto-configured one has @ConditionalOnMissingBean and steps back. - But if the two beans have the same name, it is a clash. Bean overriding is disabled by default, so startup fails. Interview questions Q1. @Component vs @Bean ? @Component marks your own class so component scanning picks it up. @Bean is a factory method inside a @Configuration class; you use it for third-party types or when building the object needs custom logic. Q2. @Component vs @Service vs @Repository ? All three register beans. @Service is only a label that shows meaning. @Repository also adds persistence exception translation — it converts database exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException types. Q3. Why are @Configuration classes proxied? So that when one @Bean method calls another, it gets back the container's singleton instead of creating a new instance.

Why? In simple words: When one interface has several implementations, you must tell Spring which one to use. You can mark a default, ask for a specific one by name, or take all of them and choose at runtime. Real systems often have several implementations of one interface. For example: - payment gateways: Razorpay, UPI, card, - notification channels: SMS, WhatsApp, email, - reward rules. You need one of three things: 1. a default one, 2. a specific one, 3. all of them, so you can pick one at runtime. This is the Strategy pattern — choose the algorithm while the program runs. What is happening internally? Say a constructor parameter has type T . The container collects every bean that can be assigned to T . Then: 1. If there is exactly one, it injects that one. 2. If there are several, a bean marked @Primary wins. 3. If there is no @Primary , a @Qualifier on the parameter filters the candidates. 4. If there is no qualifier, Spring matches the parameter name to a bean name. 5. If nothing decides it, startup fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException . Collections work differently: - For List<T , Spring injects all candidates. They are ordered by @Order or the Ordered interface. - For Map<String, T , Spring injects a map of bean name → bean. Think of an ATM that accepts several bank cards. It has a default network, but it can also route to a specific bank when the card says so. How does it work? Each gateway is a bean with its own name. RazorpayGateway is marked @Primary , so it is the default. Example - CheckoutService gets the @Primary gateway as its default. - It also gets a map of all gateways, keyed by bean name. It picks one at runtime from the method the user chose. - Refunds asks for the UPI gateway by name with @Qualifier("upi") . Now, adding a new gateway is just one new @Component class. You don't edit any existing code. This is the open/closed principle (9.4) for free — open for extension, closed for modification. When would I use it? - Strategy registries: payment methods, notification channels, incentive rule evaluators keyed by rule type. - Plugin-style extension points: new behaviour is added by dropping in a new bean. - Environment-specific defaults: @Primary on the real client, and a stub (fake) under a test profile. What can go wrong? - Two @Primary beans of the same type. Spring can't choose, so you get an ambiguity error. - Qualifier strings scattered across the code. If someone renames a bean, these strings break silently. Prefer a custom qualifier annotation, or a map keyed by a method on the interface (like code() ). - Relying on parameter-name matching. It breaks easily when someone renames a parameter during refactoring. Interview questions Q1. Two beans implement the same interface. How does Spring choose? First @Primary , then @Qualifier , then the parameter name. If none of these decides it, Spring throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. If you want all of them, inject List<T or Map<String, T . Q2. How do you implement the Strategy pattern with Spring? Make each strategy a bean that implements a common interface. Then inject Map<String, Strategy or a List , and build a registry keyed by type to pick the right strategy at runtime.

Why? In simple words: Scope decides how many copies of a bean exist and how long each one lives. Most beans are one shared copy for the whole app; a few need a new copy per request or per use. - Most beans are stateless services — they hold no per-user data. So everyone can share one instance. - Some objects must exist once per request (for example, a request context). - Some must be brand new each time (stateful helpers that collect data). Scope controls how many instances exist and how long they live . What is happening internally? Scope Instances Lifecycle managed by container --- --- --- singleton (default) One per ApplicationContext, cached Full (created at startup, destroyed at shutdown) prototype A new instance on every lookup or injection Creation only — no destroy callbacks request One per HTTP request (stored in request attributes) Web only session One per HTTP session Web only application One per ServletContext Web only A Spring singleton is one per container, not one per JVM . This is different from the classic GoF Singleton pattern (from the "Gang of Four" design patterns book). A singleton is shared by every request thread at the same time. So it must be stateless or thread-safe . Think of a railway enquiry counter with one clerk. Everyone talks to the same clerk. If he writes your coach number on a single shared slate, the next person can overwrite it before you read it back. How does it work? Suppose you inject a shorter-lived bean (request or prototype) into a singleton. The injection happens only once — when the singleton is created. After that, the singleton keeps the same object forever. To get a fresh instance each time, you need a middle step: - ObjectProvider<T : call getObject() whenever you need a new one. - @Lookup method injection : Spring overrides the method so that it fetches a fresh bean from the container. - A scoped proxy ( @Scope(value = "request", proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET CLASS) ): the singleton holds a proxy. On every call, the proxy finds the instance for the current request. Example - ReportService gets a new ReportBuilder on each call through ObjectProvider . So two requests never share the same rows. - BadPricingService stores request data in a field of a singleton. Thread A sets the tenant to "t1". Then thread B sets it to "t2". Thread A now reads "t2" and returns the wrong tenant's price. When would I use it? - Singleton for almost all services, repositories, clients and controllers. - Request scope for request context objects. (Or use a ThreadLocal holder — a per-thread variable — that a filter sets.) - Prototype for stateful, short-lived helpers built by a factory. What can go wrong? - Mutable fields in singletons. They cause race conditions (threads overwriting each other) and cross-tenant data leaks , as shown above. - Prototype beans holding resources. The container never destroys them, so you must clean them up yourself. - Request-scoped beans used outside a request. In async threads or scheduled jobs there is no request. So they fail with "No thread-bound request found". Interview questions Q1. What bean scopes exist? singleton (the default), prototype, request, session and application — plus websocket. Q2. Are singleton beans thread-safe? Only if you make them so. Spring does not synchronise them. Keep them stateless, or use thread-safe fields. Q3. What happens when a prototype is injected into a singleton? It is injected only once, so the singleton always uses the same instance. To get a fresh one, use ObjectProvider, @Lookup, or a scoped proxy. Q4. Spring singleton vs GoF Singleton? Spring's singleton is one instance per container, so several contexts mean several instances. The GoF Singleton is one per class loader, and the class itself enforces it.

Why? In simple words: Every bean goes through fixed stages: it is created, filled with its dependencies, set up, used, and finally cleaned up. Knowing these stages tells you where to put your setup and cleanup code — and when Spring adds its proxies. Beans often need two kinds of extra work: - Setup after dependencies are injected: load a rule cache, check the config, open a connection. - Cleanup at shutdown: flush buffers, close pools. Spring itself also needs hooks to add behaviour to beans. For example, it adds proxies for transactions, security and async. The lifecycle defines exactly when each of these happens. What is happening internally? Step by step: 1. Instantiate. Spring calls the constructor. Constructor injection happens here. 2. Populate properties. Field and setter injection happen. 3. Aware callbacks. If the bean asks for it, Spring gives it its own name, the BeanFactory, or the ApplicationContext. 4. Before-init post-processing. Every BeanPostProcessor runs postProcessBeforeInitialization , in order. 5. Initialisation. First @PostConstruct , then InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet() , then any custom init-method. 6. After-init post-processing. Every BeanPostProcessor runs postProcessAfterInitialization . Here the AOP auto-proxy creator wraps the bean in a proxy. 7. Ready. If a proxy was made, the proxy is stored and injected everywhere — not the raw object. 8. Shutdown (singletons only). First @PreDestroy , then DisposableBean.destroy() , then any custom destroy-method. There are two extension points. Their names are similar, so keep them apart: - BeanFactoryPostProcessor works on the recipes . - It runs before any bean is created , and it changes bean definitions . - Examples: PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer fills in ${...} placeholders. Configuration-class processing registers more bean definitions. - BeanPostProcessor works on the finished objects . - It runs for each bean instance , and it can change the bean or replace it completely. - Examples: AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor does the @Autowired injection. AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator creates AOP proxies for @Transactional , @Async , @Cacheable and aspects. Think of a tiffin service. The BeanFactoryPostProcessor edits the menu card before anything is cooked. The BeanPostProcessor works on each packed tiffin — it can add a label, or put the box inside a bigger insulated bag (the proxy). How does it work? Order matters here. - Inside a constructor or @PostConstruct , this is the raw object. It is not the proxy , because the proxy is created later, in step 6. - So if you call your own @Transactional method from @PostConstruct , it runs without a transaction. - Work that needs the full context and the proxies should run after startup. Use ApplicationRunner or @EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class) . Example - RuleCache loads its rules in @PostConstruct (step 5), when the repository is already injected. It clears them in @PreDestroy (step 8). - WarmUp waits for ApplicationReadyEvent . At that point all proxies exist and the server is running. - TimingPostProcessor shows the hook frameworks use. It could return a proxy around bean instead of bean itself — that is exactly how AOP works. When would I use it? - @PostConstruct : cache warm-up and validation that use injected dependencies. - @PreDestroy : flushing and closing things. - ApplicationRunner : jobs that should run once at startup. - BeanPostProcessors : only when you write infrastructure or library code. What can go wrong? - Heavy or slow work in constructors or @PostConstruct . It delays startup and readiness. And if it fails, the whole startup is aborted. - Expecting @Transactional or @Async to work inside @PostConstruct . There is no proxy yet, so they do nothing. - @PreDestroy not being called. It is never called for prototype beans, or when the process is killed with kill -9 . Enable graceful shutdown ( server.shutdown=graceful ) and handle SIGTERM (the polite stop signal) in Kubernetes. Interview questions Q1. Describe the Spring bean lifecycle. Instantiate → inject dependencies → Aware callbacks → BPP before-init → @PostConstruct / afterPropertiesSet / init-method → BPP after-init (this is where proxies are created) → in use → @PreDestroy / destroy on shutdown. Q2. BeanFactoryPostProcessor vs BeanPostProcessor? A BFPP changes bean definitions (the recipes) before any bean is created. A BPP changes or wraps each bean instance, around the time it is initialised. Q3. When are AOP proxies created? In postProcessAfterInitialization , by the auto-proxy creator BeanPostProcessor. The proxy then replaces the raw bean in the container.

t: 6.7 Proxies and AOP: how @Transactional, @Async and @Cacheable really work
x: Why? In simple words: Spring puts a wrapper object (a proxy) in front of your bean. Every outside call passes through the wrapper, which adds extra work like starting a transaction. But a call from inside the bean to itself skips the wrapper — and that is the source of many Spring bugs. Some concerns cut across hundreds of methods: transactions, security checks, caching, retries, metrics and logging. If you copy-paste begin/commit/rollback or timing code into each method, you will make mistakes. Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP) solves this. You write the behaviour once, and it is applied around every matching method. Spring builds AOP using proxies . Once you understand proxies, you can explain the most common Spring bugs. Think of a bank branch. You don't walk straight to the cashier. The security guard at the door checks you first, and logs you on the way out. The cashier (your real method) only does the money work. What is happening internally? A proxy is an object that: 1. has the same type as your bean, 2. catches each call made to it, 3. runs advice — extra logic before, after or around the call, 4. and passes the call on to the real object. There are two kinds of proxy: - JDK dynamic proxy : it implements the bean's interfaces (using java.lang.reflect.Proxy ). Because it only implements interfaces, you can't cast it to the concrete class. - CGLIB proxy : it creates a subclass of your class at runtime and overrides its methods. Spring Boot uses CGLIB by default. - Result: final classes, and final or private methods, can't be intercepted. A subclass can't override them. In the diagram, the outside call goes through the proxy, so the transaction starts. But this.audit() is called on the real object directly. It never passes through the proxy. Key words you should know: - Aspect : the module that holds the cross-cutting logic. - Advice : the logic itself, and when it runs — @Before , @After , @AfterReturning , @AfterThrowing , @Around . - Pointcut : an expression that selects which methods get the advice. - Join point : one single method execution. - Weaving : applying aspects to code. Spring does it at runtime with proxies. AspectJ can also weave at compile time or when classes are loaded. How does it work? Only calls that come in through the proxy are intercepted. A call from inside the object ( this.method() ) goes straight to the real object and bypasses the proxy. This is the self-invocation problem . Because of it, these annotations silently stop working on the called method: @Transactional , @Async , @Cacheable , @Retryable , @PreAuthorize . There is no error — they just do nothing. Example What the code shows: - The bug. processBatch calls post(t) on this . The proxy is skipped, so there is no new transaction per transaction record. - Fix 1 (cleanest). Move the transactional method into another bean ( LedgerPoster ). Now the call goes through that bean's proxy. - Fix 2. Use programmatic transactions with TransactionTemplate . You start each transaction in code, so no proxy is needed. - Your own aspect. TimingAspect times any method marked @Timed . @Around wraps the call, and pjp.proceed() runs the real method. When would I use it? - Use the built-in proxied annotations every day: @Transactional , @Async , @Cacheable , @PreAuthorize , @Retryable . - Write custom aspects only for truly cross-cutting concerns: timing and metrics, audit logging, tenant checks, and idempotency guards (checks that make a repeated request safe — doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once). - Keep business logic out of aspects. What can go wrong? - Self-invocation (explained above). This is the 1 Spring interview trap. - Annotations on private or final methods. They are ignored, with no error at all. - Calling the bean before it is proxied. For example, in the constructor or in @PostConstruct . - Objects created with new . Spring never sees them, so they are not proxied. - Aspect ordering surprises. For example, is the retry inside the transaction or outside it? Set the order explicitly with @Order . - Over-broad pointcuts like execution( com.. (..)) . They slow everything down and make the code hard to reason about. Interview questions Q1. How does Spring AOP work? Spring creates proxies — CGLIB subclasses or JDK interface proxies — inside a BeanPostProcessor. The proxy runs the advice around each call and then passes the call to the target bean. Q2. Why doesn't @Transactional work when I call the method from the same class? The internal call goes through this , not through the proxy, so the transaction interceptor never runs. Move the method to another bean, or use TransactionTemplate. Q3. JDK proxy vs CGLIB? A JDK proxy can only implement interfaces. CGLIB creates a subclass of the class, and it is Boot's default. Because it subclasses, final classes and final methods can't be advised. Q4. Name the advice types. @Before, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @After (runs always, like finally ), and @Around (wraps the call and decides whether and when to proceed).

Why? In simple words: Build the app once, and change its settings from outside — through files, environment variables and secrets. The same JAR then runs on your laptop, in QA and in production. The same JAR must run in different places: on a laptop, in QA and in production. Each place has different databases, URLs, credentials and feature settings. If you hard-code these values, you must rebuild the app for every environment. Externalised configuration fixes this. You keep one artefact (one built JAR). Only the files, environment variables and secrets change. What is happening internally? Spring builds an Environment object from an ordered list of property sources (places where settings come from). If two sources set the same key, the higher one wins. Simplified order, highest first: 1. Command-line arguments ( --server.port=9090 ) 2. SPRING APPLICATION JSON 3. OS environment variables ( SPRING DATASOURCE URL , LOYALTY REDEMPTION MAXPOINTSPERDAY ). Relaxed binding maps these to normal keys — so SPRING DATASOURCE URL becomes spring.datasource.url . 4. Profile-specific files: application-prod.yml 5. application.yml / application.properties 6. @PropertySource , then defaults @ConfigurationProperties takes all properties under one prefix and loads them into a typed object at startup. A record works well for this. It also: - converts values — durations like 10s , data sizes like 10MB , - validates values — with @Validated . So bad config fails at startup, not at 2 a.m. in production. Profiles ( spring.profiles.active=prod ) switch on profile-specific files, and beans marked @Profile("prod") . Think of a mobile phone. The phone is the same everywhere. When you change the SIM card, it picks up a different network and number. The JAR is the phone; the config is the SIM. How does it work? Key points in this file: - ${DB USER:loyalty} reads an environment variable, and uses loyalty if it is not set. - ${DB PASSWORD} has no default. It must come from the environment or a secret store. - The part after --- applies only when the prod profile is active. Example - RedemptionProps is a typed, validated record for everything under loyalty.redemption . A negative limit or a missing timeout stops startup. - @ConfigurationPropertiesScan tells Spring to find such records. - SmsConfig gives a fake SMS sender in every profile except prod , and the real Gupshup sender in prod . In Kubernetes: - Non-secret config comes through ConfigMaps — as mounted files or environment variables. - Secrets come through Kubernetes Secrets or Azure Key Vault. Spring Cloud Azure can load Key Vault secrets as a property source. When would I use it? For every value that changes per environment: URLs, timeouts, limits, feature flags, pool sizes and credentials. Prefer typed @ConfigurationProperties over many scattered @Value("${...}") strings. What can go wrong? - Secrets committed to application.yml in Git. Use environment variables or a vault instead. - A typo in a property name is silently ignored. This happens with @Value plus a default, or with properties that nothing binds to. Validated properties records catch type errors. Add the configuration processor to get IDE hints for property names. - Too many profiles that combine in surprising ways ( dev,local,kafka-off ). Keep only a few profiles, one per environment. - Different values in different pods because of a stale ConfigMap. A config change needs a rollout or a refresh mechanism to reach every pod. Interview questions Q1. How does Spring Boot resolve a property that's defined in several places? By property-source precedence. Command-line arguments beat environment variables. Environment variables beat profile-specific files. Profile-specific files beat application.yml. Q2. @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties ? @Value injects one value at a time by its string key. @ConfigurationProperties loads a whole prefix into a typed object that can be validated. It is better for groups of related settings. Q3. How do you manage secrets? Never in source control. Inject them through environment variables from Kubernetes Secrets, or from a vault (Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault), and rotate them regularly.

Why? In simple words: Boot looks at which libraries you added and sets up the matching objects for you. If you define your own version of an object, Boot sees it and steps back. Without Boot, every app wrote the same 200 lines of setup: - a DataSource and a connection pool, - an EntityManagerFactory, - a transaction manager, - Jackson's ObjectMapper, - the DispatcherServlet, - Tomcat… Auto-configuration does this for you when it sees that you need it. And it steps aside the moment you define your own. Think of a hotel room. The basic things — bed, towel, kettle — are already set up when you arrive. If you bring your own kettle, housekeeping doesn't add a second one. What is happening internally? 1. @EnableAutoConfiguration reads a file inside each JAR on the classpath: META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports . It lists the candidate configuration classes. The spring-boot-autoconfigure JAR alone lists about 150. 2. Each candidate is an @AutoConfiguration class. It is guarded by conditions that are checked at startup: Condition The config applies when… --- --- @ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class) that class is on the classpath (a driver or library is present) @ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class) you haven't defined your own bean of that type @ConditionalOnProperty("spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers") a property is set (or has a given value) @ConditionalOnBean some other bean exists @ConditionalOnWebApplication it's a web app 3. Auto-configurations are processed after your own configuration. So @ConditionalOnMissingBean can already see your beans, and it backs off. 4. Properties classes feed values into the auto-configured beans. For example, DataSourceProperties is bound to spring.datasource. . How does it work? Here is a real chain. You add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa and the Postgres driver. Then: 1. DataSourceAutoConfiguration creates a HikariCP connection pool from spring.datasource. . 2. HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration creates the EntityManagerFactory and a JpaTransactionManager . 3. JpaRepositoriesAutoConfiguration scans for repository interfaces and creates proxies for them. If you define your own DataSource bean, step 1 backs off. To debug what was configured: - Run with --debug . This prints the condition evaluation report . It lists positive matches (applied) and negative matches (skipped), each with a reason. - Or call the Actuator endpoint /actuator/conditions . To switch something off explicitly: @SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class) . Example This is your own starter. It gives every service on the platform the same multi-tenancy support: - It only applies when TenantResolver is on the classpath. - Each bean has @ConditionalOnMissingBean , so a service can still replace it. - You register it with one line in the AutoConfiguration.imports file. A platform team publishing a "tenant starter" is a great senior-level example to mention in interviews. Every service then gets the same tenant header handling, MDC tagging (adding the tenant to every log line) and Hibernate filter. When would I use it? - Every day, as a user. Read the condition report when something is configured (or not configured) unexpectedly. - Write your own starter for conventions shared across services: tenancy, auth, log format, standard error responses. What can go wrong? - Surprise auto-config from a transitive dependency (a library pulled in by another library). For example, Spring Security on the classpath suddenly protects every endpoint with a generated password. Or a Kafka client starts trying to connect. - Defining a bean with the "wrong" type or name. The auto-config doesn't recognise it, so it doesn't back off. You end up with two beans. - Startup failure "Failed to configure a DataSource". JPA is on the classpath, but no database URL is set. Interview questions Q1. How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work? Starters put auto-configuration classes on the classpath, listed in AutoConfiguration.imports . Each class applies only if its @Conditional checks pass. It backs off if you have already defined that bean yourself. Q2. How do you see why something was or wasn't auto-configured? Run with --debug to get the condition evaluation report, or use Actuator's /conditions endpoint. Q3. How do you disable a specific auto-configuration? Use @SpringBootApplication(exclude = …) or spring.autoconfigure.exclude in properties. Or simply define your own bean of that type.

Why? In simple words: Know what Spring does, step by step, from java -jar until the app is ready. And learn Spring events: one part of your app announces "this happened", and other parts react, without the two knowing about each other. Knowing what happens between java -jar and "Started in 4.2 seconds" helps you: - debug startup failures, - put initialisation code in the right place, - make startup faster, - and decouple parts of your app with events (inside one process). What is happening internally? 1. SpringApplication.run decides the app type (servlet, reactive, or none). It loads initializers and listeners. 2. It prepares the Environment (property sources and profiles) and prints the banner. 3. It creates the ApplicationContext . 4. Bean definition loading. Component scan, @Configuration processing and auto-configuration all run. These are done by BeanFactoryPostProcessors. 5. Singleton instantiation. Spring resolves the dependency graph. Beans are created, injected, initialised and proxied (by BeanPostProcessors). 6. The embedded web server starts. The port opens. 7. ApplicationStartedEvent fires. Then the ApplicationRunner / CommandLineRunner beans run. Then ApplicationReadyEvent fires, and readiness becomes UP. 8. On shutdown: stop accepting new traffic (graceful), destroy beans, close pools. Application events are a publish–subscribe system inside one process. - You call ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(obj) . - Spring calls every matching @EventListener method. - By default this is synchronous, on the same thread . If a transaction is open, the listener runs inside that same transaction. Think of the announcement system at a railway station. The station master announces once, and every passenger waiting for that train reacts. He doesn't need to know who they are. How does it work? @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER COMMIT) waits until the surrounding transaction commits. If the transaction rolls back, the listener is skipped. That makes it the correct place to send notifications about database changes. Example What happens here: 1. redeem runs inside a transaction and publishes PointsRedeemed . 2. The listener does not run yet. It waits for the commit. 3. If the transaction commits, the listener runs. If it rolls back, the listener never runs. 4. @Async("notificationExecutor") runs the SMS on another thread pool, so the request thread is not blocked. When would I use it? To separate side effects from core logic inside one service: notifications, audit, cache eviction (removing stale cache entries) and metrics. For cross-service reliability, in-process events are not enough. If the process crashes right after the commit, the in-process event is lost. When the event must reach Kafka no matter what, use the transactional outbox pattern (11.15). What can go wrong? - Synchronous listeners hurting the publisher. A slow listener slows the publisher's request. An exception in a plain @EventListener goes back up to the publisher and can roll back its transaction. - @TransactionalEventListener with no active transaction. By default the event is silently dropped. Set fallbackExecution = true if you need it to run anyway. - Slow startup from eagerly creating heavy beans. Measure it with the /actuator/startup endpoint (with BufferingApplicationStartup ). Consider lazy init for beans that aren't critical, and keep @PostConstruct light. Interview questions Q1. What happens when a Spring Boot application starts? Spring prepares the environment, creates the context, and loads bean definitions (scan, config, auto-config). Then it creates the singletons, running post-processors and creating proxies. It starts the embedded server, runs the runners, and finally fires ApplicationReadyEvent. Q2. Are Spring events synchronous? Yes, by default — they run on the publisher's thread. Add @Async to handle them asynchronously. @TransactionalEventListener ties delivery to a transaction phase, such as after commit. Q3. Why use @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER COMMIT) for notifications? So users are never told about changes that later roll back. For guaranteed delivery across services, use an outbox instead.

t: 7.1 How a request flows through Spring MVC
x: Why? In simple words: A request does not jump straight into your controller. It passes through a fixed line of "counters" — Tomcat, filters, the DispatcherServlet, interceptors — and if you know that line, you can find where any problem happens. Sometimes a request is slow. Sometimes it returns the wrong status code. Sometimes it skips your validation, or it never reaches your controller at all. To debug any of these, you must know every component the request passes through, and in which order. Interviewers ask "What happens when a request hits a Spring Boot app?" to check exactly this. What is happening internally? Here is the same flow in plain steps: 1. Tomcat (the web server inside Spring Boot) accepts the connection. It gives the request to one worker thread from its thread pool. The default maximum is 200 threads. 2. Filters run one after another. A filter is code that runs for every request before Spring MVC sees it — for example, security checks or reading the tenant ID. 3. The DispatcherServlet receives the request. It is the front controller — one single entry point for the whole app that sends each request to the right place. 4. Inside it: find the controller method, run interceptors, convert JSON into Java objects, validate them, call your code, convert the result back to JSON. 5. If anything throws an exception, your @ControllerAdvice handler turns it into an error response. 6. The response goes back out through the filters and onto the network. One request = one Tomcat thread for its whole life. This is true unless you use async MVC, WebFlux or virtual threads. So every blocking call — a DB query, an HTTP call to another service — keeps that thread busy while it waits. Because of this, timeouts on outbound calls and pool sizes matter a lot. Think of a bank with 200 counters: if every clerk is stuck waiting on a phone call, new customers stand in the queue. How does it work? - HandlerMapping builds its lookup table once, at startup, from all @RequestMapping methods. So if two methods map to the same URL and method, the app fails at startup — not later. - Content negotiation means choosing the format of the data. Spring looks at the Accept header (what the client wants back) and the Content-Type header (what the client sent). Based on these, it picks a converter. For JSON, Jackson is used by default. - The HTTP status code comes from one of three places: - the return type ( ResponseEntity ), - the @ResponseStatus annotation, - or an exception handler. Example Note step 8. Tomcat threads are reused for the next request. So the filters must clear TenantContext and MDC in a finally block. Otherwise the next request on that thread could see the previous tenant's data. When would I use it? Use this knowledge when you are: - Debugging a 404 (no controller matched the URL). - Debugging a 415 (the client sent the wrong Content-Type ). - Debugging a 406 (the client's Accept header asks for a format you can't produce). - Finding out why validation did not run. - Fixing filter order problems — for example, auth must run before tenant resolution. - Planning capacity. The number of requests you can handle depends on threads × time per request. What can go wrong? - Slow downstream calls use up all Tomcat threads. New requests then wait in a queue (the size is set by accept count ). When that queue is full too, new connections are refused. - A filter forgets to call chain.doFilter , so the request stops there. Or a filter does not clean up its ThreadLocals in finally , so data leaks to the next request on the same thread. - Large request bodies are read fully into memory , which can cause memory pressure. Interview questions Q1. What happens when a request hits a Spring Boot app? Tomcat gives the request a thread from its pool. Then servlet filters run, such as security. Next the DispatcherServlet takes over: HandlerMapping finds the controller method, interceptors run, and the HandlerAdapter prepares the method arguments — Jackson turns the JSON into objects and validation runs. Then the controller runs, and a message converter writes the response as JSON. If an exception is thrown anywhere, @ControllerAdvice handles it. Q2. What is the DispatcherServlet? It is Spring MVC's front controller — one single servlet that receives every request. It sends each request to the right handler using mappings, adapters, resolvers and converters.
