Why? In simple words: Your API is a promise to everyone who calls it. If you use the right URLs, HTTP methods and status codes, callers know what to expect and can safely retry. If you use the wrong ones, you get duplicate orders and confused clients. An API is a contract. Mobile apps, partner systems and other services all depend on it. When resources, methods and status codes are correct, the API is: - predictable — callers know what each call does, - cacheable — GET responses can be cached, - safe to retry — a retry does not cause damage. When they are wrong, you get duplicate orders, broken clients and confusing support tickets. What is happening internally? - Methods in a @RestController return normal Java objects. Spring converts these to JSON for you. This conversion is called serialisation . - ResponseEntity<T gives you full control of the response: the status, the headers and the body. - Method parameters get their values from different parts of the request: - the URL path → @PathVariable , - the query string ( ?page=2 ) → @RequestParam , - the headers → @RequestHeader , - the JSON body → @RequestBody . - For paging, Spring can fill a Pageable object from the page , size and sort parameters. How does it work? First, one important word. Idempotent means: doing the same call two times has the same effect as doing it once. Deleting order 5 twice still leaves order 5 deleted. Safe means the call changes nothing at all. Method Meaning Idempotent? Typical success status --- --- --- --- GET Read Yes (and safe — changes nothing) 200 POST Create / action No (make it idempotent with an idempotency key) 201 + Location, or 202 for async PUT Replace the whole resource Yes 200 / 204 PATCH Update only some fields Not guaranteed 200 / 204 DELETE Remove Yes 204 Error status codes: - 400 — the request is malformed or fails validation. - 401 — the caller is not logged in (unauthenticated). - 403 — the caller is logged in but not allowed (forbidden). - 404 — not found. - 409 — conflict, such as a duplicate or a version clash. - 422 — the input is valid, but a business rule says no. - 429 — too many requests (rate limited). - 500 — a bug on the server. - 502 / 503 / 504 — a service you depend on has a problem. Example Points to notice: - The POST returns 201 Created with a Location header that points to the new redemption. - The POST requires an Idempotency-Key header, so a retry is safe. - The GET uses a cursor ( afterId ) for paging and limits size to at most 100. - The request and response are small record DTOs. When would I use it? In every API. Always return DTO records — small classes made only for the API. Never return JPA entities. Entities cause three problems: 1. They leak internal fields to the outside world. 2. They trigger lazy loading while JSON is being written. 3. They tie your API to your database schema, so a schema change breaks clients. What can go wrong? - Returning entities. While Jackson writes JSON, it touches lazy fields. This causes a LazyInitializationException , or N+1 queries (one query for the list, plus one more for each item). Two-way relationships cause infinite recursion. Internal columns get exposed. - Returning 200 for everything , with an "error" field in the body. Clients and monitoring tools then can't tell a failure from a success. - Non-idempotent POSTs retried by mobile apps. On a flaky network the app retries, and you get duplicate redemptions. Require an Idempotency-Key header (11.14). - Offset paging on huge tables. OFFSET 1000000 makes the DB walk past a million rows — slow. Results also shift when new rows arrive. Use keyset/cursor paging instead ("give me rows after ID X"). Interview questions Q1. PUT vs PATCH vs POST? PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent — repeating it gives the same result. PATCH updates only some fields. POST creates something or triggers an action, and it is not idempotent unless you add an idempotency key. Q2. Which status code for a business-rule failure such as insufficient points? 422 Unprocessable Entity — the input is fine but the rule says no. Use 409 if it is a conflict with the current state. 400 is for input that is malformed or invalid. Q3. Why not return JPA entities from controllers? Because of lazy-loading exceptions, accidental N+1 queries, infinite recursion on two-way mappings, leaking internal fields, and tying the API to the database schema.

Why? In simple words: Never trust input from outside. Put simple annotations like @NotBlank on your request class, and Spring checks every request for you — and sends back a clear 400 error if something is wrong. Every input from outside must be checked before it reaches business logic or the database. "Outside" means mobile apps, partners, admin panels — anything. Declarative validation means you declare the rules as annotations instead of writing if checks by hand. This has three benefits: - The rules live next to the DTO, so they are easy to find. - They are consistent and easy to test. - Bad input gets a clear 400 error. Without this, the bad data goes deep into the code and fails later with a confusing 500. What is happening internally? Spring does not validate by itself. It hands the job to Bean Validation — the standard Java validation API (Jakarta Validation). The library that actually does the work is Hibernate Validator. The steps for a request body: 1. Jackson converts the JSON into your object. 2. Because the parameter has @Valid , Spring now validates the object. 3. Each constraint annotation (like @NotBlank ) has a matching ConstraintValidator class that does the check. 4. If any check fails, Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException . For @PathVariable and @RequestParam constraints, it is different. You need @Validated on the class. Failures then throw HandlerMethodValidationException (Spring 6.1+) or ConstraintViolationException . If you put @Valid on a nested field, validation also goes inside that nested object. This is called cascading . How does it work? What this shows: - Simple field rules: @NotBlank , @Size , @NotNull , @FutureOrPresent . - Rules on list items: List<@NotBlank String checks every SKU code in the list. - @Valid on reward means the rules inside RewardSpec are also checked. - @AssertTrue on a method checks a rule that needs two fields together — the end date must be after the start date. Example To make a custom rule, you need two pieces: 1. An annotation ( @IndianMobile ) marked with @Constraint(validatedBy = …) . 2. A validator class that implements isValid . Note that isValid returns true for null . This is the usual habit: let @NotNull handle "missing", and let the custom rule handle only "wrong format". Validation groups ( @Validated(OnCreate.class) ) let one DTO have different rules for create and update. But usually it is clearer to write a separate request record for each operation. When would I use it? On all request DTOs, and on @ConfigurationProperties classes (so bad config fails at startup). Keep business rules that need data in the service layer, not in annotations. For example, "points ≤ balance" needs the account's balance from the DB, so it belongs in the service. What can go wrong? - Forgetting @Valid . The constraints are then silently ignored — no error, no check. - Validating only on the client (the app or web page). Anyone can call the API directly with curl or Postman and skip those checks. - Putting DB lookups inside validators. They become slow and hard to test, and they hide business logic in a place nobody looks. - Sending the raw validation exception text to clients. Section 7.4 shows how to shape it into a clean response. Interview questions Q1. How does @Valid work in Spring MVC? After Jackson turns the body into an object, Spring calls Bean Validation on it. Any broken rule throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, which you map to a 400 response. Q2. How do you write a custom validator? Create a constraint annotation marked with @Constraint(validatedBy = …) , and write a class that implements ConstraintValidator<A, T .isValid . Q3. Where should business-rule validation live? In the service or domain layer, because that layer has the data and context to decide. Annotations are only for checking the shape of the input.

Why? In simple words: Instead of every controller catching and formatting errors in its own way, you write one class that catches all exceptions. It decides the status code, builds a clean error body, and logs real bugs once. Without one central handler, three bad things happen: 1. Every controller catches and formats errors differently. 2. Stack traces leak to clients. 3. Unexpected exceptions become plain 500s with no useful information. A single @RestControllerAdvice class fixes all of this. It maps each exception type to the right status code and a consistent body. It also logs unexpected errors exactly once. What is happening internally? When a controller method throws an exception, this happens: 1. DispatcherServlet asks its HandlerExceptionResolver s to deal with it. 2. One of them, ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver , looks for the best matching @ExceptionHandler for that exception type. 3. It looks first inside the controller itself. Then it looks in @ControllerAdvice beans, in the order set by @Order . It picks the most specific match. 4. It calls that handler method. 5. Whatever the handler returns is written out like a normal response. Spring 6 gives you ProblemDetail . It is the standard error body format from RFC 9457. It has the fields type , title , status , detail and instance , and you can add your own extra properties. How does it work? What each handler does: - Validation failure → 400, with a list of which field failed and why. - InsufficientPointsException (a business rule) → 422, with a clear title and a type link. - Optimistic lock or unique-key clash → 409, "please retry". - Anything else → 500 with a generic message. The full stack trace is logged here, once — and never sent to the client. Example When would I use it? In every service. Pair it with domain exceptions — your own unchecked exceptions (1.15) such as InsufficientPointsException . Services throw them, and the advice turns them into responses. So controllers stay free of try/catch. What can go wrong? - Wrong order of handlers. A catch-all handler wins over specific ones because of class order, or you have several advice classes without @Order . Then the same error gets different responses. - Logging and rethrowing in every layer. The same stack trace then appears five times in the logs. - Leaking internals in detail — SQL, class names or stack traces. - Exceptions thrown inside filters. Filters run before the DispatcherServlet. So @ControllerAdvice never sees these exceptions. Handle them inside the filter itself, or in Spring Security's entry points. Interview questions Q1. How do you handle exceptions globally in Spring? With a @RestControllerAdvice class that has @ExceptionHandler methods. Each one maps an exception type to a status code and a ProblemDetail body. Unexpected errors are logged once, there. Q2. Why doesn't my @ControllerAdvice catch an exception thrown in a filter? Filters run before the DispatcherServlet, so Spring's exception resolvers are not involved yet. Handle it in the filter itself or in the security entry point.

Why? In simple words: Both let you run code for every request. A filter sits at the building's main gate and sees everyone. An interceptor sits at the office door, after Spring already knows which controller method will handle the request. Some logic must run for every request. Examples: authentication, finding the tenant, adding correlation IDs, request logging, rate limiting. You can put such logic in a Servlet filter or a Spring MVC interceptor . The right choice depends on two things: what the logic needs to see, and when it must run. What is happening internally? - A Filter ( jakarta.servlet.Filter , usually written by extending Spring's OncePerRequestFilter ) runs in the servlet container, around the DispatcherServlet. - It runs for every request — including static files and error pages. - It can wrap or replace the request and response objects. - It can stop the chain, so the request goes no further. - A HandlerInterceptor runs inside the DispatcherServlet, after the controller method has been chosen. - It knows which handler method will run, and can read its annotations. - It has three hooks: preHandle (before the controller), postHandle (after the controller) and afterCompletion (after the response is done). How does it work? Filter Interceptor --- --- --- Level Servlet container Spring MVC Sees Raw request/response (can wrap them) The handler method and its annotations Runs for Everything Only requests that map to a handler Typical use Security, tenant, correlation ID, CORS, compression, request/response logging Auth checks per endpoint based on annotations, metrics per handler, locale Example What the code does: - CorrelationIdFilter runs first for every request. It takes the X-Request-Id header, or makes a new UUID. It puts the ID in the logging context (MDC) and in the response header. In finally , it removes the ID — because Tomcat threads are reused, and the next request must not see the old ID. - FeatureFlagInterceptor reads the @RequiresFeature annotation on the chosen controller method. If the feature is off for this tenant, it returns 404 and stops. A filter could not do this, because a filter doesn't know which method will run. - WebConfig registers the interceptor for paths under /api/ . When would I use it? - Use a filter for anything that must happen before Spring MVC, or for all traffic — security, tenancy, tracing. - Use an interceptor for logic that depends on which handler was chosen. What can go wrong? - Wrong filter order. For example, tenant resolution runs before security has checked who the caller is. Or it runs after another filter that already needed the tenant. - Reading the request body in a filter. The body is a stream, and reading it uses it up. Then the controller gets an empty body. Wrap the request with ContentCachingRequestWrapper to fix this. - Expecting interceptors to run for errors or static files. They don't run for those, though you may expect them to. Interview questions Q1. Filter vs interceptor? A filter works at the servlet level. It runs for every request and can wrap the request and response. An interceptor works at the Spring MVC level. It runs around the chosen handler and can see its method and annotations. Q2. Where would you put tenant resolution and why? In a filter, early in the chain. Then every later component — security rules, controllers, repositories — has the tenant context. Clear it in finally so the next request on that thread starts clean.

t: 7.6 Calling other services: RestClient, timeouts and connection pools
x: Why? In simple words: Every time your service calls another service, it can get stuck waiting. Set timeouts, reuse connections, and keep one configured client per downstream — otherwise one slow service can bring yours down too. Microservices call each other and partners all the time — pricing, inventory, SMS, payment gateways. Every outbound call is a risk. Your service can hang there, leak connections, or spread someone else's outage to your own callers. So configuring the HTTP client correctly is basic production hygiene. It also comes up often in SDE2 interviews. What is happening internally? The client options in Spring: - RestClient (Spring 6.1+) — the modern, synchronous client with a fluent (chained-method) style. - WebClient — the reactive, non-blocking client. - RestTemplate — the old client; it is in maintenance mode (only bug fixes). - HTTP interfaces ( @HttpExchange ) — you write an annotated interface, and Spring generates the client for you. Connection pools: Under the hood, an HTTP library does the real work — JDK HttpClient , Apache HttpClient 5 or Reactor Netty. It keeps a connection pool for each host — a set of open connections ready to reuse. - Reusing a connection skips the TCP and TLS handshakes, which saves time. - The pool's limit caps how many calls can go to one host at the same time. Timeouts — there are three: 1. Connect timeout — how long to wait to open the TCP connection. 2. Read/response timeout — how long to wait for data after connecting. 3. Pool-acquire timeout — how long to wait for a free connection from the pool. Without a read timeout, a stuck downstream service holds your thread forever. How does it work? Follow these rules: 1. Set timeouts shorter than your own SLA (the response time you promise). 2. Also keep them shorter than the timeout your caller uses for you. This is called a timeout budget — each hop gets a share of the total time. 3. Add retries only for idempotent calls — calls that are safe to repeat. 4. Add a circuit breaker for unhealthy dependencies (8.7). A circuit breaker stops calling a service that keeps failing, for a short while, like a fuse in your house. Example What the code does: - One RestClient bean for the pricing service, with a 500 ms connect timeout and a 2 s read timeout. - PricingClient wraps it. A 4xx response from pricing becomes your own PriceNotFoundException . - InventoryApi shows the declarative style: Spring generates the client from the interface. When would I use it? For every outbound HTTP call. Make one client bean per downstream service. Each one gets: - its own timeouts and pool limits — this is a bulkhead , so one slow service can't use up the connections meant for others; - observability — metrics, and tracing headers that pass along automatically when you build from the injected RestClient.Builder ; - resilience policies such as retries and circuit breakers. What can go wrong? - No timeouts. Your threads fill up with requests stuck on a slow dependency. Then the outage spreads to everyone who calls you. - Creating a new client for every request. There is no connection reuse. You pay for a TLS handshake on every call, and you can run out of ports (sockets stuck in TIME WAIT). - Retrying non-idempotent POSTs. This causes duplicate payments or orders. - Not reading or closing response bodies. The connection never goes back to the pool, so the pool slowly leaks. - Calling remote services inside a DB transaction. The DB connection and its locks stay held while you wait on the network (7.12). Interview questions Q1. What timeouts do you configure on an HTTP client? Connect timeout, read/response timeout, and pool-acquisition timeout. All of them must fit inside the caller's latency budget. Q2. RestTemplate vs RestClient vs WebClient? RestTemplate is the old synchronous client. RestClient is the modern synchronous client with a fluent style. WebClient is reactive and non-blocking, used with WebFlux or for high-concurrency async calls. Q3. Why reuse HTTP clients? To reuse pooled TCP/TLS connections, avoid handshake costs and port exhaustion, and keep timeouts and limits in one central place.

t: 7.7 JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data repositories
x: Why? In simple words: You write Java classes, and the library turns them into database tables and SQL for you. With Spring Data, you only write an interface; Spring writes the code behind it. With plain JDBC (Java's low-level database API), you do everything by hand: - You copy every column into every field, one by one. - You open and close connections and statements yourself. - You write the same insert, select, update and delete SQL for every table. This basic set is called CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete). This is boring and easy to get wrong. A tool that maps Java objects to database tables is called an ORM (Object-Relational Mapper). In Java: - JPA is the specification — a set of rules and annotations. It is like an interface. - Hibernate is the implementation of JPA — the real engine. It is like EF Core in .NET. Hibernate maps Java objects to tables, generates the SQL, tracks what you changed and manages links between objects. Spring Data JPA goes one step further. You only declare a repository interface . Spring writes the class that implements it for you. Think of a tiffin service. You just say "veg thali, no onion" on the order slip. The kitchen knows how to cook it. You never enter the kitchen. What is happening internally? - Entity : a class marked with @Entity . It maps to one table. - Hibernate needs a constructor with no arguments, so it can create the object itself. - The class and its methods must not be final . Why? Hibernate creates a subclass at runtime (a proxy ) to support lazy loading. A final class cannot be subclassed. - EntityManager (called Session in Hibernate): the object that does the actual work with the database. - It holds the persistence context (7.9) — a list of the objects loaded in this transaction. - This pattern is called a unit of work : collect all changes, then write them together. - Spring does not give you a raw EntityManager. It injects a shared proxy that finds the EntityManager of the current transaction. - Spring Data repositories : at startup, Spring does these steps: 1. It scans for interfaces that extend Repository . 2. For each one, it creates a JDK proxy — a fake object generated at runtime that implements your interface. 3. Basic CRUD calls go to a ready-made class, SimpleJpaRepository . 4. Your own query methods get generated code. They come in a few kinds: - Derived queries : Spring reads the method name and builds the query. For example, findByTenantIdAndStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc is parsed into JPQL at startup. (JPQL is SQL-like, but written against classes and fields, not tables and columns.) If you make a typo in the name, the app fails at startup. This is good — you find the bug early, not in production. - @Query : you write the JPQL or native SQL yourself. - Projections : an interface or record that selects only some columns, not the full entity. - Specifications : build filters at runtime, for search screens where the user picks the filters. - ID generation — how a new row gets its primary key: - IDENTITY : the database auto-increments the ID. Hibernate does not know the ID until the row is inserted. So it must insert each row immediately. Because of this, JDBC batch inserts are disabled (no sending 50 inserts in one go). - SEQUENCE : Hibernate fetches a block of IDs from a database sequence in advance. The block size is allocationSize . Since Hibernate already knows the IDs, it can batch inserts. This is the preferred choice on Postgres. - UUID : the app makes the ID itself, with no need to ask the database. Use time-ordered UUIDv7. Its values grow over time, so new rows land next to each other in the index. This is called better index locality, and it makes inserts faster. How does it work? Example The repository interfaces build on each other. Each level adds more methods: Repository → CrudRepository / ListCrudRepository → PagingAndSortingRepository → JpaRepository . JpaRepository is the top level. It adds flush, batch delete and getReferenceById . When would I use it? Use it for domain services that do a lot of CRUD and have clear aggregates — a main object with its child objects, saved and loaded together. Examples: accounts, orders, campaigns. Use something else for: - complex reporting queries, - bulk operations, - anything where performance is critical. For these, use native SQL, JdbcTemplate (Spring's thin JDBC helper) or jOOQ (a type-safe SQL builder). Mixing both approaches in one service is normal. What can go wrong? - ORDINAL enums : the enum is saved as its position number (0, 1, 2). If someone reorders the enum values later, old rows now point to the wrong value. Your data is silently corrupted. Always use STRING . - IDENTITY IDs : they disable batch inserts, so bulk inserts become slow. - ddl-auto=update in production : Hibernate changes the schema on its own at startup. Schema changes must go through versioned migrations instead (7.16). - Bulk @Modifying updates : they run directly in the database and skip the persistence context. So entities you already loaded in memory now hold old values (they are stale ). Fix: use clearAutomatically = true , or reload the entities. - Derived query names that grow silly , like findByAAndBOrCAndDOrderBy… . Nobody can read them. Switch to @Query . - findAll() on a big table : it loads every row into memory. Interview questions Q1. JPA vs Hibernate vs Spring Data JPA? JPA is the ORM specification — the rules and annotations. Hibernate is the implementation that actually does the work. Spring Data JPA sits on top of JPA and generates repository implementations from your interfaces. Q2. How does Spring Data create a repository implementation from an interface? At startup, it creates a proxy for the interface, backed by SimpleJpaRepository for CRUD. It parses method names, or reads @Query annotations, and turns them into queries. Q3. IDENTITY vs SEQUENCE generation? IDENTITY uses the database's auto-increment. Hibernate must insert each row immediately to learn its ID, so batching is disabled. SEQUENCE fetches IDs in advance in blocks, so Hibernate can batch the inserts.

Why? In simple words: You tell JPA how your objects are linked — an order has lines, a line belongs to an order. Then you can just call order.getLines() . But each link can secretly fire extra queries, so you must control how and when it loads. Domain objects point to each other. For example: - An order has many lines. - An order belongs to an outlet. - A scheme has many rules. If you map these links, you can move from one object to another in plain Java code. This web of linked objects is called the object graph . But every link has a cost. It can: - fire a hidden query, - cause a surprise cascade (an action on the parent spreading to children), - or become a performance trap. What is happening internally? - Owning side vs inverse side : - The owning side is the side that holds the foreign key. It uses @ManyToOne with @JoinColumn . Only this side decides what gets written to the database. - The inverse side uses @OneToMany(mappedBy = …) . It is only a mirror, so you can navigate in the other direction. Changes made only here are not saved. - Fetch types — when the linked data is loaded: - EAGER : load the link immediately, together with the parent. Hibernate uses a join or an extra query. - LAZY : do not load it yet. Hibernate puts a placeholder in the field instead. For a single object, the placeholder is a proxy . For a collection, it is a PersistentCollection wrapper. The data is loaded the first time you touch it. - Defaults : @ManyToOne and @OneToOne are EAGER . @OneToMany and @ManyToMany are LAZY . - Cascade : an operation on the parent (persist, merge, remove) is passed on to its children automatically. - orphanRemoval = true : if you remove a child from the parent's collection, Hibernate deletes that child row. Think of a lazy proxy like a restaurant token. You get the token now. The food (the data) comes only when you go to the counter and ask for it. How does it work? Example Sometimes a many-to-many link has its own data. For example, an outlet joins a scheme on a certain date. That joining date belongs to the link itself. In this case, do not use @ManyToMany . Make the join table its own entity instead. When would I use it? Map relationships inside an aggregate — for example, order → lines. Across aggregates or across services, store only the ID (like outletId ), not the object. Because of this: - loading stays predictable (no surprise queries), and - the boundaries between services stay clean. What can go wrong? - EAGER @ManyToOne everywhere : every query drags in a chain of joined entities. - Updating only one side of a two-way link : the objects in memory disagree with each other until you reload them. - CascadeType.REMOVE on @ManyToMany : deleting one parent deletes children that other parents still share. - toString , equals , hashCode or JSON serialisation touching lazy collections : this causes extra queries, endless recursion (A prints B, B prints A …), or LazyInitializationException . Interview questions Q1. What are the default fetch types? ToOne links ( @ManyToOne , @OneToOne ) are EAGER. ToMany links are LAZY. You should set ToOne links to LAZY explicitly. Q2. What is the owning side of a relationship? It is the side that holds the foreign key ( @JoinColumn ). JPA writes the relationship to the database from this side. mappedBy marks the other side, the inverse side. Q3. When would you avoid @ManyToMany ? When the link has its own data or its own lifecycle. Then model the join table as an entity, with two ManyToOne relations.

t: 7.9 The persistence context, entity states and dirty checking
x: Why? In simple words: Inside a transaction, Hibernate keeps a notebook of every object it loaded and what it looked like at load time. At the end, it compares, finds what you changed, and writes the UPDATE for you — even if you never call save() . Hibernate does more than run SQL. It keeps a unit of work — it collects changes and writes them together. In detail, it: - tracks every entity it loaded, - makes sure one database row = one Java object within a transaction, - groups writes into batches, - writes your changes to the database automatically. Sending pending changes to the database is called flushing . If you do not understand this, you will see puzzles like: - "Why did this UPDATE happen? I never called save." - "Why is my change not saved?" - "Why does my batch job run out of memory?" What is happening internally? The persistence context is also called the first-level cache . It holds two things: 1. A map: (EntityClass, id) → entity instance . 2. A snapshot of each entity — a copy of its values as they were when loaded. In Spring, the persistence context lives as long as the transaction. Think of a library register. Every book issued is written down with its condition. When it comes back, the clerk compares it with the register and notes any damage. An entity moves through these states: - Transient : a new object that Hibernate does not know about yet. - Managed : Hibernate is tracking it. - Detached : Hibernate tracked it earlier, but the context is closed or cleared now. - Removed : marked for delete; the DELETE runs at flush. Key behaviour: - find / findById first checks the persistence context. Within one transaction, the same ID always gives you the same Java object . - Dirty checking : an entity is dirty when its values differ from its snapshot. At flush , Hibernate compares each managed entity with its snapshot. It issues UPDATE s for the changed ones. So you do not call save() to update a managed entity. - When does flush happen? Before commit. Also, in the default AUTO mode, before a query that touches the affected tables — so the query sees your changes. - Writes wait in a queue (the action queue ). At flush they run in a fixed order: inserts, then updates, then collection changes, then deletes. How does it work? What save() does in Spring Data: - For a new entity, it calls persist . - For an entity with an existing ID, it calls merge . merge first runs a SELECT for that row, then copies your values onto it. That is an extra query you often do not need. Example Without the flush + clear , all 1 million objects (and their snapshots) stay in memory. With it, every 500 rows are written and then dropped from the context. When would I use it? - Everyday updates : load the entity, change it, and let the commit flush it. - Read-only queries : use @Transactional(readOnly = true) . Hibernate then skips the snapshots and the dirty checking, which saves memory and CPU. - Bulk jobs : flush and clear every few hundred rows. Or use JDBC batching or plain SQL directly. What can go wrong? - Unexpected UPDATEs : some code changed a managed entity — even a setter called only "for display". Hibernate sees the change and saves it. - Running out of memory : a long transaction loads too many entities, and they all stay in the context. - Stale state : a bulk JPQL or SQL update skips the context. Entities already in memory now hold old values. - Detached entity confusion : - Changing an entity after the transaction has ended changes nothing in the database. - merge returns a different managed object. Keep using the returned one, not the one you passed in. - Flush order surprises : an error such as a unique-constraint violation may appear later, on some other query (when AUTO flush runs). It does not appear on the line where you called save . Interview questions Q1. What is the persistence context? It is Hibernate's first-level cache and unit of work, one per transaction. It maps IDs to managed entity objects, keeps a snapshot of each, and flushes changes at commit. Q2. What is dirty checking? At flush, Hibernate compares each managed entity with its snapshot. For every changed entity, it generates an UPDATE automatically. Q3. Do you need to call save() after modifying an entity? Not for a managed entity inside a transaction — the change is flushed at commit. save matters only for new or detached entities. Q4. persist vs merge? persist makes a new object managed. merge copies a detached object's values onto a managed object (loading it first if needed) and returns that managed object.

t: 7.10 The N+1 query problem and fetching strategies
x: Why? In simple words: You load 500 orders with one query. Then, for each order, you read its outlet name — and Hibernate quietly fires one more query each time. So 1 query becomes 501. This is the most common ORM performance bug. The code looks like one query, but it runs hundreds. A typical story: - A list endpoint is fast in dev, with 10 rows. - In production, with 500 rows, it takes 8 seconds. - Why? Each row triggers more queries. What is happening internally? Step by step: 1. Loading N parent rows runs 1 query . 2. Your code touches a lazy link on each parent (for example, order.getOutlet().getName() ). 3. Each touch loads that proxy or collection with 1 more query . 4. Total: N+1 round trips to the database. Each query alone is cheap. But the network delay adds up: 500 × 2 ms = 1 second. And the whole time, the request holds a connection from the pool, so other requests may have to wait. Think of a shopkeeper who walks to the godown separately for each item on your list, instead of picking all items in one trip. How does it work? Fixes, from most targeted to least targeted: 1. Fetch join (JPQL): load the linked data in the same query, using join fetch . 2. @EntityGraph : on a repository method, list which links should be loaded together with the parent. 3. Batch fetching : set hibernate.default batch fetch size=50 . Hibernate then loads lazy links for many parents at once, using IN (?, ?, …) . So N+1 queries become 1 + N/50. 4. DTO projection : select exactly the columns the response needs, straight into a DTO (a plain data object). This is often the best choice for read endpoints. Example How to detect it: - In dev and tests, log the SQL: logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG . - Turn on hibernate.generate statistics to see query counts. - In integration tests, assert the number of queries (for example, with datasource-proxy). - In production, look at APM traces (application performance monitoring). Hundreds of identical SELECTs in one request is the sign. When would I use it? On every list or report endpoint. Decide what to load for each use case — a list view needs less than a detail view. Do not decide it once for the whole app by making links EAGER. What can go wrong? - Fetch-joining a collection while paginating : Hibernate cannot apply the page limit in SQL. So it loads all rows and pages them in memory . You will see warning HHH90003004. Fix: first fetch only the parent IDs for the page, then fetch the links for those IDs. Or use batch fetching. - Fetch-joining two collections (Hibernate calls a List mapping a "bag"): you get MultipleBagFetchException , or a Cartesian product — every line row multiplied by every other row. Fix: fetch one collection per query, or use Set s, or batch fetching. - Making links EAGER to "fix" N+1 : this does not fix it. It just moves the problem to every other place that loads the entity. Interview questions Q1. What is the N+1 problem? One query loads N parent rows. Then reading a lazy link on each parent fires one more query per parent. That is N+1 queries in total. Q2. How do you fix it? Use fetch joins, @EntityGraph, batch fetching ( default batch fetch size ), or DTO projections that select exactly what is needed. Detect it by logging and counting the SQL. Q3. Why is join fetch with pagination dangerous? When you fetch a collection, Hibernate cannot apply LIMIT in SQL. So it loads all the rows and does the paging in memory.

Why? In simple words: A lazy link can load its data only while the database session is open. If you touch it after the transaction has ended, it crashes. Spring Boot's default "fix" keeps the session open for the whole web request — which creates bigger problems. Lazy loading is good: you do not load data you do not need. But there is a catch: - A lazy proxy can load only while its session (the persistence context) is still open. - If you touch it after the transaction ends, you get LazyInitializationException . - This usually happens in the controller, or while converting the object to JSON ( serialisation ). By default, Spring Boot "solves" this with Open-Session-in-View (OSIV) . But OSIV causes worse problems, as you will see below. What is happening internally? - A lazy link is a Hibernate proxy or PersistentCollection . It keeps a reference to the session that created it. - On first access, it asks that session to load the data. - If the session is already closed, it throws LazyInitializationException: could not initialize proxy - no Session . Think of a railway counter that closes at 5 pm. Your token is valid, but if you come at 6 pm, nobody is there to serve you. OSIV is controlled by spring.jpa.open-in-view=true . It is on by default, and Spring prints a warning about it at startup. Here is what it does: 1. An interceptor opens an EntityManager at the start of the web request . 2. It closes it only after the response has been written. So lazy loading now works in controllers and in JSON serialisers. But: - Queries now run in the web layer, outside your service transaction . N+1 queries can hide inside the JSON writing, where nobody looks. - A database connection is held for the whole request. That includes slow calls to other services and the serialisation time. Under load, this uses up the whole connection pool. How does it work? The correct approach has two parts: 1. Turn OSIV off. 2. Load everything the response needs inside the service transaction . Then convert it to DTOs before you return. Example When would I use it? Always, in services that give data to controllers. Use clear fetch plans (what to load, decided per use case), and map to DTOs inside the transactional service. What can go wrong? - Leaving OSIV on : the pool runs out under load, and queries hide in the web layer. - "Fixing" LazyInitializationException the wrong way : making links EAGER, or calling Hibernate.initialize everywhere. - Serialising entities directly with Jackson : lazy proxies fire queries or throw errors. Return DTOs instead. Interview questions Q1. What causes LazyInitializationException? Touching a lazy link that is not loaded yet, after its persistence context (session) has closed. This usually happens outside the transaction. Q2. What is Open-Session-in-View and why disable it? It keeps the persistence context open for the whole web request, so lazy loading works in the view layer. But it hides queries outside transactions and holds a DB connection for the full request. Disable it and load data explicitly in services.

t: 7.12 @Transactional: how it works and its rollback rules
x: Why? In simple words: You put @Transactional on a method. Spring then starts a transaction before the method, and commits it after — or rolls everything back if a runtime exception escapes. You write the boundary once, not in every method. A business operation must be atomic — all steps happen, or none do. For example: - debit the account, - and write the ledger entry, - and write the outbox event. Either all three are saved, or none are. Think of an ATM. Either the cash comes out and your account is debited, or neither happens. Doing this by hand in every method is repetitive and easy to get wrong. You would call connection.setAutoCommit(false) , then commit, then roll back on errors — every single time. @Transactional lets you declare the boundary once. What is happening internally? 1. Spring wraps your bean in a proxy (6.7) — a wrapper object that sits in front of it. The proxy has a TransactionInterceptor . 2. When a call comes through the proxy, the interceptor asks the PlatformTransactionManager to begin a transaction. For JPA, this is the JpaTransactionManager . It uses the settings you gave: propagation, isolation, timeout and readOnly. 3. The manager gets a DB connection and turns autocommit off. Then it binds the connection and the EntityManager to the current thread. It does this through TransactionSynchronizationManager , which uses a ThreadLocal (4.15) — a variable that each thread has its own copy of. Any repository called in the same thread finds this connection and reuses it. 4. Your method runs. 5. If the method returns normally → flush + commit . If it throws an exception → rollback , but only if the rollback rules match. Otherwise, it still commits. 6. The connection is unbound and returned to the pool. Then after-commit callbacks ( @TransactionalEventListener ) run. Default rollback rules: - Roll back on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException) and Errors . - Commit on checked exceptions (like IOException ). - You can change this with rollbackFor / noRollbackFor . How does it work? A note on the "idempotent replay" line: idempotent means doing the same request twice gives the same result as doing it once. If the same idempotency key comes again, we return the old result instead of debiting again. Example When would I use it? - Put it on service-layer methods. Each such method should be one business operation. - Use @Transactional(readOnly = true) on query services. It turns on read optimisations, and it can send the reads to a replica database. - Keep transaction boundaries out of controllers and repositories. What can go wrong? (where @Transactional silently doesn't work) - Self-invocation (6.7): a method calls another method in the same class. The call does not go through the proxy, so the annotation is ignored. The same is true for private or final methods , and for objects you create with new . - Checked exceptions commit by default. Swallowed exceptions (caught and not rethrown) also commit. - Work on another thread ( @Async , executors, CompletableFuture ) runs outside the transaction. Why? The transaction is bound to the original thread only. - Multiple data sources without saying which transactionManager to use. - Long transactions with remote calls inside : they hold a connection and row locks while waiting on the network. Also, the remote side effect cannot be rolled back. Better: do the DB work, commit, then call out. Or use the outbox pattern. - UnexpectedRollbackException : this happens in three steps: 1. An inner REQUIRED method throws. This marks the shared transaction as rollback-only . 2. The outer method catches the exception. 3. The outer method tries to commit — and Spring throws this exception, because the transaction can only roll back. Interview questions Q1. How does @Transactional work? A proxy's TransactionInterceptor begins a transaction through the PlatformTransactionManager and binds the connection to the current thread. Then it calls the method. At the end, it commits, or rolls back according to the rollback rules. Q2. What are the default rollback rules? Roll back on RuntimeException and Error. Commit on checked exceptions, unless rollbackFor says otherwise. Q3. List cases where @Transactional is silently ignored. Self-invocation, private or final methods, objects not managed by Spring, work on other threads, and the wrong transaction manager. Also, it still commits when a checked exception is thrown or an exception is swallowed. Q4. Why shouldn't you call external APIs inside a transaction? The DB connection and locks stay held while you wait on the network. This hurts throughput and risks pool exhaustion and deadlocks. Also, if the DB transaction fails, you cannot roll back the external effect.

Why? In simple words: When one transactional method calls another, propagation decides: does the inner one join the outer transaction, start its own separate one, or insist that one already exists? Transactional methods often call other transactional methods. So a question comes up. Should the inner method: - join the caller's transaction, - start its own transaction, or - require that a transaction already exists? The propagation setting decides this. A wrong choice causes one of two problems: - You lose data you wanted to keep. For example, an audit record is rolled back together with the failed operation. - You commit half-done work that you wanted to undo. What is happening internally? Propagation If a transaction exists If none exists --- --- --- REQUIRED (default) Join it Start a new one REQUIRES NEW Pause it; start a separate one (on a separate connection) Start a new one NESTED Create a savepoint inside it; if the inner part fails, roll back only to the savepoint Start a new one SUPPORTS Join Run without a transaction NOT SUPPORTED Pause it; run without a transaction Run without a transaction MANDATORY Join Throw an error NEVER Throw an error Run without a transaction (Pausing a transaction is officially called suspending it. A savepoint is a bookmark inside a transaction that you can roll back to.) With REQUIRED , the inner and outer methods share one physical transaction . So if the inner method throws an unchecked exception, the whole transaction is marked rollback-only. This happens even if the outer method catches the exception. How does it work? Example NESTED uses JDBC savepoints. DataSourceTransactionManager supports it. With JPA's transaction manager, it works only in limited setups. It is useful for "try this sub-step; if it fails, undo only that step and carry on". When would I use it? - REQUIRED : for almost everything. - REQUIRES NEW : for work that must be saved whatever happens to the outer transaction. Examples: audit logs, failure records, idempotency-key reservations, or sequence allocation. - MANDATORY : on repository-like methods that must never run outside a transaction. - SUPPORTS : for readOnly queries that work fine with or without a transaction. What can go wrong? - Pool deadlock with REQUIRES NEW : it needs a second connection while the first one is still held. Under load, with a small pool, every thread holds one connection and waits for another. Nobody can move forward. - REQUIRES NEW cannot see the outer transaction's writes : the paused outer transaction has written rows but not committed them. The new transaction won't see them . It may even block, waiting on their locks. - Expecting a caught inner exception to be harmless : with REQUIRED , the outer transaction is already marked rollback-only. You get UnexpectedRollbackException at commit. Interview questions Q1. REQUIRED vs REQUIRES NEW vs NESTED? REQUIRED joins the current transaction, or creates one; everything shares it. REQUIRES NEW pauses the current one and runs a separate transaction that commits or rolls back on its own. NESTED creates a savepoint inside the current transaction. Q2. When would you use REQUIRES NEW? For work that must be saved no matter what happens to the caller, such as audit or failure logs. But remember it needs an extra connection. Q3. Why might REQUIRES NEW cause a deadlock? Each request holds one connection and needs a second. If such requests fill the whole pool, they all wait for each other forever.

Why? In simple words: Many transactions touch the same rows at the same time. The isolation level decides how much one transaction can see of another's unfinished work. Too loose gives wrong data; too strict makes everything slow. Many transactions run at the same time on the same rows. Isolation decides how much they see of each other's changes — changes that are not committed yet, or that happen in parallel. - Too weak : you get double redemptions and wrong balances. - Too strong : you get blocking, retries and lower throughput. Choosing the level on purpose, not by accident, is a senior skill. What is happening internally? These are the problems ( anomalies ) that can happen. T1 and T2 are two transactions running at the same time. Anomaly What happens --- --- Dirty read T2 reads T1's change before T1 commits it; then T1 rolls back, so T2 used data that never existed Non-repeatable read T1 reads the same row twice and gets different values, because T2 committed an update in between Phantom read T1 runs the same range query twice and sees new or missing rows, because T2 inserted or deleted rows in between Lost update T1 and T2 both read balance 100, and each writes its own result; one of the updates is lost Write skew T1 and T2 read the same data, then each writes a different row based on it, and together they break a rule (two doctors both go off call, leaving nobody) Isolation level Dirty Non-repeatable Phantom Default in --- --- --- --- --- READ UNCOMMITTED possible possible possible — READ COMMITTED prevented possible possible PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle REPEATABLE READ prevented prevented possible (prevented in Postgres's snapshot implementation; mostly prevented in InnoDB using gap locks) MySQL InnoDB SERIALIZABLE prevented prevented prevented — How do databases build these levels? Two main ways: - MVCC snapshots (multi-version concurrency control): each transaction reads a consistent snapshot of the data, as of a point in time. Used by PostgreSQL, Oracle, InnoDB, and SQL Server with snapshot isolation. - Locks : readers and writers block each other. SQL Server's default READ COMMITTED works this way. More details are in 12.7. Remember: Lost updates and write skew are not prevented by READ COMMITTED. To stop them, you need row locks, optimistic versions or atomic statements (7.15), or SERIALIZABLE. How does it work? (An invariant is a rule that must always stay true — for example, "balance never goes below zero".) Example When would I use it? - Most OLTP work (normal day-to-day transactions): keep the default, READ COMMITTED. Protect specific rules with locking or atomic statements. - Several reads that must agree with each other (reports, statements): use REPEATABLE READ or a snapshot. - Complex rules across many rows : use SERIALIZABLE, but only rarely, and with automatic retry. What can go wrong? - Raising isolation for the whole app "to be safe" : you get more blocking, more deadlocks and more serialisation failures. - Assuming a level behaves the same in every database : it does not. Postgres REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation; MySQL's REPEATABLE READ is not the same thing. - Forgetting to retry serialisation failures (SQLSTATE 40001). At SERIALIZABLE, the database cancels some transactions on purpose. You must retry them. Interview questions Q1. Name the isolation levels and the anomalies each prevents. Read uncommitted prevents none. Read committed prevents dirty reads. Repeatable read also prevents non-repeatable reads. Serializable also prevents phantoms and write skew. Q2. What is a lost update and how do you prevent it? Two read-modify-write transactions overwrite each other's result. Prevent it with an atomic UPDATE statement, SELECT FOR UPDATE , or an optimistic version check. Q3. What is the default isolation in PostgreSQL and MySQL? PostgreSQL uses READ COMMITTED. MySQL InnoDB uses REPEATABLE READ.

t: 7.15 Optimistic locking, pessimistic locking and atomic updates
x: Why? In simple words: When two requests change the same row at once, you have three choices. Check for a clash at save time (optimistic). Lock the row while reading (pessimistic). Or do the check and the change in one SQL statement (atomic update). Many requests change the same rows at the same time. For example: - two redemptions from the same account, - two admins editing the same campaign, - many users booking the last seat. You need a strategy that keeps the data correct, without killing throughput. Think of IRCTC tatkal booking. Many people want the last seat. Only one should get it, and nobody should be charged for a seat they did not get. What is happening internally? 1. Optimistic locking ( @Version ) — "assume no clash, but check at save time": 1. No lock is taken while reading. 2. On update, Hibernate adds WHERE id = ? AND version = ? and increases the version by one. 3. If another transaction changed the row first, the version no longer matches. The update matches 0 rows . 4. Hibernate throws OptimisticLockException . (Spring wraps it as ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException .) 5. You retry, or report a conflict to the user. No locks are held between the read and the write. 2. Pessimistic locking — "lock first, then work": - SELECT … FOR UPDATE takes a row lock at read time. - Other writers, and other FOR UPDATE readers, wait until you commit. - The lock holder is sure to succeed. The cost is that others are blocked. 3. Atomic conditional update — "let the database do it in one step": - One SQL statement does the read, the check and the write, all inside the database: UPDATE … SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance = ? . - The row lock is held only for that one statement. - The number of affected rows tells you whether it worked: 1 = success, 0 = failed. How does it work? Strategy Best when Cost --- --- --- Optimistic @Version Clashes are rare (editing campaigns, profiles); the user takes a long time between reading and saving Retries or 409 errors when a clash happens Pessimistic FOR UPDATE Clashes are frequent and retries are costly; a rule across many rows inside one transaction Blocking, risk of deadlock, lower throughput Atomic UPDATE A numeric rule on a single row (balance, stock, counters) The logic must fit in one SQL statement Example Here is what happens when two redemptions run at the same time with the atomic update. The balance is 100, and both requests ask for 80: When would I use it? - Atomic updates : for balances, stock and counters — like your loyalty ledger. - Optimistic versions : for entities and aggregates that admins edit. - Pessimistic locks : for operations on many rows that must stay consistent within one transaction. Always lock rows in the same order everywhere, to avoid deadlocks (4.13 / 12.7). What can go wrong? - Holding pessimistic locks while calling external services : others stay blocked for a long time, and the pool runs out. - Locking rows in different orders in different code paths : T1 locks A then B, T2 locks B then A. Each waits for the other — a database deadlock. - Optimistic retries without backoff under heavy contention : everyone retries at the same moment and clashes again. This is a retry storm . Also, retrying side effects that are not idempotent (not safe to repeat) can do them twice. - @Version with bulk JPQL updates : bulk updates do not increase the version, so the check is skipped. Interview questions Q1. Optimistic vs pessimistic locking? Optimistic finds clashes at write time with a version check. It takes no locks and retries on conflict, so it suits low contention. Pessimistic locks rows at read time ( FOR UPDATE ) and blocks other writers, so it suits high contention. Q2. How would you prevent double-spending of points under concurrency? Use an atomic conditional UPDATE ( balance = amount ) and check the affected row count — or use a row lock. Add an idempotency key so duplicate requests are not processed twice. Q3. What happens when an optimistic lock check fails? The update affects zero rows, and Hibernate throws OptimisticLockException. The application then retries, or returns 409.

t: 7.16 Connection pools, migrations and JPA performance settings
x: Why? In simple words: Keep a set of ready database connections and reuse them (a pool). Change the schema only through numbered SQL scripts (migrations). And switch on a few Hibernate settings so inserts go in batches. Three needs, three tools: - Pool : opening a DB connection takes milliseconds — TCP setup, TLS, login. So every app keeps a pool of open connections and reuses them. - Migrations : schema changes must be versioned and must run the same way in every environment. So you need migrations . - Settings : a few Hibernate settings make the difference between 50 and 5,000 inserts per second. Think of an auto stand. Autos wait in a line, ready to go. You take one, finish your trip, and it comes back to the line. Nobody builds a new auto for each ride. What is happening internally? - HikariCP is Spring Boot's default pool. It keeps a set of open connections. 1. A thread borrows one ( getConnection ). 2. It uses it for the transaction. 3. It gives it back. 4. If no connection is free, the thread waits up to connection-timeout , and then fails. - Pool size — more is not better. The database has limited CPU cores and disk. Beyond a point, more parallel queries just fight each other for them. - A common starting point is about 10–20 connections per app instance. - Multiply by the number of instances. The total must stay within the DB's max connections . - Flyway runs numbered SQL scripts ( V1 init.sql , V2 add index.sql ) in order at startup. It records which ones it has run in the flyway schema history table. Liquibase is the alternative, based on XML/YAML. How does it work? Example Zero-downtime schema change — the expand → migrate → contract pattern. You change the schema while the app keeps running: 1. Expand : add the new column as nullable (V4). 2. Deploy code that writes to both the old and the new column. 3. Migrate : fill in old rows (backfill) in small batches. 4. Deploy code that reads from the new column. 5. Contract : drop the old column in a later release (V5). When would I use it? In every service: - Tune the pool using its metrics ( hikaricp.connections.active , pending ). - Put every schema change in a versioned migration. - Turn on batching for jobs that write a lot. What can go wrong? - Pool exhaustion : slow queries, long transactions, OSIV or leaked connections (borrowed and never returned). Threads get stuck in getConnection . A thread dump shows this (5.8). - Too many connections during autoscaling : pool size × number of pods goes above the DB's connection limit. Use PgBouncer (a connection pooler in front of Postgres), or size the pools correctly. - Migrations that lock big tables : for example, adding a column with a volatile default (a value computed per row, like random() ), creating an index without CONCURRENTLY , or running a long backfill in one transaction. - Editing a migration file that has already run : Flyway stores a checksum of each file. The checksum no longer matches, so the app fails at startup. Interview questions Q1. How do you size a connection pool? Start small, about 10–20 per instance. Keep the total under what the DB can handle. Then tune from pool metrics and DB load. The DB's cores and I/O limit useful parallel work — not the number of app threads. Q2. Why not use ddl-auto=update in production? It is not versioned, and it cannot do safe data migrations. It may make destructive or locking changes, and it can behave differently in each environment. Use Flyway/Liquibase migrations, and set validate . Q3. How do you make a schema change with zero downtime? Use expand-migrate-contract. Make additive changes first, write to both old and new, backfill in batches, switch reads to the new structure, and remove the old structure in a later release.

Why? In simple words: Spring Security is a security guard that stands in front of your code. It checks who the caller is and what they may do, before your controller ever runs. Every endpoint must answer two questions: - Who is calling? This is called authentication . - Are they allowed to do this? This is called authorisation . In a multi-tenant SaaS there is a third question. A tenant is one customer company that shares the platform with others. So you also ask: can this caller touch this tenant's data? If you write these checks by hand in every controller, someone will forget one. One missed check can leak data. Spring Security puts all these checks in one place. It is a configurable chain of filters that runs before your code. Think of a company office. The guard at the gate checks your ID card (authentication). The lift only takes you to the floors your card allows (authorisation). You do not ask each desk to check your ID again. What is happening internally? Here is the same flow as steps: 1. Tomcat receives the request. It passes it to DelegatingFilterProxy , a normal servlet filter. 2. That filter hands over to FilterChainProxy . It picks the first SecurityFilterChain whose URL matcher fits the request. 3. The chain runs its filters in order: CORS, CSRF, then the authentication filters. 4. An authentication filter (for example, the JWT one) asks the AuthenticationManager to check the credentials. The manager uses one or more AuthenticationProvider s. If the check passes, you get an Authentication object. 5. This object is stored in SecurityContextHolder . That is a ThreadLocal — a per-thread storage box — so it lives only for this request. 6. ExceptionTranslationFilter catches security errors. An AuthenticationException becomes 401. An AccessDeniedException becomes 403. 7. AuthorizationFilter checks your URL rules ( requestMatchers … hasAuthority … ). 8. The request reaches DispatcherServlet and then your controller. 9. If a service method has @PreAuthorize , an AOP proxy (a wrapper object Spring puts around your bean) checks it before the method runs. Key objects you should know: - Authentication — holds the principal (who the user is), the credentials and the authorities (what they may do). - SecurityContextHolder — where the current Authentication is kept for this request. - AuthenticationManager / AuthenticationProvider — the classes that actually check credentials. - UserDetailsService — loads a user from your store for username/password login. - PasswordEncoder — hashes passwords with BCrypt or Argon2. Never store plain text or MD5. - GrantedAuthority — one permission. It can be a role like ROLE ADMIN or a scope like SCOPE points.redeem . 401 vs 403 : - 401 Unauthorized means "I don't know who you are". Credentials are missing or invalid. The name is confusing — it really means not authenticated . - 403 Forbidden means "I know who you are, but you are not allowed to do this". How does it work? You define one or more SecurityFilterChain beans. You write them with the lambda DSL — the http.csrf(...).authorizeHttpRequests(...) style shown below. Spring Boot auto-configures everything else. You protect at two levels: - URL rules give coarse protection. For example, "everything under /admin needs ADMIN". - Method security ( @PreAuthorize ) gives fine-grained checks. It sits close to the business logic, so it can look at method arguments like tenantId . Example When would I use it? In every service that exposes HTTP. Use three layers together: 1. URL rules — coarse checks. 2. Method security — fine checks near the business logic. 3. Data-level tenant filtering — every query is scoped by tenant. You can use a Hibernate filter or an explicit WHERE tenant id = ? condition. Why all three? Because in a multi-tenant system, one authorisation bug can show one customer's data to another customer. That is the worst kind of bug in SaaS. What can go wrong? - When you add the security starter, every endpoint suddenly needs login. Spring prints a generated password at startup. This surprises people, but it is the safe default. - Rule order matters. Rules are matched from top to bottom. If you put anyRequest().permitAll() before the specific rules, everything is open. - Trusting a tenant ID from a request header without checking it against the token's tenant claim. A user can just change the header and read another tenant's data. This is called an IDOR : insecure direct object reference. - Disabling CSRF for a browser app that uses cookie sessions. CSRF protection is needed there. (It is only safe to disable for stateless bearer-token APIs.) - The SecurityContext does not move to @Async threads on its own, because it is stored in a ThreadLocal. Use DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor to carry it over. Interview questions Q1. How does Spring Security process a request? A FilterChainProxy runs the matching SecurityFilterChain. First, authentication filters check the credentials, build an Authentication object and store it in the SecurityContextHolder. Then authorisation filters check the URL rules. Security exceptions are turned into 401 or 403 responses. Finally, method security checks like @PreAuthorize run at the service proxy. Q2. Authentication vs authorisation? Authentication checks who you are; if it fails, you get 401. Authorisation decides what an already-authenticated user may do; if it fails, you get 403. Q3. How do you enforce tenant isolation? Take the tenant from the verified token, not only from a header the client sends. Check it in method security. And apply a mandatory tenant filter to every data query, so even a missed check cannot return another tenant's rows.

Why? In simple words: A JWT is a signed pass that the caller carries with every request. Any service can check the signature by itself, so nobody needs to call a central session store. OAuth2 is the set of rules for how you get that pass. In microservices, you don't want every service to call a central session store on every request. That store becomes slow and a single point of failure. - A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a self-contained, signed token. Any service can verify it locally, without a network call. - OAuth2 is the standard for how clients get tokens. - OpenID Connect (OIDC) sits on top of OAuth2 and adds the user's identity. Different callers use different OAuth2 flows. Your mobile apps use one flow, partner integrations another, and service-to-service calls another. Think of a railway ticket with an official stamp. The TT on any coach can check the stamp himself. He does not phone the booking office for every passenger. What is happening internally? A JWT has three parts joined by dots: base64url(header).base64url(payload).signature . Base64url is just a text encoding, not encryption. What this means: - Signed, not encrypted. Anyone can decode and read the payload. So never put secrets or sensitive PII (personal data like phone numbers) inside it. The signature only proves that nobody changed it. - Asymmetric signing (RS256/ES256). The identity provider (Keycloak, Azure AD/Entra ID, Auth0, Cognito) signs with its private key. Your services verify with the matching public keys. These public keys are published at the provider's JWKS endpoint (JSON Web Key Set). Services cache them. When keys rotate, the kid (key ID) in the header tells which key to use. - What a resource server checks. A resource server is your API that receives the token. It checks: 1. the signature; 2. exp (expiry) and nbf (not-before), allowing a small clock skew; 3. iss — who issued it; 4. aud — which API it was made for. Then it maps scope and roles to Spring authorities. - Stateless — but revocation is hard. There is no server-side session to look up. The downside: you cannot easily cancel a token before it expires. So keep access tokens short-lived (5–15 min). Pair them with refresh tokens . Refresh tokens live longer, are rotated on use, can be revoked, and must be stored securely. OAuth2 flows: Flow Who uses it --- --- Authorization Code + PKCE Mobile and web apps acting for a user (no client secret is stored on the device) Client Credentials Service-to-service calls (a machine identity, no user) Refresh Token Getting new access tokens without logging in again Device Code TVs and CLIs (Implicit, Password — deprecated) Don't use them PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) is a one-time secret the app creates for each login. It stops a stolen authorisation code from being used by another app. OIDC adds two things: an ID token (it says who the user is) and a userinfo endpoint. The access token is still the one your APIs check. How does it work? You point Spring at the identity provider. From the issuer-uri , Spring discovers the JWKS URL and also validates iss . You list the expected audience. Often your provider puts roles in a custom claim, like roles . Spring does not know about it by default. This converter maps that claim to ROLE authorities: Example A service-to-service call using client credentials (loyalty service → voucher partner gateway). The interceptor gets a token, attaches it to each request and refreshes it when it expires: When would I use it? - JWT resource server — for every API behind an identity provider. - Client credentials — for calls between services. - Authorization Code + PKCE — for mobile app login. - mTLS or service-mesh identity — for internal calls in high-security setups. mTLS means both sides show certificates to each other. What can go wrong? - Accepting alg: none (no signature at all), or HS256 with a secret that can be guessed. Good libraries block this if you configure them correctly. - Not checking aud . Then a token made for some other API is accepted by yours. - Long-lived access tokens that cannot be revoked. - Storing tokens in browser localStorage . An XSS attack (injected script) can steal them. Use secure cookies or keep them in memory instead. - Huge tokens with too many claims. They can hit HTTP header size limits. - Clocks on servers that differ slightly (clock skew). This causes random "token expired" errors. Interview questions Q1. How does JWT authentication work? The client sends a signed token with the request. The service checks the signature using the issuer's public key from the JWKS endpoint. It then checks expiry, issuer and audience, and builds the security context from the claims. There is no session lookup. Q2. How do you revoke a JWT? You cannot revoke it directly. So you keep access tokens short-lived and revoke the refresh tokens instead. For sensitive actions, use token introspection (ask the provider if the token is still valid) or keep a deny-list of token IDs ( jti ). Q3. OAuth2 vs OpenID Connect? OAuth2 is delegated authorisation — it gives access tokens for calling APIs. OIDC is an identity layer on top of it — it adds ID tokens and user info, so you know who the user is. Q4. Which flow for a mobile app, and which for service-to-service? Authorization Code with PKCE for a mobile app. Client Credentials for service-to-service.

t: 8.3 Unit testing with JUnit 5 and Mockito
x: Why? In simple words: Unit tests are small, fast checks of one class at a time. You replace its neighbours with fakes, so you test only your logic. They let you change code later without fear. Tests let you change code without fear. Unit tests give the fastest feedback — they run in milliseconds. They are also the cheapest way to lock down business rules, such as redemption limits, rule evaluation and idempotency behaviour. ( Idempotent means doing the same thing twice has the same effect as doing it once.) Interviewers also judge your code quality by asking: can you test what you design? What is happening internally? - JUnit 5 (Jupiter) finds methods marked @Test and runs them. It gives you: - lifecycle hooks such as @BeforeEach and @AfterEach (run before/after each test); - parameterised tests ( @ParameterizedTest + @CsvSource / @MethodSource ) — one test method run with many inputs; - extensions ( @ExtendWith ) that plug in extra behaviour. - Mockito creates fake objects: - Mocks are generated subclasses or proxies. They record the calls they get and return the answers you stubbed. - Spies wrap a real object. - @InjectMocks builds the class under test and passes the mocks into it. - AssertJ gives fluent, readable assertions, like assertThat(x).isEqualTo(…) and assertThatThrownBy(…) . The test pyramid tells you the mix: many fast unit tests at the bottom, fewer slice and integration tests in the middle (8.4), and only a handful of end-to-end tests at the top. Think of a car-mechanic testing an engine on a stand. He does not fit the whole car. He feeds fake fuel and fake signals and checks what the engine does. How does it work? Every test has three parts: 1. Arrange — set up data and stubs. 2. Act — call the method. 3. Assert — check the result and the important interactions. Mock only collaborators at the boundaries : repositories, HTTP clients, clocks. Never mock the class under test, and never mock value objects (simple data holders). Example What each test shows: - rejectsWhenBalanceIsInsufficient — a failed debit throws the right exception, and nothing is saved to the ledger or outbox. - replayingSameIdempotencyKeyDoesNotDebitAgain — the same key sent twice does not debit twice. - tierMultiplier — one parameterised test covers three tiers. - capturesPublishedEvent — an ArgumentCaptor grabs the object passed to outbox.save , so you can check its contents. When would I use it? For all domain logic and service orchestration (services that call other services in order). Inject Clock , ID generators and random sources instead of calling them directly. Then tests can control them, and results are deterministic — the same every run. What can go wrong? - Over-mocking. Tests copy the implementation line by line. They break on every refactor and prove nothing. Check behaviour — outputs and important interactions — not every single call. - Mocking value objects or the class under test. - Unused stubs. Mockito's strict stubs fail the test when a stub is never used. This is good: it catches outdated tests. - Tests that depend on time, randomness, HashMap ordering or the state left by other tests. They pass sometimes and fail sometimes (flaky tests). Interview questions Q1. Mock vs stub vs spy? A stub just returns canned answers. A mock also lets you verify which calls were made. A spy wraps a real object and calls the real methods unless you stub them. Q2. What should you mock? External boundaries and collaborators — repositories, HTTP clients, clocks and message publishers. Do not mock value objects or the logic you are testing. Q3. How do you test time-dependent code? Inject a Clock into the class. In tests, pass Clock.fixed so "now" is always the same.

t: 8.4 Slice tests and integration tests with Testcontainers
x: Why? In simple words: Mocks can't tell you if your SQL is wrong or your JSON mapping is broken. So you also run tests with real Spring wiring and a real database in Docker. Testcontainers starts that database for you inside the test. Unit tests with mocks cannot catch: - a wrong JPQL query; - a broken JSON mapping; - a missing index; - a Postgres-specific SQL feature; - a misconfigured Kafka listener. You need tests that run the real Spring wiring against real infrastructure . These tests must still be fast and give the same result on every laptop and every CI run. What is happening internally? - Slice tests start only part of the application context — one layer: - @WebMvcTest(Controller.class) loads the MVC setup, the controller, its advice and Jackson. Services are replaced by @MockitoBean s. MockMvc sends fake requests without starting a real server. - @DataJpaTest loads JPA and your repositories. Each test runs in a transaction that is rolled back at the end. - There are others too, like @JsonTest and @RestClientTest . - @SpringBootTest starts the full context. It can also start a real server on a random port. - Testcontainers starts real Docker containers (PostgreSQL, Kafka, Redis) from inside the test. With @ServiceConnection (Boot 3.1+), Spring automatically picks up their dynamic URLs and ports. Containers can be reused across test classes. - The context cache : Spring keeps an application context and reuses it for other test classes with the same configuration. But each different set of @MockitoBean s creates a new context. That slows the suite. Think of a dress rehearsal for a wedding. Practising each dance alone is a unit test. The rehearsal on the real stage, with the real sound system, is the integration test. How does it work? A web-slice test. It checks that bad input gives a 400 with two field errors, without any real service: Example A full integration test against real Postgres. Twenty threads try to redeem 100 points each from an account holding 1,000: Exactly 10 redemptions should succeed and the balance must end at zero — never negative. This concurrency test against real Postgres is the single most convincing thing to show in your Java project (8.11). When would I use it? - @WebMvcTest — for request mapping, validation, error format and security rules. - @DataJpaTest + Testcontainers — for custom queries and constraints. - @SpringBootTest + Testcontainers — for end-to-end flows (API → DB → Kafka) and concurrency guarantees. Run all of them in CI on every pull request. What can go wrong? - Using H2 (an in-memory database) instead of your real database. H2 has a different SQL dialect, different locking, different JSONB and constraint behaviour. Tests pass and production breaks. - Slow suites because of many unique contexts. Each different mock set or property set builds a new context. Standardise your test configurations so they share one. - Tests that share data and don't clean up. Then a test passes or fails depending on run order. - @Transactional on integration tests can hide bugs. The data never really commits. Lazy loading works only because the test's transaction is still open — in production it would fail. Interview questions Q1. @WebMvcTest vs @DataJpaTest vs @SpringBootTest? @WebMvcTest is a web-layer slice with mocked services. @DataJpaTest is a JPA slice with repositories, each test in a rolled-back transaction. @SpringBootTest loads the full application context. Q2. Why use Testcontainers instead of H2? Your tests run against the same database engine and version as production. So they catch differences in SQL dialect, locking, constraints and features that H2 would hide. Q3. How would you test that concurrent redemptions never overdraw? Write an integration test against real Postgres. Fire N concurrent redemptions, each with a different idempotency key. Then assert the final balance and the exact number of successes.

t: 8.5 Kafka with Spring: producers, consumers, idempotency and dead letters
x: Why? In simple words: Kafka is a durable notice board of events. One service pins up "order completed", and other services read it whenever they are ready — even if they were down for an hour. Spring Kafka makes writing and reading these events easy. Services must react to each other's events. For example: order completed → accrue points → notify the retailer → update analytics. But they should not depend on each other synchronously (waiting for a direct reply): - If the loyalty service is down, ordering must still work. - When loyalty comes back, it must process everything it missed. Kafka gives you an event log that is durable (survives crashes), ordered and replayable (you can read it again). Spring Kafka makes producing and consuming events simple. The Kafka concepts are in 11.12–11.13; this section covers the Spring side. What is happening internally? - Producer side. KafkaTemplate wraps a thread-safe KafkaProducer .
