The producer groups records per partition into batches and sends them asynchronously. With acks=all plus producer idempotence (on by default since Kafka 3.0), producer retries cause neither lost nor duplicate records. - Consumer side. @KafkaListener creates a listener container : 1. It starts one or more consumer threads (set by concurrency ). 2. Each thread owns a KafkaConsumer in the consumer group. 3. Each consumer polls records from the partitions assigned to it and calls your method. 4. After your method returns, the container commits the offset (the "read up to here" bookmark). The default is AckMode.BATCH . - So delivery is at-least-once. If the app crashes after processing but before the commit, the same record comes again. Your code must handle duplicates. - Error handling. DefaultErrorHandler retries a failed record with a backoff (wait) by seeking back to it. After the retries run out, it gives the record to a recoverer . Usually that is DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer . It publishes the record to <topic .DLT (dead-letter topic) with headers explaining the error. - Ordering is only per partition. If you use accountId as the key, all events of one account go to the same partition, so they stay in order. Think of the railway parcel office register. Each parcel is noted down. Every godown clerk marks the last entry he handled. If he goes on leave, he restarts from his mark — and may handle one parcel twice, so he must check before acting. How does it work? Example How the consumer stays safe against duplicates: 1. It checks if this eventId was already processed. If yes, it returns and does nothing. 2. It applies the accrual. 3. It saves the eventId in processed event — in the same database transaction as the accrual. 4. The primary key on event id blocks two consumers that race on the same redelivered record. The error handler retries 3 times with exponential backoff (500 ms, then doubling). Validation and deserialisation errors skip the retries — those records are poison (they will never succeed), so they go to the DLT at once. For non-blocking retries , use @RetryableTopic . It sends failed records through separate retry topics with delays, and finally to the DLT. This way one failing record does not stall its whole partition. When would I use it? - Event-driven integration between services. - Asynchronous processing of high-volume events: accruals, notifications, analytics. - CDC pipelines (Change Data Capture — streaming every database change as an event). - Audit streams. When the event must not be lost, publish from the outbox relay (11.15), not directly inside the business transaction. What can go wrong? - Non-idempotent consumers apply the effect twice when a record is redelivered. This is the root cause of "duplicate reward postings under retries". - Dual writes : repo.save(); kafka.send(); — two separate systems. The DB may commit while the send fails, or the reverse. Use the outbox pattern. - Poison messages retried forever, blocking the partition. Classify exceptions as retryable or not, and use a DLT. - Slow processing. If one poll takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms , Kafka kicks the consumer out of the group. This causes rebalance storms and redeliveries. Keep handlers fast, or reduce max.poll.records . - Hot keys. If one huge tenant is the key, all its events land in one partition. So one consumer does all the work. - Schema changes that break consumers. Use a schema registry, or allow only additive JSON changes (add fields, never remove or rename). Interview questions Q1. How does Spring Kafka deliver messages — exactly once? No — by default it is at-least-once. Offsets are committed after the listener returns, so a failure causes redelivery. So you make consumers idempotent. Kafka transactions give exactly-once only for Kafka-to-Kafka processing. Q2. How do you make a consumer idempotent? Store the processed event ID, with a unique constraint, in the same DB transaction as the business effect. Or make the effect itself idempotent, for example an upsert by business key. Q3. What is a dead-letter topic and when do you send to it? It is a separate topic for records that failed after all retries, or that can never succeed (validation or deserialisation errors). Moving them out stops them from blocking the partition. The DLT is monitored; records are fixed and replayed. Q4. How do you preserve ordering per account? Use the account ID as the record key. All of that account's events then go to one partition and are processed by one consumer thread, in order.

t: 8.6 Caching with Spring Cache and Redis
x: Why? In simple words: A cache keeps a copy of often-read data in fast memory. Next time, you read the copy instead of asking the database again. Some data is read far more often than it changes: scheme definitions, SKU catalogues, tenant settings, computed balances. Reading it from the database every time wastes DB capacity and adds latency. A cache serves repeated reads from memory: - a local in-process cache answers in microseconds; - Redis answers in about a millisecond. Think of a shopkeeper who keeps the 20 most-sold items on the counter. He only goes to the godown for the rest. What is happening internally? - @EnableCaching makes Spring wrap beans that use caching annotations in a proxy (6.7). A proxy is a wrapper object that runs extra logic before and after your method. - @Cacheable works like this: 1. Build the key. By default it comes from the method arguments. You can customise it with SpEL (Spring's expression language). 2. Look up the key in the CacheManager . 3. Hit (found): return the cached value. Your method is not called. 4. Miss (not found): call your method and store the result. - @CacheEvict removes entries. @CachePut always calls the method and updates the cache. - The CacheManager implementation decides where data is stored: - Caffeine — in-process, one copy per instance, nanosecond access, bounded by size and TTL (time to live). - Redis — shared by all instances, one network hop away, values are serialised, TTL per cache. - sync = true : if many requests miss the same key at once on one instance, only one loads it; the others wait. This is local protection against a stampede (many requests hitting the DB together). How does it work? The pattern is called cache-aside : 1. On a read, look in the cache first. On a miss, load from the DB and store it. 2. On a write, update the DB, then evict (delete) the key. Why delete instead of writing the new value into the cache? Because writing can race with a concurrent reader. That reader may put the old, stale value back in after your update. Deleting forces the next read to load fresh data. Example Redis is useful for much more than caching (11.5, 13.x): - atomic counters ( INCR ); - rate limiting (a token bucket written in Lua); - distributed locks ( SET key value NX PX 30000 , or Redisson); - leaderboards (sorted sets); - idempotency keys with a TTL; - pub/sub and streams. When would I use it? For read-heavy, change-light data, expensive computations and per-tenant configuration. - Caffeine — for small reference data where brief per-instance staleness is fine. - Redis — when instances must share results, or the data set is large. - Both together — a two-level cache: Caffeine first, then Redis, then the DB. What can go wrong? - Stale data. Two common causes: - You evict before the transaction commits. Another request then caches the old value again. - You evict on only one instance, while others still hold local copies. Fix: evict after commit ( @TransactionalEventListener ), and keep TTLs as a safety net. - Self-invocation. @Cacheable on a method called from the same class does not cache. The call skips the proxy. - Stampede. A hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the DB at once. See 11.5: single-flight, jitter, early refresh. - Unbounded caches. The default ConcurrentMapCacheManager has no limits, so memory keeps growing — a memory leak. Always set a size limit and a TTL. - Caching mutable objects locally. Callers change the shared cached object, and everyone sees the change. Cache immutable DTOs or records. - Serialisation changes. After a deploy, old Redis entries may no longer be readable. Version your cache keys, or clear the cache on deploy. Interview questions Q1. How does @Cacheable work? A proxy builds a key from the method arguments. On a hit, it returns the cached value without calling the method. On a miss, it calls the method and stores the result. Q2. Why evict on write instead of updating the cache? Updating can race with a concurrent read that reloads old data and writes it to the cache last, leaving stale data. Deleting forces the next read to load fresh data. Q3. Local cache vs Redis? A local cache (Caffeine) is fastest, but each instance has its own copy and they can drift apart. Redis is shared and consistent across instances, but costs a network hop and serialisation.

t: 8.7 Resilience: timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and bulkheads (Resilience4j)
x: Why? In simple words: Other services will sometimes be slow or down. These patterns make sure one sick dependency doesn't drag your whole service down with it — you stop waiting, stop calling it for a while, and show a sensible fallback. In a distributed system, dependencies will be slow or down. Without protection, this happens: 1. One partner API becomes slow. 2. Your threads wait on it, and your thread pool fills up. 3. Your service stops responding to anyone. 4. Your callers' thread pools fill up too. 5. The outage cascades across the whole platform. Resilience patterns contain the failure: - fail fast instead of waiting; - retry only what is safe to retry; - isolate what is slow; - degrade gracefully (give a reduced but useful answer). Think of the electrical circuit breaker (MCB) in your house. When there is a short circuit, it trips and cuts power to that line, so the whole house doesn't catch fire. After the fault is fixed, you switch it back on. What is happening internally? Resilience4j wraps (decorates) your calls. You use it with annotations and Spring AOP, or in functional style. - TimeLimiter / client timeouts — limit how long you wait. Always set this first. - Retry — calls again on the transient exceptions you list. It waits longer each time (exponential backoff), plus some randomness (jitter) so clients don't retry together. - CircuitBreaker — keeps a sliding window of recent results (by call count or by time). - If the failure rate or slow-call rate goes above a threshold, the breaker opens . - While open, calls fail at once with CallNotPermittedException . The dependency is not touched. - After a wait, it becomes half-open and lets a few trial calls through. - If they succeed, it closes. If they fail, it opens again. - Bulkhead — caps how many calls can run at once (with a semaphore), or gives the dependency its own thread pool. So one dependency cannot use up all your threads. (The name comes from the walls inside a ship that stop one leak from sinking the whole ship.) - RateLimiter — caps the number of calls per time unit, to respect a partner's quota. Order of decorators with annotations, outermost first: Retry → CircuitBreaker → RateLimiter → TimeLimiter → Bulkhead → your call. Because Retry is outside the CircuitBreaker: - every retry attempt is recorded by the breaker; and - once the breaker opens, the retries fail fast too, so they stop quickly. How does it work? With this config, the breaker looks at the last 50 calls (and needs at least 20 before it decides). It opens if 50% fail, or if 60% take longer than 2 s. It stays open for 30 s, then allows 5 trial calls. Retry tries up to 3 times, starting at 200 ms and doubling, only for I/O and timeout errors. The bulkhead allows 20 calls at once and waits at most 50 ms for a free slot. Example Two points to notice: - The Idempotency-Key header makes the retried POST safe. The partner sees the same key and does not issue a second voucher. - queueForLater is the fallback. When the breaker is open, the request goes into a queue, a background job retries it later, and the user sees "processing". This is graceful degradation. When would I use it? Around every remote dependency: partner APIs, other microservices, even the database for non-critical reads. Combine it with: - client timeouts (7.6); - idempotency keys on any write that may be retried; - fallbacks that keep core flows working — cached prices, "processing" states, hiding optional widgets. What can go wrong? - Retrying non-idempotent operations creates duplicates — double vouchers, double payments. - Retry storms. If every layer retries 3 times, three layers multiply the load 27 times (3 × 3 × 3) on a dependency that is already struggling. Retry at one layer only, with backoff, jitter and a retry budget (a cap on total retries). - No timeout. Calls just hang, so the circuit breaker never sees a failure. - Fallbacks that hide real outages and raise no alert. - Breaker windows that are too small, so the breaker keeps flipping open and closed (flapping). Or thresholds so high that it never opens. - Self-invocation again: the annotations only work when the call goes through the proxy. Interview questions Q1. Explain the circuit breaker states. Closed: calls flow normally and results are recorded. It moves to Open when the failure or slow-call rate crosses a threshold; now calls fail fast. After a wait, it moves to Half-open and allows a few trial calls. If they succeed, it goes back to Closed; if they fail, it goes back to Open. Q2. Which calls should you retry? Only idempotent operations that fail with transient errors — timeouts, 503s, connection resets. Use exponential backoff with jitter, a limited number of attempts, and ideally retry at one layer only. Q3. What is a bulkhead? It isolates resources per dependency, using a semaphore or a thread-pool limit. So one slow dependency cannot use up all your threads. Q4. How do these patterns prevent cascading failures? Timeouts limit how long you wait. Circuit breakers stop calling a failing dependency. Bulkheads limit how many resources one dependency can use. Fallbacks keep the caller responsive.

Why? In simple words: @Async runs a task in the background so the user doesn't wait for it. @Scheduled runs a task at fixed times. The big catch: with many pods, every pod runs the scheduled job unless you add a lock. Some work should not make the request wait: sending an SMS after a redemption, generating a report, warming a cache. Other work runs on a timetable: daily point expiry at 02:00, hourly reconciliation, retrying pending vouchers. Spring gives you @Async and @Scheduled for these. Both have pitfalls that matter when you run many instances. What is happening internally? - @Async . Add @EnableAsync . Then a proxy intercepts every @Async method. It hands the call to a TaskExecutor (a thread pool) and returns at once. The method returns void or a CompletableFuture . If you configure nothing, Boot gives you a ThreadPoolTaskExecutor — or virtual threads when spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true . - @Scheduled . Add @EnableScheduling . A TaskScheduler then triggers @Scheduled methods by fixedRate , fixedDelay or cron . Note: by default it has only one thread ! - Many instances. If you run several pods, every pod runs every @Scheduled method. So a daily job runs N times unless you coordinate. Think of a society with three watchmen and one rule: "lock the main gate at 10 pm". If nobody coordinates, all three walk to the gate. ShedLock is the register at the gate — the first one to sign does the job. How does it work? This config sets up a dedicated pool for notifications and a DB-based lock for jobs: - 4 core threads, up to 8, and a queue of 500 tasks. - When the queue is full, CallerRunsPolicy makes the caller run the task itself. This slows the caller down instead of dropping work. - A TaskDecorator copies MDC and tenant context into the worker thread (4.15). - ShedLock stores its locks in a shedlock table in your DB, so only one instance runs each job. Example The expiry job runs at 02:00 IST every day. ShedLock holds the lock for at least 5 minutes and at most 2 hours. The work is chunked, resumable and idempotent per lot, so a crash in the middle is safe to restart. When would I use it? - @Async — for fire-and-forget side effects where losing one on a crash is acceptable (or a later job will fix it). - Durable queue (Kafka/outbox) — for work that must not be lost. - @Scheduled + ShedLock — for periodic maintenance. - Kubernetes CronJobs or a workflow engine — for heavy or long batch jobs. What can go wrong? - Self-invocation and private methods. Proxy rules again — these calls skip the proxy, so they run synchronously. - An exception in a void @Async method disappears silently, unless you configure an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler . - ThreadLocal context (tenant, security, MDC) is lost in async threads. Use a TaskDecorator to copy it. - The default single scheduler thread. One slow job delays all the others. Configure a pool ( spring.task.scheduling.pool.size ). - Jobs running on every pod — duplicate expiry or duplicate payouts — when there is no ShedLock or leader election. Also, jobs that are not idempotent and cannot resume after a crash. - Time zones and DST (daylight-saving time changes) in cron expressions. Always set the zone . Interview questions Q1. How does @Async work and what are its limits? A proxy hands the call to an executor and returns immediately. Limits: it does not work on self-invocation or private methods; it loses ThreadLocal context unless you propagate it; and the work is lost if the app crashes. Q2. How do you ensure a scheduled job runs once across multiple instances? Use a distributed lock (ShedLock on a DB or Redis), or leader election. Or run the job outside the app — a Kubernetes CronJob, or Quartz in clustered mode.

t: 8.9 Observability: health, metrics, logs and traces
x: Why? In simple words: In production you can't debug line by line. So the service must report on itself: numbers that say something is wrong, traces that show where, and logs that explain why. In production you cannot attach a debugger. You find problems only through what the system emits: - Metrics tell you that something is wrong — for example, the error rate went up. - Traces tell you where — which hop in the request is slow. - Logs tell you why — the exception and its context. Health endpoints let Kubernetes send traffic only to healthy instances. Think of a car dashboard. The warning light (metric) says something is wrong. The mechanic's diagnostic scan (trace) finds which part. The service record (logs) explains what happened. What is happening internally? - Actuator adds management endpoints: - /actuator/health , with liveness and readiness groups for Kubernetes probes; - /info , /metrics , /prometheus ; - /loggers — change log levels at runtime; - /threaddump , /heapdump , /conditions , /startup . - Micrometer is the metrics facade — like SLF4J, but for metrics. You write counters, gauges, timers and distribution summaries, each with tags (labels). It exports them to Prometheus, Azure Monitor or Datadog. Boot measures many things for you automatically: HTTP server and client requests, JVM memory/GC/threads, Hikari connection pools, Kafka clients and caches. - Micrometer Tracing + OpenTelemetry work like this: 1. Each request gets a trace ID. 2. A span (one timed step) is created for each HTTP call, DB query and Kafka message. 3. The trace context travels to the next service in W3C traceparent HTTP headers and in Kafka headers. 4. Spans are exported to Jaeger, Tempo, Zipkin or Application Insights. - Structured logging means logs written as JSON. It is built into Boot 3.4+. Put the trace ID and tenant ID in every line using MDC (a per-thread map of log fields). Then logs are searchable and you can join them with traces. How does it work? What to measure: - RED for each endpoint and dependency: R ate (requests per second), E rrors, D uration (p50/p95/p99). p95 means 95% of requests were faster than this. - USE for each resource: U tilisation, S aturation (queue lengths, waits for a pool), E rrors. Apply it to thread pools, connection pools, Kafka consumer lag and GC. - Business KPIs : redemptions per minute, accrual lag, failed vouchers. Alert on symptoms measured against SLOs , not on every CPU blip. An SLO (service level objective) is a target such as "99.9% of redemptions succeed in < 500 ms". The error budget is the 0.1% you are allowed to fail. Alert when you are burning that budget too fast (the burn rate). Example This config exposes only health, info and prometheus. It turns on the liveness and readiness probes, samples 10% of traces in production, and writes JSON logs. When would I use it? From day one, in every service: - a dashboard per service (RED + USE); - alerts on SLO burn; - traces to investigate slow requests; - logs linked to traces by trace ID. In interviews, the question "how would you know it's working in production?" is answered with exactly these. What can go wrong? - High-cardinality tags. Cardinality means how many different values a tag can have. User IDs, order IDs or raw URLs as tags create millions of series. This blows up the metrics backend's memory and cost. Use tags with a small, fixed set of values: status, endpoint template, tenant tier. - Exposing /heapdump or /env to the public. They can leak data. Keep management endpoints on an internal port or network. - Liveness probes that check the database. If the DB has a short blip, Kubernetes restarts every pod. Liveness should reflect only the app process itself. Put dependency checks in readiness — and carefully. - Logging PII or secrets. Logging at DEBUG in production. Logging the same exception in many layers. Interview questions Q1. Metrics vs logs vs traces? Metrics are aggregated numbers, used to detect problems and alert. Traces follow one request across services to find where the latency or error is. Logs are detailed events that explain what happened. Q2. Liveness vs readiness probes? Liveness asks: is the process healthy, or should Kubernetes restart it? Readiness asks: can it serve traffic right now — is it warmed up and are its dependencies reachable? A failing readiness probe takes the pod out of load balancing without restarting it. Q3. What are RED and USE? RED (rate, errors, duration) is for request-driven services. USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) is for resources such as pools, queues and CPU.

t: 8.10 Microservices patterns in the Spring ecosystem
x: Why? In simple words: Breaking an app into many small services gives teams freedom, but brings new problems — network calls fail, data is spread out. Each common problem has a well-known pattern and a well-known tool. Splitting a system into services gives you: - independent deployment; - independent scaling; - clear team ownership. The price is network calls, partial failures, data spread across services, and more operational work. A set of well-known patterns solves the recurring problems. Interviewers expect you to: 1. name the patterns; 2. know the Spring or Kubernetes tool for each; 3. say when not to use microservices. What is happening internally? Concern Pattern Typical implementation --- --- --- One entry point for all calls: routing, auth, rate limits API Gateway / BFF (Backend for Frontend) Spring Cloud Gateway, Azure API Management, Kong, Envoy Finding where service instances are running Service discovery Kubernetes Services + DNS; Eureka outside Kubernetes Keeping configuration in one central place Externalised config ConfigMaps/Secrets, Azure App Configuration, Spring Cloud Config One failure spreading to others (cascading failures) Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads Resilience4j (8.7) Who owns which data Database per service Each service owns its schema; no shared tables Keeping data consistent across services Saga (choreography/orchestration) + outbox Kafka, Temporal/Camunda, outbox relay or Debezium CDC (11.15) Queries that need data from many services API composition, CQRS read models An aggregator service; a read model fed by events Moving away from a monolith Strangler fig Gateway sends new paths to new services, step by step Seeing what happens across services Correlation IDs, distributed tracing, central logs Micrometer Tracing + OpenTelemetry (8.9) Deployment Containers, orchestration, progressive delivery Docker, Kubernetes, Helm/Kustomize, Argo/Flagger canaries Security between services mTLS, OAuth2 client credentials Istio/Linkerd service mesh, Spring Security (8.2) A few terms from the table: - Saga — a long business process split into local steps. Each step has a compensation (an undo step) if a later step fails. In choreography , services react to each other's events. In orchestration , one coordinator tells each service what to do. - CQRS — keep separate models for writing and for reading. The read model is built from events. - Strangler fig — named after a plant that slowly grows around a tree. You move features out of the monolith one route at a time. - Canary — send a small share of traffic to the new version first. How does it work? Draw service boundaries around business capabilities , also called bounded contexts : Ordering, Loyalty, Incentives, Notifications, Catalogue. - Each service owns its own data. - It publishes events when its data changes. - Other services keep a local copy of what they need, instead of calling synchronously for everything. The copy may be a little behind for a short time. This is called eventual consistency . Think of the departments in a big hospital. Billing, pharmacy and lab each keep their own records. When the lab finishes a test, it sends a slip to billing. Billing does not walk into the lab and read its register. Example When would I use it? When teams and domains are large enough that independent deployment and scaling pay for the extra complexity. For a small team or a new product, a modular monolith is often the better senior answer. That means one deployable app with clear internal modules. Extract a module into a service only when its scaling or ownership needs become different from the rest. What can go wrong? - Distributed monolith. Services must be deployed together, and they call each other synchronously in long chains. Latency adds up. Availability multiplies down: 5 services at 99.9% each, called in series, give about 99.5% (0.999⁵). - Shared database between services. This is hidden coupling. One team's schema change breaks another team's service. - Chatty APIs (N calls to render one page), missing timeouts, no idempotency, and data that drifts apart with no reconciliation job. - Operational load without platform support — no proper CI/CD, observability or on-call setup for each service. Interview questions Q1. Monolith vs microservices — how do you decide? Weigh the benefits — team size, clear domain boundaries, need for independent scaling and deployment — against the costs: operational complexity, network failure modes and data consistency. Start with a modular monolith, and split along bounded contexts when it is justified. Q2. How do services stay consistent without distributed transactions? Use local transactions plus events (the outbox pattern), sagas with compensation steps, idempotent consumers and reconciliation jobs. You accept eventual consistency. Q3. What does an API gateway do? Routing, authentication and token validation, rate limiting, TLS termination, request shaping, CORS, observability and canary routing. It should contain no business logic.

t: 8.11 The Java project — your proof of the switch
x: In simple words: Build one real Spring Boot service from your own loyalty domain. It proves you can write production Java, and it gives you strong stories for every interview round. Build this in Weeks 8–12. Use the Sunday 2-hour slots, plus whatever spare time you find. It is deliberately taken from your own domain. So every interview question about it lands on ground you already know well. Loyalty Ledger Service — spec Purpose : a multi-tenant points ledger. It supports: - accrual (from order events); - redemption (through the API); - reversal; - expiry; - balance queries. It must stay correct under retries and concurrency — no double postings, no negative balances. Stack : Java 21, Spring Boot 3.x, PostgreSQL, Spring Data JPA, Flyway, Kafka, Redis, Resilience4j, Spring Security (JWT resource server), Testcontainers, Docker Compose, GitHub Actions. Endpoints Method Path Notes --- --- --- POST /api/v1/accounts Creates an account for a tenant + outlet GET /api/v1/accounts/{id}/balance Cached in Redis; evicted when the balance changes POST /api/v1/accounts/{id}/redemptions Idempotency-Key header is required; returns 201 / 422 / 409 POST /api/v1/accounts/{id}/reversals Reverses a ledger entry by its id GET /api/v1/accounts/{id}/ledger?after=<cursor Keyset pagination (page by "after this id", not by offset) — Kafka order-completed Idempotent consumer → accrual — Kafka points-events Published through the outbox — Daily 02:00 IST job Expires points older than N months (ShedLock) Schema (Flyway V1) Key points of the schema: - CHECK (balance = 0) — the database itself refuses a negative balance. - UNIQUE (tenant id, idempotency key) — the same request can never create two ledger entries. - The index on (account id, created at DESC, id DESC) serves the keyset-paginated ledger query. - The partial index on outbox covers only unpublished rows, so the relay's poll stays fast. Package layout Milestones 1. Week 8: create the repo; Docker Compose with Postgres, Kafka and Redis; Flyway V1; the Account + LedgerEntry entities; create/get endpoints; CI running the tests. 2. Week 9: redemption with an idempotency key + an atomic conditional debit (one SQL update that subtracts only if the balance is enough); ProblemDetail errors; validation. 3. Week 10: reversal; keyset pagination; the concurrency integration test (20 threads); a note in the README comparing optimistic locking with the atomic update. 4. Week 11: the Kafka idempotent accrual consumer; the outbox table + relay (a @Scheduled poller that publishes unpublished rows); the DLT. 5. Week 12: Redis balance cache; Resilience4j around a fake "rewards catalogue" client; JWT security; Actuator + Prometheus metrics; a k6 load test (record p95 and throughput); a README with an architecture diagram and trade-offs. README must contain : - an architecture diagram; - how idempotency works, in both the API and the consumer; - why you chose an atomic SQL update over @Version for the balance, and when you would choose each; - the concurrency test; - the load-test numbers; - what you would do next at 10× scale — partition the ledger by tenant, add read replicas, use CDC instead of polling the outbox. Say this: "At FieldAssist the loyalty workflows run on .NET. To make my Java switch concrete I rebuilt the core of that ledger in Spring Boot — idempotent redemption, an idempotent Kafka consumer, transactional outbox, and a test that fires 20 concurrent redemptions and proves we never overdraw."

Why? In simple words: The four OOP pillars are not definitions to recite. They are questions you ask while designing. If your design skips one, the interviewer will notice and ask about it. Interviewers will not ask you to define encapsulation. Instead, they watch whether your design actually uses it. Each pillar answers one design question. If you forget a pillar, the design shows a clear warning sign. This warning sign is called a smell . Interviewers know these smells well, and they will dig into them. What is happening internally? The table shows the question each pillar answers, and the smell you see when it is missing. Pillar Design question it answers Smell when missing --- --- --- Encapsulation Who owns this data, and who checks its rules? Public setters everywhere; logic sits in "manager" classes that change other objects' fields directly Abstraction What does the caller really need to know? Callers depend on concrete classes and their inner details Inheritance Is this truly an "is-a" relationship, with shared behaviour that rarely changes? Very deep class trees; subclasses override methods just to throw UnsupportedOperationException Polymorphism How do I add a new type without editing old code? if/else or switch on type codes copied all over the codebase Rich vs anaemic domain model - In a rich model , behaviour lives next to the data it protects. For example, account.debit(points) itself refuses to let the balance go negative. - In an anaemic model , entities are just bags of data. Services read the fields, do the calculation and write the values back. So every service must remember every rule. If one service forgets, the rule is broken. Think of a bank locker. In a rich model, the locker has its own lock and checks your key. In an anaemic model, the locker is an open box, and every staff member must remember to check your key. How does it work? While designing, ask three questions for each class: 1. What rules ( invariants — things that must always be true, like "balance is never negative") does this class own? 2. What is the smallest public API that still lets callers do their job? 3. Where will change come from? New types, new rules, new channels? Put an interface exactly at the place where change will come from — and nowhere else. Example When would I use it? In every LLD answer. Say these things out loud: - which class owns which rule, - where the abstraction boundary is (what callers can and cannot see), and - how a new variant plugs in without editing old code. What can go wrong? - Over-abstraction: making an interface for every class "just in case". - Fake encapsulation: thinking that private fields with getters and setters is encapsulation. It is not, if anyone can still set any value. - Inheritance only to reuse code: using extends just to borrow methods, when there is no real "is-a" relationship. Interview questions Q1. How do OOP principles show up in your design? Encapsulation: each entity checks and protects its own rules (invariants). Abstraction: callers depend on interfaces such as PaymentGateway , not on concrete classes. Polymorphism: a new variant is just a new class. Inheritance: I use it only for a real is-a relationship; otherwise I use composition (one object holding another). Q2. What's an anaemic domain model and why is it a smell? It is a model where entities have only data plus getters and setters, and all the logic sits in services. It is a smell because no class owns the rules. So rules get copied into many services, or someone forgets them.

t: 9.2 Class relationships and UML in interviews
x: Why? In simple words: Draw a quick box-and-arrow picture of your classes before you code. It gets you and the interviewer on the same page, and the arrows show who owns what. A quick class diagram takes about five minutes. It makes sure you and the interviewer agree on the design before you write code. The relationship types are association, aggregation, composition, inheritance and dependency. Using them correctly tells the interviewer you understand ownership and lifecycles . Ownership means "who is in charge of this object". Lifecycle means "when it is created and when it is deleted". These two things decide which class creates and deletes which object. What is happening internally? Relationship Meaning Java shape UML --- --- --- --- Dependency Uses another class for a short time A method parameter or a local variable dashed arrow Association Knows about another object A field that points to another object plain line Aggregation Has-a; the part can live on its own A field holding objects created somewhere else ( Team → Player ) hollow diamond at the whole Composition Owns; the part dies when the whole dies The whole creates and manages its parts ( Order → OrderLine ) filled diamond at the whole Inheritance Is-a extends hollow triangle Realisation Implements an interface implements dashed line + hollow triangle Multiplicity means "how many objects are on each side of the link". You write it as 1 , 0..1 , (any number) or 1.. (one or more). A simple way to remember aggregation vs composition: a cricket team has players, but if the team is dissolved, the players still exist (aggregation). A tiffin box has compartments, and if you throw away the box, the compartments go with it (composition). How does it work? 1. Draw a box for each class. 2. In the box, write the class name, 2–4 key fields and the key methods. 3. Draw the arrows between boxes. 4. Mark interfaces with «interface». 5. Do not draw getters, setters or every field. 6. Spend five to eight minutes at most. Example When would I use it? - At the start of every LLD round, right after you clarify the requirements. - In behavioural rounds, when you explain the design of a system you built. What can go wrong? - Spending 20 minutes making a perfect diagram. - Drawing implementation details instead of the main structure. - Forgetting multiplicities. These matter because they decide your data structures. For example, "1.. spots" means you need a collection of spots, keyed by spot type. Interview questions Q1. Aggregation vs composition? Both are has-a relationships. In composition, the whole owns the part's lifecycle — an order's lines are deleted with the order. In aggregation, the part lives independently — players still exist after a team is broken up. Q2. Association vs dependency? Association is a lasting link in the structure, usually a field. Dependency is short-term use, usually a method parameter or a local variable.

Why? In simple words: A class should do one kind of job, for one kind of person. Then a change asked by one team touches only that team's class. Suppose one class does many jobs. Then it changes for many reasons. A tax rule change, a database change and an email template change all edit the same file. Because of this: - Different people's changes clash in code reviews. - A change for one reason can break something unrelated. SRP keeps each class focused on one job. So changes stay local, and testing is simple. What is happening internally? The rule is: "A class should have one reason to change." "One reason" means one actor — one person, team or concern that asks for changes. Examples: finance rules, saving to the database ( persistence ), or how things look on screen ( presentation ). So you split responsibilities by who asks for changes . You do not split them by counting methods. How does it work? 1. Look at a class. 2. List everyone who could ask for a change to it. 3. If there is more than one such stakeholder, split the class along those lines. 4. Add a small coordinator class that calls the pieces in the right order. Example When would I use it? Split a class when you see any of these signs: - It has grown beyond about 200–300 lines. - It has unrelated dependencies — for example a repository and an SMTP (email) client and a PDF library. - Its tests need many unrelated mocks. What can go wrong? You can over-split. Dozens of one-method classes are hard to find your way around. Group by cohesion instead: things that change together should stay together. Interview questions Q1. Explain SRP with an example. Each class should have one reason to change. For invoices, I keep calculation (finance rules), persistence (database), PDF rendering and delivery (email) in separate classes. A workflow class coordinates them.

Why? In simple words: When you need a new type of something, you should add a new class — not edit an old, tested switch . Old code stays safe; new code plugs in. Imagine every new reward type, payment method or notification channel means editing one central switch . Each edit can break the cases that already work. So you must retest all of them every time. OCP says code should be open for extension, closed for modification . In plain words: add new behaviour by adding new code, not by editing code that is already tested. What is happening internally? 1. Each place where behaviour varies (a variation point ) becomes an abstraction — an interface. 2. Each variant becomes one class that implements this interface. 3. The core logic depends only on the interface. 4. The core logic receives the variants from outside — through dependency injection or a registry (a lookup map). So polymorphism replaces the if/else chains. Think of a mobile charger socket. The socket stays the same. To support a new phone, you buy a new cable that fits the socket — you do not rewire the wall. How does it work? 1. Find a switch or if-else on a type code that keeps growing. 2. Pull out an interface with the operation that varies. 3. Move each branch into its own class. 4. Pick the right class at runtime from a map or a factory. Example When would I use it? Wherever you expect new variants to keep coming: pricing, fees, rule types, channels, export formats, payment providers. What can go wrong? You may predict change that never comes. This is speculative abstraction . It breaks YAGNI — "You Aren't Gonna Need It". So apply OCP where change has already happened, or is clearly planned. Interview questions Q1. Explain OCP with an example from your work. In our incentive and reward system, each new rule type is a new Strategy class, registered by its type name. The evaluation engine does not change when we add a type.

Why? In simple words: A child class must behave the way its parent promised. If code works with the parent, it must still work when you pass in the child. Polymorphism only works if every subtype can replace its base type without surprising the caller. Suppose a subclass breaks the base class's promise (its contract ). For example, it throws where the base does not, ignores an input, or gives a weaker guarantee. Then bugs appear in other code — code that was correct — far away from the subclass. These bugs are hard to trace. What is happening internally? A subtype must keep the base type's contract . This means four things: 1. No stronger preconditions. A precondition is what the method needs before it runs. The subtype must accept at least everything the base accepts. 2. No weaker postconditions. A postcondition is what the method promises after it runs. The subtype must promise at least what the base promises. 3. Keep the invariants. Rules that are always true for the base must stay true. 4. No new surprise exceptions. Do not throw exceptions that callers of the base would not expect. Think of a substitute driver for your office cab. You don't care who drives, as long as he follows the same route and reaches on time. If the substitute refuses to take the highway, the "substitute" has broken the deal. How does it work? Test it with this question: "Can every caller of the base type use this subtype correctly, without knowing it is a subtype?" If callers need instanceof checks or special cases, LSP is broken. To fix it, redesign the hierarchy. Use separate interfaces for separate capabilities. Example When would I use it? - When you design class hierarchies. - When you review subclasses that override a method only to throw or to do nothing. What can go wrong? Using inheritance because something is "is-a" in English. A square is a rectangle in maths class. But in code, a Square cannot behave like a Rectangle , because its width and height cannot change separately. What matters is whether one can safely replace the other in code — this is called behavioural substitutability . Interview questions Q1. What is LSP and give a violation? You must be able to use a subtype anywhere the base type is expected, without breaking correctness. Two classic violations: Square overriding Rectangle 's setters so width and height change together, and a subclass that throws UnsupportedOperationException for a base-class method.

Why? In simple words: Don't make one giant interface for everything. Make small interfaces, so each class implements only what it can really do, and each caller sees only what it really uses. A "fat" interface has too many methods. This causes two problems: 1. Every class that implements it must provide methods it cannot support. Usually it just throws for them. 2. Every client depends on methods it never calls. So a change to an unrelated method still affects it. What is happening internally? Split a large interface into small role interfaces . Each role interface covers one need of one kind of client. - One class can implement several roles. - A client depends only on the role it uses. Think of a restaurant menu. A tea stall does not need to print the full five-star menu and then write "not available" next to most items. It prints only what it serves. How does it work? 1. Group the methods by which client calls them. 2. Turn each group into its own interface. Example When would I use it? - When an interface has many methods, and some implementations leave methods empty or make them throw. - When read clients and write clients are different. This read/write split is also the basis of CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation — separate models for writes and reads). What can go wrong? Splitting into one method per interface with no reason. Keep each interface cohesive — its methods should belong together. Interview questions Q1. What is ISP? Clients should not depend on methods they don't use. So I prefer small, role-specific interfaces over one fat interface.

Why? In simple words: Your business logic should not know which SMS company or which database you use. It talks to an interface it owns; the SMS or database code plugs into that interface from outside. Suppose business logic directly creates infrastructure objects, like new TwilioClient() or new PostgresRepo() . Then two problems follow: - Every infrastructure change ripples into business code. - You cannot test the business logic without the real infrastructure. DIP fixes this. It makes both sides depend on an abstraction (an interface), and the business side owns that interface. What is happening internally? 1. The high-level policy (for example, the redemption rules) defines ports . A port is an interface the business needs, such as NotificationSender or LedgerRepository . 2. The low-level details (Twilio, Postgres) implement these ports. These implementations are called adapters . 3. Now the source-code dependency points from the detail to the abstraction. Normally the business code would point to the detail. This direction is now flipped — that is the "inversion". This idea is the core of hexagonal architecture (also called ports and adapters ) and of clean architecture. DI containers like Spring connect the adapters to the ports for you (6.2). Think of a wall plug socket. The socket's shape is fixed by the house, not by the appliance. Any appliance — a fan, a mixer, a phone charger — makes its plug fit the socket. How does it work? The diagram shows the dependency before and after. Example When would I use it? At every boundary with infrastructure or outside systems: the database, messaging, HTTP partners, clocks, file storage. What can go wrong? - Leaky interfaces: the interface copies one vendor's API exactly. Then the abstraction leaks that vendor's concepts into your business code. - Needless interfaces: making interfaces for internal classes that will never have a second version. Interview questions Q1. Explain DIP. Both high-level and low-level modules depend on abstractions. The high-level (business) side owns these abstractions. The low-level details implement them and are injected from outside. Q2. DIP vs DI? DIP is a design principle — it is about which direction dependencies point. DI (dependency injection) is a technique — you pass dependencies in from outside instead of creating them inside. Containers like Spring automate DI.

Why? In simple words: Some objects should exist only once in the whole program. A Singleton makes sure only one is ever created, and everyone shares it. Some things must exist exactly once per process. Examples: a configuration registry, an ID generator, a metrics registry. If you create many of them, you waste resources. Worse, each copy may hold different data, so the state becomes inconsistent. For example, two ID generators could hand out the same ID. What is happening internally? The class hides its constructor, so nobody else can call new . It gives out one shared instance instead. In Java, the safe versions depend on guarantees from the JVM: - Holder idiom: the JVM loads a class only when it is first used (lazy), and it does this in a thread-safe way. So a static field inside a nested holder class is created once, safely, on first use. - Enum: each enum constant is created exactly once. Java also protects enums from the two common attacks on singletons — creating a second copy using reflection, or by serialising and deserialising. How does it work? Example long id = IdGenerator.INSTANCE.next(); . In Spring, you rarely write singletons yourself. Every bean is already a singleton per container by default. Spring injects it wherever it is needed, and you can replace it with a fake in tests. When would I use it? - In plain Java (LLD rounds without Spring): for stateless utilities or truly global resources. - In Spring apps: prefer singleton-scoped beans instead. What can go wrong? - Hidden global state: tests share the same instance, so one test can affect another. - Tight coupling: calls like X.getInstance() all over the code cannot be mocked easily. - Thread safety: if the singleton holds data that changes (mutable), you must make it thread-safe. - Bad lazy initialisation: if you create it lazily without proper synchronisation, two threads can create two instances. Or one thread can see a half-built object. Interview questions Q1. How do you implement a thread-safe singleton? Use an enum singleton, or the holder idiom. Another option is double-checked locking with a volatile field. Q2. Why are singletons criticised? They create global state that can change, hide dependencies, make testing hard and couple code tightly. A single instance supplied through dependency injection avoids these problems.

t: 9.9 Factory patterns: simple factory, factory method, abstract factory
x: Why? In simple words: A factory is one place that decides which class to create and how to set it up. The rest of the code just asks the factory and gets an object. Suppose new ConcreteClass() is written all over the code. Two problems follow: - Callers are tied to concrete types. - The creation logic is copied everywhere — which class to pick for which input, and how to configure it. A factory puts this in one place. It decides which class to create and how . Think of a railway reservation counter. You say "Sleeper, Delhi to Varanasi". The clerk decides which coach and berth to give you. You don't walk into the train and pick a seat yourself. What is happening internally? There are three kinds of factory: - Simple factory. It is not an official GoF ("Gang of Four" design patterns book) pattern, but it is the most common. A static method picks the class based on a parameter. - Factory Method (GoF). An abstract creator class declares a create() method. Subclasses decide which concrete product to return. The creator's other logic works only with the product interface. - Abstract Factory (GoF). An interface that produces a family of related products that must be used together. For example, all the components for one payment provider. How does it work? Example When would I use it? - When the concrete type depends on input or configuration — vehicle type, file format, provider. - When creating the object is complex. - When a family of objects must match each other. In Spring, a Map<String, Bean registry often replaces a hand-written factory (6.4). What can go wrong? - Factories that grow a giant switch . Combine the factory with a registry (a map from key to implementation) instead. - Abstract factories for families that never actually change. Interview questions Q1. Factory Method vs Abstract Factory? Factory Method lets subclasses decide one product type. Abstract Factory creates a whole family of related products through one interface. Q2. Factory vs Builder? A factory decides which class to create, usually in one step. A builder constructs one complex object step by step.

Why? In simple words: When an object has many optional settings, a Builder lets you set them one by one, by name, and then gives you a finished object that cannot be changed. Objects with many optional parameters usually end up in one of two bad shapes: 1. Telescoping constructors — long constructors like new Notification(to, null, body, null, 5, true, null) . You cannot tell which argument is which. 2. Setter-based objects that can change. These can be left half-configured. A builder fixes both. It gives readable, named, step-by-step construction, with validation. The end result is an immutable object — one that cannot change after it is built. Think of ordering a dosa at a counter. You say "masala, extra butter, no onion". The cook checks the order makes sense, then hands you the finished plate. You don't get a half-made dosa. What is happening internally? 1. A static nested Builder class holds the settings while you configure them. These settings can change. 2. Each setter-like method returns this . So you can chain calls one after another. This is called a fluent interface . 3. build() checks rules that involve more than one field (cross-field rules). 4. Then build() calls the private constructor of the immutable target class. How does it work? Example (Lombok's @Builder generates this same pattern for you. Records with only a few fields usually don't need a builder.) When would I use it? - Objects with 4 or more parameters, where several are optional. - Immutable configuration objects and request objects. - Test data builders. What can go wrong? - No validation in build() — so invalid objects can be created again. - Builders for 2-field objects — just noise. - build() returning an object that can still change (mutable). Interview questions Q1. When do you use a Builder? For complex objects with many optional parameters. It gives readable construction, validation inside build() , and an immutable result.

Why? In simple words: Instead of building a complex object from zero each time, keep one ready-made sample and make copies of it, changing only what is different. Sometimes creating an object from scratch is costly or complicated. For example, it is loaded from config, or it has many nested settings. And you often need many similar copies with small changes. Examples: campaign templates, document templates, game units. Think of a wedding invitation card. The printer designs one card. For each guest, he only changes the name — he does not redesign the card each time. What is happening internally? 1. You keep one fully configured object. This is the prototype . 2. You create new objects by copying it. 3. Then you customise the copy. In Java, prefer copy constructors or copy() / with… methods. Avoid Object.clone() , because: - it makes a shallow copy by default, - it needs the Cloneable marker interface, and - it skips the constructor, so your constructor's checks don't run. How does it work? Example CampaignTemplate diwali = festiveTemplate.copyFor("Diwali 2026"); — you set up one template, then stamp out a copy for each tenant or season. When would I use it? - Templates. - Cloning objects that are already configured. - Undo snapshots (together with the Memento pattern). What can go wrong? - Shallow copies share the nested objects that can change. So changing one copy also changes the other. - The pitfalls of clone() listed above. Interview questions Q1. Shallow vs deep copy in Prototype? A shallow copy shares the nested mutable objects with the original. A deep copy makes its own copies of them. I prefer immutable components or explicit copy constructors, so sharing is safe.

Why? In simple words: An Adapter is like a travel plug adapter. Your laptop charger has one shape, the wall socket has another, and the adapter sits in between so both work without changing either. Sometimes you must connect to an outside API (a third-party API) or an old system (a legacy system). Its methods do not match what your code expects. For example: - An SMS vendor's SDK has strange method names and its own number-based error codes. - An old SOAP service sends and receives data in a different format. You do not want the vendor's classes spread all over your business code. If they spread, changing the vendor later means touching many files. You want to swap vendors later with one small change. What is happening internally? An adapter is a small class that sits between your code and the vendor: 1. It implements your interface. This is called the target . 2. Inside, it holds the vendor class. This is called the adaptee . 3. When your code calls the adapter, it translates the call for the vendor. It converts method names, parameters, data formats and errors. This is composition : the adapter wraps (holds) the adaptee. It does not extend it. How does it work? RedemptionService only knows about the SmsSender interface. The adapter implements that interface and forwards each call to the vendor client. Example In the code below, the adapter does two translations. First, it changes the phone format (removes the + ). Second, it turns the vendor's number error code into a proper Java exception. When would I use it? - Every third-party integration: payment gateways, SMS/WhatsApp providers, partner APIs. - Connecting to legacy (old) systems. - Making several different providers fit behind one common interface. What can go wrong? - Leaking vendor details. If vendor types or vendor exceptions come out of the adapter, your business code depends on the vendor again. - Business logic creeping in. Adapters slowly collect business rules. Keep them thin — they should only translate. Interview questions Q1. What does an Adapter do? It converts one interface into a different interface that the client expects. It wraps the incompatible class and translates the calls, the data and the errors.

Why? In simple words: A Decorator wraps an object to add one extra feature, like putting a gift wrap on a box. You can wrap the same box many times, and each layer adds something. You want to add behaviour to an object. For example: - Add tax on top of a price. - Add logging or caching around a client. - Add compression around a stream. You also want to choose the combination at runtime. Without Decorator, you would need a subclass for every combination: TaxedDiscountedPrice , LoggedCachedClient , and so on. The number of classes explodes. What is happening internally? A decorator has three properties: 1. It implements the same interface as the object it wraps. 2. It holds a reference to that wrapped object. 3. It adds its own behaviour before or after passing the call on ( delegating ) to the wrapped object. Because the decorator has the same interface, you can wrap a decorator inside another decorator. So decorators can be stacked . Java I/O is the classic example: new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(f))) . Each layer adds one feature. How does it work? The outer layer calls the inner layer, gets its result, and changes it. Here, the base price goes in, then the discount is applied, then GST is added. Example The order is ₹100 (10,000 paise). The 10% discount makes it 9,000. Then 18% GST makes it 10,620. When would I use it? - Pricing pipelines (base price → discount → tax). - Common behaviour around clients, such as retry, cache and metrics. These are called cross-cutting concerns. Spring often does this with AOP proxies. - Stream processing. - Add-ons, such as an extra shot on a coffee (10.16). What can go wrong? - Order matters. Tax-then-discount does not give the same result as discount-then-tax. - Long chains are hard to debug. You must step through many layers to find the bug. - Broken contract. A decorator might behave differently from what the interface promises. Interview questions Q1. Decorator vs inheritance? Decorators add behaviour at runtime by wrapping objects (composition), and you can combine them freely. Inheritance fixes behaviour at compile time, and you need a new subclass for every combination, so the number of classes explodes.

Why? In simple words: A Proxy is a stand-in that sits in front of the real object. Like a receptionist, it decides who gets through, may answer some questions itself, and only calls the real person when needed. Sometimes you need to control access to an object without changing the object itself. You may want to: - Create it only when it is first needed ( lazy loading ). - Cache its results. - Check permissions before allowing a call. - Count or log calls. - Represent a remote object as if it were local. A proxy stands in for the real object and does these jobs. What is happening internally? A proxy implements the same interface as the real object (the real subject ). For every call, it decides whether, when and how to pass the call to the real object. Common types of proxy: - Virtual proxy : creates the real object lazily, only on first use. - Caching proxy : remembers results and returns them without calling the real object again. - Protection proxy : checks access before forwarding the call. - Remote proxy : a local stub that hides a network call. - Smart reference : adds counting or logging. You use proxies daily without noticing. Spring AOP, Hibernate lazy-loaded entities and Spring Data repositories are all proxies (6.7, 7.8). How does it work? The structure looks the same as Decorator. The difference is the purpose ( intent ): - A decorator adds features . The client builds the chain of decorators itself. - A proxy controls access . It usually hides the fact that it exists — the client thinks it is talking to the real object. Example CachingCatalogProxy saves each product after the first slow network call. TenantGuardProxy blocks SKUs that are not in this tenant's catalogue. When would I use it? - Caching layers. - Lazy loading of heavy objects. - Access control. - Stubs for remote services. - Wrappers for metrics and tracing. What can go wrong? - Unbounded caching. A caching proxy with no size limit keeps growing. This is a memory leak. - Hidden cost. A simple-looking method call may actually be an expensive remote call behind the proxy. - Self-invocation. When an object calls its own method ( this.method() ), the call does not go through the proxy. So the proxy's behaviour (for example, a transaction) is skipped. Interview questions Q1. Proxy vs Decorator vs Adapter? A Proxy keeps the same interface and controls access. A Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behaviour. An Adapter changes the call to a different interface.

Why? In simple words: A Facade is one simple front door to a complicated system. Like a hotel reception desk, you make one request and it coordinates housekeeping, kitchen and billing for you. Placing an order touches five subsystems: inventory reservation, pricing, payment, loyalty accrual and notification. Now imagine every client does this coordination itself — the mobile API, the partner API and the admin tool. Two problems follow: 1. The same coordination code is copied in three places. 2. Every client depends on the details of all five subsystems. This is called tight coupling . What is happening internally? A facade gives one simple, high-level method over a complex subsystem. ( Coarse-grained means one big call instead of many small ones.) The facade makes all the inner calls in the right order. The subsystems are still there. Code that really needs them can still call them directly. How does it work? All three clients call one method. The facade talks to the five subsystems. Example The steps are: 1. Reserve the stock. 2. Calculate the total price. 3. Charge the payment. 4. Confirm (commit) the stock reservation. 5. Add loyalty points. 6. Send the notification. If anything fails, the catch block releases the reserved stock. This undo step is called a compensation . When would I use it? - Application services that coordinate several domain services. - A simple SDK on top of a complex library. - BFF layers ( Backend for Frontend — one backend API shaped for one specific app). What can go wrong? - God class. The facade slowly collects all the business logic and becomes one huge class. - Hidden distributed-transaction problems. If the subsystems are separate microservices, one try/catch is not enough. You need a saga — a series of local steps, each with an undo step (11.15). Interview questions Q1. What problem does a Facade solve? It hides a complex subsystem behind one simple interface. This reduces coupling, and clients no longer copy the same coordination code.

Why? In simple words: Composite lets you treat one item and a group of items in the same way. A folder and a file both answer "what is your size?" — the folder just asks its children and adds up. Some data is a tree, where groups and single items must be handled the same way. Examples: - Folders and files. - Organisation charts. - Menus. - Product bundles. - Rule conditions joined with AND/OR. Without Composite, the client code is full of checks like "if it is a group, loop over it; else handle the single item". What is happening internally? There is one common interface, called the component . Two kinds of classes implement it: - Leaves : single items with no children. - Composites : containers that hold child components. When you call an operation on a composite, it calls the same operation on each child. Then it combines the results. Because a child can itself be a composite, this happens recursively down the tree. How does it work? The tree below means: sales must be at least 50,000, AND (visits at least 20 OR at least 5 new outlets). Example AllOf and AnyOf are composites. MinSales and MinVisits are leaves. The client just calls scheme.test(...) and does not care which is which. When would I use it? - Rules engines (10.12). - File systems. - Permission hierarchies. - Bundle pricing. - UI trees (a panel holding buttons and other panels). What can go wrong? - Deep recursion. A very deep tree can cause a stack overflow. - Type checks leaking into clients. If clients ask "is this a composite?", the pattern is not doing its job. - Cycles. If a node ends up as its own child, recursion never ends. Interview questions Q1. Where have you seen Composite? In rule trees that combine conditions with AND/OR, such as incentive schemes. Also in file systems and organisation charts.

Why? In simple words: Strategy means "put each way of doing a job in its own class, and plug in the one you need". Like choosing Ola, Uber or auto for the same trip — the trip stays the same, only the method changes. Often one step of the logic changes depending on the situation. Examples: - Parking fee depends on vehicle type. - Split rules in Splitwise (equal, exact, percentage). - Eviction policy in a cache (LRU, LFU). - Rate-limiting algorithm. - Pricing per tenant. If you hard-code all of these with if/else or switch , every new variant means editing old code. This breaks OCP (the Open/Closed Principle : open for adding, closed for editing). Strategy makes each algorithm a separate, pluggable object. It is the most-used pattern in LLD rounds. What is happening internally? There are three parts: 1. A strategy interface declares the operation. 2. Concrete strategies each implement it in their own way. 3. The context holds a strategy and passes the work to it. The strategy is either injected or picked from a registry (a map of strategies). It is simply polymorphism plus composition. How does it work? The parking lot does not know how fees are calculated. It just asks its FeeStrategy . Example HourlyFee rounds up to whole hours, with a minimum of one hour. ParkingTicketing keeps a map from vehicle type to fee strategy. How to justify it in an interview: "I used Strategy for fees because pricing varies independently of the parking flow, and I want to add weekend or event pricing without modifying ticketing logic." When would I use it? Use it for any behaviour that has several swappable versions: - Pricing, discounts, payouts. - Routing, ranking. - Retry policies. - Serialisation formats (JSON, XML, CSV). Simple strategies can just be lambdas, for example Function<Duration, Long . What can go wrong? - Too many strategies. Making a new class for a tiny difference is overkill. A parameter would do. - The giant switch moves. The client still picks the strategy with a big switch . Use a registry or a factory instead. Interview questions Q1. Strategy vs State? They have the same structure. In Strategy, the client chooses the strategy, and it stays fixed for the whole operation. In State, the state objects themselves move the context to other states as events happen. Q2. How does Strategy support OCP? A new algorithm is just a new class, registered with the context. The context and the existing strategies do not change.

Why? In simple words: Observer is a subscription system. Interested parties sign up once, and when something happens, everyone on the list is told — like a WhatsApp group getting a message. When an order is placed, many things must happen: - Loyalty must add points. - Inventory must update. - Notifications must go out. - Analytics must record it. If OrderService calls each of these directly, it depends on all of them. Every new reaction means editing OrderService again. Observer fixes this. Interested parties subscribe to events, and OrderService just announces what happened. What is happening internally? 1. The subject keeps a list of observers (also called listeners ). 2. When an event happens, the subject notifies each observer in the list. The direction of dependency is important. Observers depend on the subject's event type. The subject does not depend on the observers. - Inside one service (in-process): Spring gives you ApplicationEventPublisher and @EventListener (6.10). - Across services: the same idea becomes pub/sub messaging , for example Kafka topics (11.12). How does it work? Example Note two details in the code. First, CopyOnWriteArrayList lets you loop safely even if someone subscribes or unsubscribes at the same time. Second, each listener call is inside its own try/catch , so one bad listener cannot break the others or the order. When would I use it? - Separating side effects from the main action. - UI updates. - Domain events inside one service. - Low-stock alerts (10.16). Use durable messaging (such as Kafka) when the observers live in other services, or when they must never miss an event. What can go wrong? - Listener exceptions break the subject if not caught. - Slow listeners that run synchronously block the caller. - Memory leaks from listeners that are never unsubscribed. - Unclear ordering — you cannot be sure which listener runs first. - Lost events on crash — in-memory events disappear if the process dies, when they should have been stored durably. Interview questions Q1. Where is Observer used in Java/Spring? Spring application events and listeners, GUI listeners, and reactive streams. Across services, it becomes pub/sub messaging.

Why? In simple words: The State pattern gives each status its own class, and that class decides what is allowed next. Like a railway ticket: a "confirmed" ticket can be cancelled with refund, but a "journey done" ticket cannot. Some objects behave differently depending on their current state. Examples: orders, vending machines, elevators, tickets and trips. For example, you can cancel a paid order (with a refund), but you cannot cancel a shipped one. If you write if (status == …) inside every method, two problems follow: 1. The rules for moving between states ( transitions ) are scattered everywhere. 2. It is easy to make an illegal transition by mistake. What is happening internally? 1. Each state is its own class. All states implement one common interface, with one method per event (pay, ship, cancel). 2. The object (the context ) holds the current state object. 3. When an event arrives, the context passes it to the current state. 4. The state handles only the events it allows. It returns the next state — or rejects the event. For simple machines, you do not need classes. An enum with a transition table is enough. How does it work? Example The interface has default methods that throw an error. Each state class overrides only the events it allows. So any event not allowed fails automatically. In a database, enforce transitions with a conditional update: UPDATE orders SET status='PAID' WHERE id=? AND status='CREATED' . The WHERE status='CREATED' part makes it safe: - It is atomic — the check and the change happen as one step. - It is idempotent — running it twice has the same effect as running it once. The second run simply updates zero rows. When would I use it? Use it for lifecycles where each state has its own rules: - Orders and payments. - Trips (10.17). - Vending machines (10.7). - Elevators (10.8). - Approval workflows. - Ticket holds (10.10). What can go wrong? - Huge state classes. One state class grows too big. - Scattered transitions. Transition rules spread across many states and services. - Concurrent transitions without atomicity. Two threads both move PAID → CANCELLED at the same time, and the customer is refunded twice. Interview questions Q1. When do you use the State pattern instead of an enum? When each state has its own distinct behaviour and transitions involve real logic. For a simple status machine, an enum with a transition table is enough.

Why? In simple words: Command turns an action into an object — like a written order slip in a restaurant. Because it is written down, you can queue it, keep a record of it, repeat it, or cancel it. Sometimes you want to treat an action as data . Then you can: - Put it in a queue. - Log it. - Retry it. - Schedule it for later. - Undo it. Many systems need this: - Text editors (undo/redo). - Job queues. - Macro recording. - Ledgers, where accrue, redeem and reverse are stored as recorded operations. What is happening internally? A command object packs one request into an object ( encapsulates it). It holds: - What to do. - On which object (the receiver ). - With which parameters. - Optionally, how to undo it. There are two other roles: - The invoker runs commands and keeps the history. - The receiver does the real work. How does it work? The editor keeps a stack of commands it has run. Undo takes the last one off the stack and calls its undo() . Example The editor uses two stacks: 1. Running a command pushes it on the undo stack and clears the redo stack. 2. Undo pops from the undo stack, reverses the command, and pushes it on the redo stack. 3. Redo pops from the redo stack, runs it again, and pushes it back on the undo stack. When would I use it? - Undo/redo. - Job and task queues. - Scheduled operations. - Operations that must be recorded in an audit log. - Compensating actions in sagas — each step has an "execute" and a "compensate" (undo). - Command handlers in CQRS (a design that separates writes/commands from reads/queries). What can go wrong? - Undo is not a true reverse. If other changes happened since, simply undoing may give the wrong result. - Unbounded history. The history stack grows forever and uses up memory. - Heavy commands. Commands that hold large state use a lot of memory. Interview questions Q1. How would you implement undo/redo? Make each action a command with execute and undo . Keep an undo stack and a redo stack. When a new command is executed, clear the redo stack.

Why? In simple words: Chain of Responsibility passes a request through a line of checkers, one after another. Like airport security: ID check, then baggage scan, then body scan — anyone can stop you, and you can add or reorder checks easily. A request must pass through a series of checks or handlers. For example: - Authentication. - Validation. - Fraud check. - Geofence check (is the user inside the allowed area?). - Photo-evidence check. The set of steps and their order change over time. If you hard-code all of them in one method, the method becomes long and hard to change. What is happening internally? 1. All handlers implement one common interface. 2. They are linked in a chain. 3. Each handler does one of two things. Either it handles the request and stops the chain, or it does its part and passes the request to the next handler. Servlet filters and Spring Security's filter chain both use this pattern. How does it work? Example Each check throws an exception to reject the claim. If every check passes, the claim is accepted. The list order is the chain order, and you can configure it per tenant. (The classic version links each handler to the next one directly. A simple list of handlers, as above, is the modern and simpler form.) When would I use it? - Validation pipelines, such as Perfect Store evidence checks. - Request filters. - Approval workflows (escalate to the next approver). - Logging levels. - Middleware. What can go wrong? - Unhandled requests. A request reaches the end of the chain and nobody handled it — silently. - Hidden order rules. One handler depends on another running first, but nobody wrote that down. - Hard debugging. Long chains are hard to trace. Log which handler made the decision. Interview questions Q1. Where is Chain of Responsibility used in Spring? Servlet filters and the Spring Security filter chain. HandlerInterceptors work in a similar way.

Why? In simple words: Template Method fixes the order of steps in a parent class and lets child classes fill in only the steps that differ. Like a standard form where the layout is printed and you only fill in the blanks. Several processes often share the same skeleton (the same overall steps) but differ in a few steps. For example: - Every report job fetches data, transforms it, and publishes it. - Every import validates, parses, saves and audits. If you copy the skeleton into each job, the fixed parts are duplicated. Over time the copies drift apart and behave differently. What is happening internally? 1. An abstract base class defines the algorithm in one final method. This is the template method . Because it is final , subclasses cannot change the order. 2. The template method calls abstract steps. Subclasses must implement these. 3. It may also call hooks . These are optional steps with a default behaviour that subclasses can override. This version is based on inheritance. There is also a callback-based version, where you pass in lambdas instead of subclassing. Spring's JdbcTemplate and TransactionTemplate use this callback version. How does it work? run() is the fixed skeleton. fetch and publish are required steps. transform has a default. shouldPublish is a hook. Example class DailyRedemptionReport extends ReportJob { … fetch from ClickHouse, publish to S3 … } — you write only the steps that change. When would I use it? - Batch jobs. - Importers. - Framework extension points, such as OncePerRequestFilter.doFilterInternal and AbstractList . What can go wrong? - Deep class hierarchies. Many levels of inheritance become hard to follow. - Rigid skeleton. A subclass needs to change the skeleton itself. In that case, prefer composition — use Strategy for the steps instead. Interview questions Q1. Template Method vs Strategy? Template Method keeps a fixed skeleton and lets subclasses change individual steps (inheritance). Strategy swaps the whole algorithm by plugging in a different object (composition).
