The yearly statistics report (analytics) is made in a separate office so the front desk is not disturbed. How does it work? 1. Upload : the app asks the API for an upload. The API returns a pre-signed PUT URL. The app uploads straight to Blob. An event triggers processing, and a metadata row is saved. 2. Search : Postgres changes go through Debezium CDC into Kafka. An indexer writes them to Elasticsearch. The search API reads from Elasticsearch. 3. Analytics : data flows from Postgres/Kafka into ClickHouse (MergeTree tables, materialised views). Dashboards read from ClickHouse. Example Perfect Store audits: 1. Photos (2–5 MB each) go straight to Azure Blob through pre-signed URLs. 2. The audit row stores only the blob keys. 3. An AI verification worker processes the photos. 4. Compliance dashboards per region come from ClickHouse, not from the transactional database. When would I use it? - Object storage — for any user-uploaded media or documents. - Search engine — for product, outlet or text search. - OLAP (analytics store) — for dashboards and reports over a large history. What can go wrong? - Uploads through app servers. They use up memory and hit timeouts. - Public buckets. Anyone can read the files, so data leaks. - Search index drift. The index slowly differs from the source. You need reindexing and reconciliation (comparing and fixing). - Analytics on the OLTP primary. Heavy reports slow down live transactions. Interview questions Q1. How would you handle large file uploads? Give the client a pre-signed URL so it uploads directly to object storage, using multipart/resumable upload for big files. Keep metadata in the DB, start processing from storage events, and deliver files through a CDN. Q2. Why not use the database for full-text search? A search engine has inverted indexes, analysers and relevance scoring. It handles fuzzy, multilingual, ranked search at scale far better than SQL. Feed it via CDC, and keep the DB as the source of truth.

Why? In simple words: In a big system, something is always broken somewhere. Good design expects this, and makes sure one broken part can't take down everything else. At scale, something is always failing — a pod, a zone, a dependency or a deploy. Reliable systems assume failure will happen. They limit its blast radius — how much of the system one failure can damage. Interviewers expect you to discuss how each component you draw can fail. Think of a building with fuses on each floor. A short circuit on one floor trips that fuse only. The rest of the building keeps its lights on. What is happening internally? - Timeouts : put a timeout on every network call. Each timeout must be shorter than the caller's own timeout, so the whole chain fits in its timeout budget . - Retries : - Use exponential backoff (wait longer each time) with jitter (random spread, so clients don't retry together). - Retry only idempotent operations and transient errors (temporary ones, like a timeout). - Use retry budgets to avoid retry storms. - Circuit breakers : if a dependency is unhealthy, stop calling it for a while and fail fast (8.7). - Bulkheads : give each dependency its own thread or connection pool. Then one slow dependency can't use up everything. (The name comes from the walls inside a ship that stop water spreading.) - Graceful degradation : serve stale or cached data, or a smaller set of features. For example, hide recommendations but keep checkout working. - Load shedding : under overload, reject low-priority work early (429/503). This protects the core flows. - Redundancy : run N+1 instances (one more than you need) across availability zones. For critical paths, use multi-region active-passive (one region on standby) or active-active (both serve traffic). - Backups and DR (disaster recovery): - RPO (recovery point objective) — how much data you can afford to lose. - RTO (recovery time objective) — how fast you must be back up. These two numbers decide your replication and backup design. Test restores regularly. - Health checks : liveness ("is it alive?") vs readiness ("can it take traffic?") (8.9). - Safe deployments : - Rolling, blue-green or canary releases, with automatic rollback if the SLO is breached. - Feature flags. - Backward-compatible schema changes (7.16). - Coordination : leader election and distributed locks use etcd, ZooKeeper or Kubernetes leases. Always add fencing tokens . A fencing token is a number that goes up with every new lock. If an old lock holder was paused and wakes up with a stale lock, its writes carry an old number and get rejected. - Clocks : machine wall clocks drift apart. So don't order distributed events by timestamps alone. Use sequence numbers, partitions or logical clocks (counters that only go up). How does it work? For each box in your diagram, ask three questions: 1. What if it is slow? 2. What if it is down? 3. What if it is wrong (bad data, duplicate messages)? Then add the matching pattern and the alert for each answer. Example The voucher partner is down for 20 minutes during a festival campaign. Here is what happens: 1. The circuit breaker opens after 50% of calls fail. 2. Redemptions are still accepted and points are debited. 3. The saga parks the voucher step for a later retry. The user sees "voucher arriving shortly". 4. The bulkhead keeps the other APIs responsive. 5. The breaker goes half-open (lets a few test calls through). When they succeed, the backlog drains with rate limiting. 6. Alerts fire when the breaker opens and when the saga backlog gets too old. When would I use it? In the "failure handling" step of every design, and in production readiness reviews. What can go wrong? - Retry storms. Everyone retries at once and makes the outage worse. - Silent fallbacks. Fallbacks hide failures, and no alert fires. - Untested backups. You find out they don't restore only during a disaster. - Single-AZ deployments. One zone outage takes everything down. - Distributed locks without fencing. A stale lock holder can still write. - Deploys that can't roll back. A schema change makes the old version incompatible. Interview questions Q1. How do you prevent cascading failures? Use timeouts, limited retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding and graceful degradation. Together they stop one failing part from pulling down the services that call it. Q2. What are RPO and RTO? RPO is the maximum data loss you can accept, measured in time. RTO is the maximum time you can take to restore service. Together they decide your replication, backup and failover design. Q3. Why do distributed locks need fencing tokens? A client can pause (because of GC or the network) and its lock can expire while another client takes the lock. A token that always increases lets the resource reject writes from the old, stale holder.

Why? In simple words: Observability means you can see what your system is doing from the outside. SLOs turn "is it healthy?" into a clear number that everyone agrees on. You can't run what you can't see. And "is the system healthy?" needs an exact definition, based on what users experience. An SLO (service level objective) turns reliability into a measurable target. That target then guides your alerts and your release decisions. Think of a car dashboard. The speedometer and fuel gauge are your metrics. The rule "keep the speed under 80" is your objective. What is happening internally? - Metrics (Prometheus/Grafana, Azure Monitor): numbers measured over time. - RED per service: rate (requests/sec), errors, duration. - USE per resource: utilisation, saturation (how much work is waiting), errors. - Business KPIs. - Logs (ELK/OpenSearch/Loki): structured JSON, with trace, tenant and request IDs in every line. - Traces (OpenTelemetry → Jaeger/Tempo/App Insights): one request's journey across services, queues and DB calls, split into timed steps called spans . - SLI (service level indicator): what you measure. For example, "% of redemption requests completing successfully in < 500 ms". - SLO (objective): the target. For example, 99.9% over 30 days. - Error budget : 100% − SLO. Here that is 0.1%, which is about 43 minutes of "bad" per month. If the budget is burning fast, slow down releases and fix reliability. - SLA (service level agreement): the promise in the customer contract, with penalties. It is looser than the internal SLO, so you get warned before you break it. - Alerting on burn rate : page someone when the error budget is being used up fast. For example, 2% of the monthly budget in 1 hour. Don't page on every CPU spike. How does it work? 1. Instrument the code once (Micrometer/OpenTelemetry). 2. Build a dashboard for each service. 3. Define 2–4 SLOs for each critical user journey. 4. Alert on symptoms (what users feel), not on causes. 5. Link every alert to a runbook (a step-by-step fix guide). Example Loyalty SLOs: - Redemption availability: 99.9%. - Redemption p99 latency: < 800 ms (99% of requests finish faster than this). - Accrual freshness: 99% of order events appear in balances within 60 s. You measure this from consumer lag and event timestamps. When would I use it? From the first deploy of any service. Also in the "monitoring" step of every design interview. What can go wrong? - Alert fatigue. Alerts on causes (like CPU) fire all the time, so people start ignoring them. - Dashboards without SLOs. Lots of charts, but no clear "good or bad" line. - High-cardinality metrics cost. Labels with too many unique values (like user ID) make the metrics store huge and expensive. - Sampling away the traces you need. Use tail-based sampling — decide what to keep after the request ends, so errors and slow requests are always kept. Interview questions Q1. SLI vs SLO vs SLA? The SLI is the measured indicator. The SLO is the internal target for it. The SLA is the external promise in the customer contract. Q2. What is an error budget used for? It puts a number on how much unreliability is allowed. When it burns fast, alerts fire and feature releases slow down so the team can focus on reliability work.

Why? In simple words: Security means only the right person can do the right thing on the right data. In a multi-tenant system, the biggest job is making sure one company can never see another company's data. Security failures are the most expensive kind. They cause data breaches, fraud, regulatory penalties and lost customer trust. In a multi-tenant SaaS, many customer companies (tenants) share the same system. So one authorisation bug can show one brand's data to another brand. That is why designs are expected to cover security explicitly. Think of a bank locker room. The guard checks your ID at the door (authentication). Your key opens only your own locker (authorisation). Every visit is written in the register (audit). What is happening internally? - Authentication (who are you?): OAuth2/OIDC with an identity provider. JWT access tokens are validated at the gateway and in the services (8.2). - Authorisation (what can you do?): check roles and scopes. Also check resource- and tenant-level access on every query. The most common real-world vulnerability is broken access control — OWASP 1. - Transport : TLS everywhere. Use mTLS (both sides show certificates) between services, often through a service mesh. - Secrets : keep them in a vault (Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault) and rotate them. Never put them in code or images. - Data : - Encrypt data at rest. - For sensitive data, use field-level encryption or tokenisation (replace the real value with a stand-in token). This covers PII (personal data) and payment data. For cards, use a PSP (payment service provider). - Keep as little PII as possible, and mask it in logs. - Input : - Validate all input. - Use parameterised queries (stops SQL injection). - Encode output (stops XSS — cross-site scripting). - Protect URL fetches against SSRF (tricking your server into calling internal addresses). - Edge : WAF (web application firewall), DDoS protection and rate limits (11.16). - Audit : keep immutable (unchangeable) audit logs for sensitive actions, like admin adjustments and payouts. Add maker-checker approvals: one person makes the change, a second person approves it. - Webhooks and partners : signed requests, IP allow-lists and idempotency. How does it work? Threat-model each flow. That means asking: 1. Who can call it? 2. With which identity? 3. Which tenant's data does it touch? 4. What could an attacker replay or forge? 5. What gets logged? Example Admin points adjustment: 1. It needs ROLE ADMIN and the same tenant claim as the account. 2. It creates a pending adjustment (the maker). 3. A second admin approves it (the checker). 4. The ledger entry records both identities. 5. The action is audited. If it is above a threshold, an alert fires. When would I use it? In the API and data steps of every design. Also when reviewing any feature that touches money, PII or cross-tenant data. What can go wrong? - Trusting client-supplied tenant or user IDs. The client can simply change them. - Secrets in Git. Anyone with repo access, or a leak, gets them. - Verbose errors. Error messages leak internal details. - Logging tokens or PII. Logs become a security risk. - No rate limits on OTP/login. Attackers can guess codes or passwords. - Overly broad service credentials. One stolen credential opens too much. Interview questions Q1. How do you ensure tenant isolation in a multi-tenant system? Take the tenant from the authenticated token, never from the request body. Enforce it in authorisation checks, and apply mandatory tenant filters at the data layer — or use separate schemas/databases for strong isolation. Add tests that try cross-tenant access. Q2. What security measures would you add to a payments or points system? Strong auth, idempotency, maker-checker for manual adjustments, audit logs, encryption, rate limits, anomaly alerts and reconciliation.

Why? In simple words: When many servers create records at the same time, each record still needs a unique ID. The trick is to make IDs unique without all servers asking one central place every time. Orders, messages, events and short links all need unique IDs. There are two simple options, and both have problems: - One auto-increment database sequence. With many shards and regions, everyone waits on this one counter. It becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure (SPOF). - Random UUIDs. They are unique, but large and unordered. That is bad for B-tree index locality (new rows land all over the index) and for sorting by time. Think of restaurant token numbers. If each counter prints tokens starting with its own counter number, two counters can never give out the same token — and they don't need to talk to each other. What is happening internally? Approach Properties --- --- DB auto-increment / sequence Simple and ordered; a bottleneck/SPOF across shards UUIDv4 (random) No coordination needed; 128 bits; random → poor index locality UUIDv7 Starts with a timestamp, then randomness; no coordination; friendly to indexes Snowflake (Twitter) 64-bit: 1 sign bit + 41-bit millisecond timestamp (~69 years) + 10-bit machine ID (1,024 nodes) + 12-bit sequence (4,096 IDs per ms per node) → roughly sorted by time, compact Range allocation Each service instance leases a block (e.g., 1M IDs) from a coordinator and hands them out locally How does it work? Each node makes Snowflake IDs like this: 1. On each request, read the current millisecond. 2. If it is the same millisecond as last time, add 1 to the sequence. 3. If the sequence goes past 4,095 (overflows), wait for the next millisecond. 4. If it is a new millisecond, reset the sequence to 0. 5. Combine the parts: (timestamp − epoch) << 22 machineId << 12 sequence . The epoch is a fixed starting date. Subtracting it keeps the timestamp small enough to fit in 41 bits. Example When would I use it? - Snowflake-style or UUIDv7 IDs — for high-volume entities across shards: orders, events, messages, tweets (13.17). - Range allocation — for short-link codes (13.1). - DB sequences — when one database is enough. What can go wrong? - Duplicate machine IDs. Two nodes with the same ID can create the same IDs. Assign machine IDs through config, a coordinator or Kubernetes StatefulSet ordinals (each pod gets a fixed number). - Clock moving backwards. NTP (time sync) can move the clock back. Refuse to create IDs, or wait until the clock catches up. - Exposing sequential IDs publicly. Attackers can guess other IDs by counting (enumeration attacks). Use opaque public IDs instead. Interview questions Q1. How would you generate unique IDs across many servers? Use Snowflake-style IDs (timestamp + machine ID + sequence) or UUIDv7. Both are time-ordered and need no coordination. Use range leasing when IDs must be dense or short. Q2. Why are random UUIDs bad as primary keys in B-tree indexes? Random inserts land all over the index. This causes page splits, poor cache locality and larger indexes. Time-ordered IDs are added near the end of the index instead.

t: 12.1 Joins and how the engine executes them
x: Why? In simple words: A join stitches rows from two tables together using a matching column. Picking the right join gives the right answer. Knowing how the database runs the join tells you why the same query is fast today and slow tomorrow. Real questions almost always need more than one table. For example: - "Outlets that never placed an order." - "Each rep with their manager." - "Revenue per city." If you choose the right join type, you get the correct answer. If you also know how the engine executes the join, you can explain performance changes. The same query can be fast one day and slow the next, because the database picked a different way to run it. What is happening internally? There are two layers. First, the logical join type — what rows you want back: Join Returns --- --- INNER JOIN Only rows that have a match on both sides LEFT JOIN All left rows; the right-side columns are NULL where there is no match FULL OUTER JOIN All rows from both sides, with NULLs where there is no match CROSS JOIN Every left row paired with every right row (Cartesian product) Self join A table joined to itself (rep → manager) Semi join ( EXISTS , IN ) Left rows that have at least one match — each left row appears once, not duplicated Anti join ( NOT EXISTS ) Left rows that have no match at all Second, the physical algorithm — how the database actually does the matching. A component called the query planner picks the algorithm. It decides using table statistics : stored facts like row counts and how values are spread. Algorithm How it works Best when --- --- --- Nested loop For each row on the outer side, look up the matching inner rows (ideally using an index) The outer input is small and the inner side has an index Hash join Build a hash table from the smaller input, then check each row of the larger input against it Both inputs are large and unsorted, and the join uses equality ( = ) Merge join Both inputs are sorted on the join key; walk through them side by side Both inputs are already sorted (for example, by indexes), or large range joins Think of a nested loop like a shopkeeper checking each customer's name in a register. It is fast when there are only a few customers and the register has an alphabetical index. It is very slow for 10 lakh customers. How does it work? The planner works like this: 1. It estimates how many rows each step will produce. 2. It tries different join orders and different algorithms. 3. It gives each option a cost. 4. It picks the cheapest plan. The plan is only as good as the estimates. Estimates go wrong when statistics are old ( stale ), or when two columns are related in a way the planner does not know ( correlated columns ). Then the planner makes a bad choice. The most common bad choice is a nested loop that runs over far more rows than it expected. Example When would I use it? In every reporting query and API query that needs more than one table. Interviews often ask you to write anti joins, self joins and LEFT JOIN aggregations live, on the spot. What can go wrong? - NOT IN with NULLs. If the subquery returns even one NULL, NOT IN returns no rows at all. - LEFT JOIN filter in WHERE. A WHERE condition on the right table quietly turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN. - Accidental Cartesian product. You forget the join condition, so every row pairs with every other row. - Duplicate rows from a one-to-many join before aggregating. One outlet with ten orders becomes ten rows, so sums get multiplied. Aggregate first, then join. - Stale statistics. The planner thinks a table is small and picks a nested loop over millions of rows. Refresh statistics with ANALYZE in PostgreSQL or UPDATE STATISTICS in SQL Server. Interview questions Q1. Why NOT EXISTS instead of NOT IN? If the subquery returns even one NULL, NOT IN returns no rows at all. NOT EXISTS gives the correct result in that case, and the database usually runs it as an efficient anti join. Q2. Nested loop vs hash vs merge join? Use a nested loop when the outer input is small and the inner side has an index. A hash join suits large, unsorted inputs joined on equality. A merge join is best when both inputs are already sorted on the join key. Q3. Why does a LEFT JOIN sometimes behave like an INNER JOIN? For unmatched rows, the right table's columns are NULL. A WHERE condition on those columns removes exactly those rows. To keep them, move the condition into the ON clause.

Why? In simple words: A window function lets each row look at its neighbours — rows in the same group — and calculate something like a rank or a running total. Unlike GROUP BY, it does not squash the rows together; every row stays in the result. Many questions need a result on each row that depends on other rows. For example: - The rank of a rep within their team. - A running total of sales. - The previous month's value. - The top N items in each category. GROUP BY does not help here, because it collapses many rows into one. Self joins and correlated subqueries (a subquery that runs once per outer row) work, but they are slow and messy. Window functions solve this. They calculate over a "window" of related rows while keeping every row . They come up again and again in live SQL rounds. What is happening internally? The general shape is: What the engine does: 1. It sorts (or hashes) the rows by the partition key and the order key. 2. For each row, it works out the frame — the set of rows the function should look at. 3. It computes the function for that row over its frame. When windows run: they are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, but before ORDER BY and LIMIT. Because of this, you cannot filter on a window result in the WHERE of the same query. Wrap the query in a subquery or CTE, and filter outside. The main function families: - Ranking: ROW NUMBER (1,2,3,4 — always unique), RANK (1,2,2,4 — ties share a rank, then a gap), DENSE RANK (1,2,2,3 — ties share a rank, no gap), NTILE(n) (splits rows into n equal buckets). - Offsets: LAG (previous row's value), LEAD (next row's value), FIRST VALUE , LAST VALUE . - Aggregates over windows: SUM , AVG , COUNT , MIN , MAX . - Frame default: if you write ORDER BY but no frame, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW . RANGE treats rows with equal ORDER BY values (ties) as one group of "peers". So in a running total, all tied rows get the same total — which surprises people. To avoid this, write ROWS explicitly. Think of a class result sheet. Each student's row stays on the sheet, but next to it you write their rank within their own section. That is a window function with PARTITION BY section ORDER BY marks DESC . How does it work? Here, R2 and R3 tie at 700. DENSE RANK gives both rank 2, and the next rep gets 3 (no gap): Example For example 6, the trick is simple. Consecutive dates go up by one each day. Row numbers also go up by one each row. So date minus row number stays the same along a streak. When a day is missed, the value jumps. That constant value labels each streak, and you group by it. When would I use it? - Leaderboards and rankings (incentive standings). - Deduplication — keeping one row per group. - Period-over-period comparisons (this month vs last month). - Running balances and account statements. - Streaks and sessionisation (grouping events into sessions). - Percent-of-total reports. What can go wrong? - Filtering on a window column in WHERE. This is not allowed. Wrap the query in a subquery and filter outside. - LAST VALUE returns the current row. This happens because the default frame ends at the current row. Set the frame to ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING . - RANGE vs ROWS surprises with ties. Tied rows get the same running total under RANGE . - Huge sorts spill to disk on big partitions. The sort no longer fits in memory and becomes slow. An index on the partition and order keys helps. Interview questions Q1. ROW NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE RANK? ROW NUMBER gives a unique sequence (1,2,3,4). RANK lets ties share a rank and then leaves a gap (1,2,2,4). DENSE RANK lets ties share a rank with no gap (1,2,2,3). Q2. How do you get the top N rows per group? In a subquery or CTE, rank rows with PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC . Then, in the outer query, keep only rows where the rank is N or less. Q3. How do you compute a running total? Use SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY t ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) . Write ROWS explicitly so tied values don't get the same total.

Why? In simple words: A CTE gives a name to one step of a big query, so you can read the query top to bottom like a recipe. A recursive CTE repeats a step again and again — perfect for walking down a manager → team tree. Long queries with subqueries nested inside subqueries are hard to read and hard to debug. A common table expression (CTE) gives each step a name. Then the query reads from top to bottom, step by step. A recursive CTE goes further. It solves hierarchy problems — manager chains, category trees, distributor networks. Without recursion, you cannot solve these in a single query, because you don't know in advance how many levels deep the tree goes. What is happening internally? - A normal CTE ( WITH name AS (…) ) defines a named subquery that lives only for that one statement. - PostgreSQL 12 and later inline CTEs. This means the CTE is copied into the main query and optimised like a normal subquery. The exception is when you mark it MATERIALIZED — then it is computed once and stored. - SQL Server always inlines CTEs. - So a CTE is a readability tool, not a performance tool. - A recursive CTE has two parts joined by UNION ALL : - An anchor member — the starting rows. - A recursive member — a query that joins the CTE back to the table to find the next level. The engine runs it in a loop: 1. Run the anchor to get the first set of rows. 2. Feed those rows into the recursive member to get the next level. 3. Feed the new rows in again. 4. Stop when a step returns no new rows. Think of a family tree. You start with one grandparent (the anchor). Then you find their children, then the children's children, and so on — until a generation has no children. How does it work? Example When would I use it? - Breaking complex reports into named steps. - Organisation and sales hierarchies — for example, rolling incentives up to managers. - Bill-of-materials (a product made of parts, which are made of smaller parts). - Graph-like walks that don't go very deep. What can go wrong? - Infinite recursion on cyclic data. If bad data says A manages B and B manages A, the loop never ends. Add a depth limit, or keep an array of the path already visited and stop when you see a repeat. - Assuming CTEs are materialised (or not). Engines behave differently. Don't assume a CTE is computed once. - Very deep or very wide recursion on big tables. This gets slow. For large hierarchies, consider a closure table (a table storing every ancestor–descendant pair) or a materialised path (storing the full path like /1/42/7/ on each row). Interview questions Q1. What is a recursive CTE? It is a CTE with two parts: an anchor query that gives the starting rows, and a recursive query that refers back to the CTE. The engine repeats the recursive part until no new rows come out. It is used for hierarchies. Q2. Do CTEs improve performance? Usually no. Modern PostgreSQL and SQL Server inline them, so they run like normal subqueries. Their real benefit is readability. In PostgreSQL, use MATERIALIZED when you deliberately want the CTE computed once.

t: 12.4 Classic SQL interview problems and evaluation order
x: Why? In simple words: Live SQL rounds keep asking the same handful of problems. Learn the templates, and learn the order in which SQL runs each clause — then you can write them fast and explain why they work. Live SQL rounds reuse a small set of patterns: - Nth highest value. - Finding and deleting duplicates. - "Did it happen in every period?" (this is called relational division ). - Pivots — turning row values into columns. - Retention — who came back next month. If you know these patterns, and the logical order in which SQL runs, you can write them quickly and explain them clearly. What is happening internally? Logical evaluation order — the order SQL conceptually runs each clause. It explains many alias and filter errors: FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → window functions → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT/OFFSET What this means in practice: - WHERE runs before SELECT. So WHERE cannot see the aliases you define in SELECT. - WHERE runs before GROUP BY. So WHERE cannot filter on aggregates like SUM . Use HAVING for that. - Window functions run after WHERE. So you cannot filter on a window result at the same level. How does it work? First, recognise which pattern the question is. Then apply that pattern's template from the examples below. Example When would I use it? In SQL rounds, in analytics questions during system-design interviews, and in your daily reporting work. What can go wrong? - Using LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1 for Nth highest. This is wrong when there are ties. Use DENSE RANK instead. - COUNT(col) vs COUNT( ) with NULLs. COUNT(col) skips NULLs; COUNT( ) counts every row. - Comparing dates using a function on the column. For example DATE(created at) = … . This stops the index from being used — it is non-sargable (see 12.5). - Integer division in percentages. 5 / 10 gives 0 in integer maths. Multiply by 100.0 to force decimal maths. Interview questions Q1. WHERE vs HAVING? WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters whole groups after aggregation. Q2. Why can't I use a SELECT alias in WHERE? In the logical order, WHERE runs before SELECT, so the alias doesn't exist yet. Either repeat the expression in WHERE, or wrap the query and filter outside.

t: 12.5 How indexes work: B+ trees, clustered and covering indexes
x: Why? In simple words: An index is like the index at the back of a book. Instead of reading every page to find a word, you look it up and jump straight to the right page. Without it, the database reads the whole table. Without an index, the database must scan the whole table to find rows. The work grows with table size — O(n) disk pages. With the right index, a lookup reads only 3–4 pages, no matter how big the table is. Most "the API takes 30 seconds" problems are really index problems. And "why isn't my index being used?" is one of the top SDE2 database questions. What is happening internally? Relational database indexes are B+ trees . A B+ tree is: - Balanced — every path from the top to the bottom has the same length. - Very wide — each 8 KB page holds hundreds of keys. It has two kinds of pages: - Internal pages hold separator keys (signposts like "keys below 1000 go left") and pointers to child pages. - Leaf pages hold the actual keys in sorted order. Each leaf is linked to its neighbours. So a range scan finds the first leaf, then simply walks along the leaves in order. Because each page fans out to about 500 children, a billion rows need only about 4 levels. The top levels are used so often that they stay in memory. Think of a library. The signboard at the entrance tells you which floor. The floor sign tells you which shelf. The shelf has books in sorted order, and you can walk along it. Three or four steps, however big the library is. The main kinds of index: - Clustered index (SQL Server, MySQL InnoDB): the table rows themselves are the leaf level. Rows are stored in primary-key order. There can be only one per table. - Secondary indexes store the primary key, not a direct row address. So a lookup through a secondary index goes: index → primary key → row. SQL Server calls this a key lookup . - Random UUID primary keys land in random places. This causes page splits (a full page is split in two to make room) and fragmentation. Sequential or time-ordered keys just add to the end neatly (11.22). - Heap + secondary indexes (PostgreSQL): rows live in an unordered pile called the heap . Every index points to a row's physical location, called the TID. - Covering index : an index that contains every column the query needs. So the engine never has to visit the table at all. In PostgreSQL this is an index-only scan . In SQL Server you add extra columns with INCLUDE . - Other index types: - Hash — equality ( = ) only. - GIN — PostgreSQL JSONB, arrays and full-text search. - GiST/BRIN — GiST for geo data; BRIN for huge tables that are naturally in order (like append-only time data). - Partial — indexes only some rows, e.g. WHERE status = 'PENDING' . - Unique — also how you enforce idempotency keys (keys that make a repeated request safe to apply only once). How does it work? Composite index column order. A composite index covers several columns. It works like a phone book sorted by (last name, first name). Follow these rules: 1. Put equality-filtered columns first ( tenant id , status ). 2. Then put the range or sort column ( created at ). 3. Leftmost-prefix rule: an index on (tenant id, status, created at) helps WHERE tenant id = ? and WHERE tenant id AND status . It does not help WHERE status = ? alone. A phone book sorted by last name can't help you find everyone with first name "Rahul". Why an index gets ignored: - A function or calculation on the column. WHERE DATE(created at) = '2026-10-01' can't use the index on created at . Rewrite it as a range: created at = '2026-10-01' AND created at < '2026-10-02' . A filter that can use an index like this is called "sargable". Or create an expression index on DATE(created at) . - An implicit type conversion. For example, a VARCHAR column compared to a number. In SQL Server, NVARCHAR vs VARCHAR mismatches do the same. - A leading wildcard. LIKE '%abc' can't use a normal index, because you don't know the start of the value. Use trigram or full-text indexes. - Low selectivity. If the filter matches roughly 10–20% or more of the rows, reading the whole table in order is cheaper than jumping around for many random lookups. - OR across different columns. Rewrite as UNION ALL , or rely on the engine's bitmap OR (combining two index results). - Stale statistics, or a cached plan built for different parameter values. In SQL Server, this second one is called parameter sniffing : the plan was built for the first parameter value it saw, and is bad for others. Example When would I use it? - On the filter, join and sort columns of every frequent query. - Unique indexes for business keys and idempotency. - Partial indexes for small "hot" subsets — for example, outbox rows not yet published, or pending payments. What can go wrong? - Too many indexes. Every write must update every index. This costs storage and multiplies write work ( write amplification ). - Duplicate or unused indexes. Check the usage statistics and drop them. - Wrong column order in a composite index. - Indexing a low-cardinality column alone , like status . A column with only a few distinct values doesn't narrow things down much. - Random UUID keys in clustered indexes. They cause page splits and fragmentation. Interview questions Q1. How does a B+ tree index speed up queries? It keeps keys sorted in a tree that is shallow and very wide. So a lookup reads only about 3–4 pages. Its leaves are linked together, so range scans read them one after another. Q2. Clustered vs non-clustered index? A clustered index stores the table rows themselves in key order, so there can be only one per table. A non-clustered index is a separate structure that points to the rows. Q3. Why might the database not use my index? Common reasons: a function or type conversion on the column, a leading wildcard, low selectivity, the wrong composite column order, stale statistics, or a bad cached plan. Q4. How do you choose composite index column order? Put equality filters first, then range or sort columns. Respect the leftmost-prefix rule. Add INCLUDE columns so the index covers the whole query.

Why? In simple words: A query plan is the database's step-by-step route for running your query. Reading it shows you exactly where the time went, so you fix the real problem instead of guessing. Guessing why a query is slow can waste days. The query plan shows exactly what the database did: - Which indexes it used. - Which join algorithms it chose. - How many rows came out of each step. - Where the time went. Reading plans is how you turn "it's slow" into a specific fix. It is also the heart of a good performance story in an interview — like your ~30 s → ~10 s API improvement. What is happening internally? - EXPLAIN shows the plan the optimiser chose. It shows estimated rows and costs. It does not run the query. - EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query. It shows the actual rows and timings for each step. - BUFFERS adds how many pages were read from memory cache vs from disk. - In SQL Server, the equivalent is the actual execution plan , plus Query Store for history over time. Think of Google Maps. EXPLAIN is the route it suggests before you leave. EXPLAIN ANALYZE is the record of the trip you actually took, with the time spent on each road. How does it work? Look for these clues in the plan: Plan clue Meaning Usual fix --- --- --- Seq Scan on a large table with a selective filter There is no index the planner can use Add a composite index that matches the filter + sort Estimated 10 rows vs actual 500,000 Bad statistics, or columns related in a way the planner doesn't know ANALYZE , extended statistics, or rewrite the query Nested Loop with a huge outer side Wrong join choice caused by a bad estimate Fix the estimates; index the inner side Sort … external merge Disk The sort did not fit in memory and spilled to disk An index that already gives the order, or more work mem Index Scan + many heap fetches / SQL Server Key Lookup in a loop The index does not cover the query, so each row needs a trip to the table Add INCLUDE columns Large Rows Removed by Filter The index finds rows, but most are thrown away afterwards Add the filtered column to the index Optimisation checklist — work through it in order: 1. Measure first. Find which query takes most of the time. Use the slow query log, pg stat statements , SQL Server Query Store, or APM traces. 2. Read the plan. Compare estimated rows with actual rows. 3. Index for the access path. Cover the filter first, then the sort, then the columns the query returns. 4. Return less data. Select only the columns you need. Use keyset pagination (continue from the last seen key, instead of a large OFFSET). Aggregate in the database, not in Java. 5. Remove N+1 patterns (7.10) — one query for a list, then one more query per item. Batch them with IN (...) or a join. 6. Pre-aggregate. Use materialised views, summary tables, or ClickHouse for analytics. 7. Partition big tables so queries skip irrelevant partitions (12.8). 8. Cache results that don't change often. Move heavy reports to read replicas or an OLAP system. 9. Verify the result using the same metrics after the change. Example Say this: "The incentive dashboard API took ~30 seconds. APM showed 90% of the time in one aggregation query. The plan was a sequential scan over the whole orders table because we filtered on DATE(created at) . I rewrote the predicate as a range, added a composite covering index on (tenant, created at) including the aggregated columns, and moved one heavy breakdown to a pre-aggregated table. The endpoint went to ~10 seconds and the DB CPU dropped." Adapt this to what you actually did — only claim the steps you took. When would I use it? - Every slow-endpoint investigation. - Every new query on a big table — check its plan before you ship it. - Design reviews of reporting features. What can go wrong? - Testing plans on tiny dev data. On production volumes, the planner chooses differently. - Adding indexes blindly. Each index adds write cost. - Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on destructive statements in production. It really executes them — an UPDATE or DELETE will change data. Wrap it in a transaction and roll back. - Fixing one query while the real problem is the number of queries. For example, an N+1 pattern firing hundreds of fast queries. Interview questions Q1. How would you find and fix a slow query? First find it, using the slow log, Query Store or APM. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and compare estimated rows with actual rows. Then fix indexes or rewrite the filters, return less data, and remove N+1 patterns. If needed, pre-aggregate or partition. Finally, confirm the improvement with metrics. Q2. EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE? EXPLAIN shows the planned strategy with estimates only. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and reports the real rows and timings for each step.

t: 12.7 Transactions, MVCC, locks and database deadlocks
x: Why? In simple words: Many users change the same data at the same time. The database must keep them from stepping on each other — without making everyone wait in one long queue. MVCC and locks are how it does this. Hundreds of transactions hit the same tables at the same moment. How the database keeps them apart ( isolation ) decides two things: - Correctness — no money spent twice, no update silently lost. - Throughput — who blocks whom, and how much work gets done per second. Once you understand MVCC and locking, you can explain strange results ( anomalies ), deadlocks, and "why is this query just waiting?". What is happening internally? MVCC stands for multi-version concurrency control. PostgreSQL, Oracle and MySQL InnoDB use it, and so does SQL Server when snapshot isolation is on. Here is how it works: - An UPDATE does not overwrite the row. It writes a new version of the row. The old version stays for transactions that started earlier. - Each transaction reads the versions that were committed as of its snapshot — a fixed point in time. In READ COMMITTED, the snapshot is taken at the start of each statement. In REPEATABLE READ, it is taken at the start of the transaction. - So readers don't block writers, and writers don't block readers. But writers still block other writers on the same row. - PostgreSQL keeps the old versions inside the table. They are called dead tuples . VACUUM cleans them up. A long-running transaction stops this cleanup, so the table grows with junk. This is called bloat . - SQL Server's default READ COMMITTED uses locks, not versions. Readers take shared locks and can block writers. If you turn on READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT , it uses row versions stored in tempdb instead. This is a real difference from your SQL Server experience, and worth mentioning in an interview. Think of a bank passbook. When a new entry is written, your earlier printout still shows the old balance. Someone reading the old printout doesn't stop the clerk from writing a new entry. Locks (simplified): - Shared (S) — taken for reads when the isolation level uses locking. - Exclusive (X) — taken for writes. - Update (U) — SQL Server only. Taken when you read a row you plan to update. It avoids conversion deadlocks , where two readers both try to upgrade to a write lock. - Intention locks — placed at table or page level to signal "someone has a lock inside here". - Range/gap locks — lock a range of keys, not just existing rows. Used in SERIALIZABLE in SQL Server and REPEATABLE READ in InnoDB. They prevent phantoms — new rows appearing in a range you already read. Explicit row locks: SELECT … FOR UPDATE (PostgreSQL/MySQL) or WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK) (SQL Server). FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets many workers each take different rows from a queue table, without waiting on each other. This is used for outbox relays and job schedulers. Lock escalation (SQL Server): if one statement holds thousands of row locks, SQL Server may swap them for a single table lock. That blocks everyone. So split big updates into smaller chunks (batches). Deadlock: transaction A locks row 1 and waits for row 2. At the same time, transaction B locks row 2 and waits for row 1. Neither can move. The database's deadlock detector finds this cycle and aborts one of the transactions. PostgreSQL reports deadlock detected . SQL Server reports error 1205, "chosen as deadlock victim". How does it work? Step by step: 1. T1 updates account A, so it locks A. 2. T2 updates account B, so it locks B. 3. T1 now wants B. B is locked by T2, so T1 waits. 4. T2 now wants A. A is locked by T1, so T2 waits. 5. Each waits for the other — a cycle. The database rolls one back. Isolation anomalies (full table in 7.14): - Dirty read — reading data another transaction hasn't committed yet. - Non-repeatable read — reading the same row twice and getting different values. - Phantom — running the same range query twice and getting new rows. - Lost update — two transactions update the same row, and one update overwrites the other. - Write skew — two transactions read the same condition, and each writes a different row. Together they break a rule that each one alone would have kept. Example: two admins each approve "the last" budget slot, so two slots get used. Write skew needs SERIALIZABLE isolation, or an explicit FOR UPDATE on the rows you read. Example When would I use it? - Designing concurrent updates — balances, inventory, seat holds. - Job tables and outbox tables. - Batch updates on busy ("hot") tables. - Debugging blocking — "which session holds the lock?". In PostgreSQL, use pg locks + pg stat activity . In SQL Server, use sys.dm tran locks and blocked process reports. What can go wrong? - Long transactions. They hold locks longer, cause bloat, and cause replication lag. - Network calls inside transactions. A slow HTTP call keeps locks held the whole time. - Inconsistent lock ordering. Different code paths lock rows in different orders, which causes deadlocks. - Missing indexes. An UPDATE without a useful index scans and locks more rows than needed. - Not retrying deadlock victims and serialisation failures. These are normal and expected. Retry them with a small backoff (a short wait), and make the retry idempotent — safe to run twice. Interview questions Q1. What is MVCC? Writers create new versions of a row instead of overwriting it. Readers see a consistent snapshot. So reads and writes don't block each other. Old versions are cleaned up later. Q2. How do database deadlocks happen and how do you handle them? Transactions wait on each other's row locks in a cycle, and the database aborts one of them. Prevent it with a consistent lock order, short transactions, good indexes and single-statement updates. Retry the victim. Q3. What is write skew and how do you prevent it? Two concurrent transactions read overlapping data. Based on it, each writes a different row, and together they break a rule (an invariant). Prevent it with SERIALIZABLE isolation, or by locking the rows you read with FOR UPDATE . Q4. What does FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED do? It locks the selected rows and skips any rows already locked by others. So parallel workers each grab different work items without blocking each other.

t: 12.8 Data modelling: normalisation, denormalisation and table partitioning
x: Why? In simple words: Normalising means storing each fact in one place, so it can't go out of sync. Denormalising means copying data on purpose to make reads faster. Partitioning means cutting one huge table into smaller pieces, usually by month. The schema decides three things: - Correctness — no update anomalies (the same fact stored twice, with one copy updated and the other not). - Performance — how many joins each request needs. - Operability — how you archive or delete old data. A senior engineer knows when to normalise, when to denormalise on purpose, and how to keep huge tables manageable. What is happening internally? Normal forms, one line each: - 1NF : each column holds a single value, and there are no repeating groups. For example, no comma-separated SKU list in one column. - 2NF : no column depends on only part of a composite key. - 3NF : no transitive dependencies — a column should not depend on another non-key column. An outlet's city belongs in outlet , not repeated in every order. - BCNF : every determinant (a column that decides another column's value) is a candidate key. Denormalisation means copying data so you avoid joins or recalculation. Use it for: - Read-heavy paths. - Analytics tables. - Cached aggregates — for example, a balance column kept next to the ledger and checked against it (reconciled) every night. - Historical snapshots that must not change when master data changes. Store the price at order time on the order line. This is a correctness requirement, not just a performance trick. Table partitioning splits a large table into child tables by a key — usually time. This is inside one database. It is different from sharding, which spreads data across servers (11.9). Benefits: - Queries that filter on the key touch only the relevant partitions. This is called partition pruning . - Dropping an old partition is instant. A huge DELETE is slow and heavy. - Each partition's indexes are smaller. Think of an office that keeps one file cabinet per month. To find last week's papers, you open only this month's cabinet. To throw away 2019, you remove the 2019 cabinets — no need to pull out papers one by one. How does it work? Example The orders table grows by 60M rows a year. You use monthly range partitions. Now: - Dashboard queries for "last 30 days" scan only one or two partitions. - GDPR or retention deletes become a simple DROP TABLE orders 2019 01 . - Vacuum and index maintenance run per partition, which is smaller and faster. When would I use it? - Normalise OLTP (transactional) schemas by default. - Denormalise on purpose, for read paths that are proven slow, and for history. - Partition tables that keep growing forever (ledgers, events, orders, logs) by time. Choose a partition key that appears in almost every query's filter. What can go wrong? - Denormalised copies drift out of sync. Decide which copy is the source of truth. Decide how the copies get updated — events, triggers, or reconciliation jobs. - Partitioning on a key that queries don't filter by. Then every query scans every partition. - Too many tiny partitions. The planner spends too long just planning. - Unique constraints must include the partition key. You can't enforce uniqueness on id alone across partitions. Interview questions Q1. When would you denormalise? For read-heavy paths where joins cost too much, for analytics, for cached aggregates, and for historical snapshots such as the price at order time. Q2. Partitioning vs sharding? Partitioning splits a table inside one database, so queries can skip partitions and old data is easy to drop. Sharding spreads data across many database servers, to get more capacity and more write throughput.

t: 12.9 OLTP vs OLAP: where ClickHouse and Trino fit
x: Why? In simple words: The database that takes orders (OLTP) is built for many tiny reads and writes. Dashboards need the opposite — a few huge scans over months of data. So analytics goes to a different kind of database (OLAP), like ClickHouse, which is built for scanning. A dashboard that adds up months of orders across thousands of outlets will crush a transactional database. It will also slow down checkout for real users. Analytical work needs a different storage design. Your experience with ClickHouse and Trino is a strength here. Be ready to explain why they are fast. What is happening internally? OLTP means online transaction processing. OLAP means online analytical processing. OLTP (PostgreSQL, SQL Server) OLAP (ClickHouse, BigQuery, Snowflake; Trino over a lake) --- --- --- Workload Many small reads and writes by key A few huge scans and aggregations Storage Row-oriented (all columns of one row stored together) Column-oriented (each column stored separately, heavily compressed) Indexes B+ trees for point lookups Sparse primary index + sort order; skip indexes; min/max per block Updates Cheap and transactional Expensive or done later in the background (mutations, ReplacingMergeTree) Joins Strong Possible but costly; prefer wide, denormalised tables Why columnar storage is fast for analytics: - A query that sums amount by outlet id reads only those two columns. It skips the rest. - Similar values are stored next to each other, so they compress 5–10×. Less data to read from disk. - Vectorised execution processes values in batches, using SIMD (one CPU instruction working on many values at once). Think of a school register. A row store is like one file per student, with all their marks. To find the class average in Maths, you open every file. A column store is like one sheet with only the Maths marks of all students — you read just that one sheet. ClickHouse MergeTree: 1. Inserted data is sorted by the table's ORDER BY key. 2. It is written as immutable (never changed) parts . 3. Parts are merged together in the background. 4. The sparse primary index stores one mark per granule (a block of 8,192 rows). So a query reads only the granules that can match. 5. Materialised views keep rollups up to date at insert time. 6. TTLs (time-to-live rules) move or drop old data automatically. Trino is a distributed SQL query engine with no storage of its own . It federates queries — one SQL query can read from many sources: Hive/Iceberg tables on object storage, PostgreSQL, Kafka, ClickHouse. It is great for ad-hoc analysis across systems. It is not meant for low-latency serving to users. How does it work? The data flow: 1. PostgreSQL holds the source of truth. 2. CDC (change data capture — Debezium reads every change from the database log) sends changes to Kafka. 3. ClickHouse reads from Kafka. A materialised view builds daily sales per outlet for dashboards and incentive metrics. 4. Batch exports go to a data lake (Iceberg on Blob storage). Trino queries the lake, Postgres and ClickHouse together for ad-hoc analysis. Example Say this: "Transactional truth stays in PostgreSQL or SQL Server; changes stream via CDC and Kafka into ClickHouse for dashboards and incentive aggregates; Trino handles ad-hoc analysis across sources. That split keeps heavy analytics from ever hurting checkout latency." When would I use it? - Dashboards and reports. - Incentive metric aggregation (13.14). - Metrics and log analytics (13.11). - Any query over months or years of events. What can go wrong? - Using ClickHouse like an OLTP database. Frequent single-row updates and deletes, or point lookups by non-key columns, perform badly. - A poor ORDER BY key. Queries can't skip granules, so they read everything. - Too many small inserts. Each insert creates a new part. Batch your inserts. - Expecting strong consistency. The analytics store is fed asynchronously, so it is always slightly behind the source. Interview questions Q1. Row store vs column store? A row store keeps each row together, which is ideal for transactional point reads and writes. A column store keeps each column together, which is ideal for scanning and aggregating a few columns over many rows, with high compression. Q2. Why is ClickHouse fast for aggregations? It uses columnar storage, so it reads only the needed columns. Data is heavily compressed. Data is sorted by the primary key, and a sparse index lets it skip granules. It uses vectorised execution. And materialised views pre-aggregate data at insert time. Q3. What is Trino used for? Distributed SQL across many data sources, without storing any data itself. It is used for ad-hoc analytics across a data lake and operational databases.

Why? In simple words: You give a long link and get back a short code. When someone opens the short code, you look up the long link and send them there — very fast, millions of times a day. Functional (what it must do): - Create a short link for a long URL. Optionally allow a custom alias and an expiry date. - Redirect from the short link to the long URL. - Basic click analytics. Non-functional (how well it must do it): - Redirects must be fast (p99 < 50 ms — 99% of requests finish within 50 ms) and highly available. - Reads are about 100 times more than writes (read:write ≈ 100:1). - Two links must never get the same code (no collisions). What it tests: ID generation, caching a path that is mostly reads, and keeping analytics off the hot path (the path every request takes). What is happening internally? Estimates : - 100M new links/month ≈ 40 writes/s (peak ~120). - Reads are ×100 → ~4,000/s (peak ~12,000). - Each record is ~500 B. So 100M × 12 × 5 years × 500 B ≈ 3 TB over 5 years. - Base62 (digits + lowercase + uppercase = 62 characters) with 7 characters gives 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion codes. That is plenty. API : Data model : url(code PK, long url, owner id, created at, expires at) . You always look a link up by its code. So a key-value store (DynamoDB/Cassandra) fits well. Postgres split into shards by code also works. Architecture : - Redirects go through a CDN/edge, then a load balancer, then the redirect service. Redis holds the ~20% of codes that are hot. On a cache miss, you go to the URL store. - The create service takes IDs from a range allocator and encodes them in base62. - Clicks are sent to Kafka. Analytics consumers read them and write to ClickHouse. How does it work? Code generation (the core deep dive). There are four common ways: Approach How Trade-off --- --- --- Hash + truncate base62(md5(longUrl))[0..7] You must detect collisions and retry; the same URL always gets the same code (deduped) Global counter + base62 Sequence → base62 No collisions; but one central counter for everyone; codes are easy to guess Pre-allocated ID ranges Each instance leases (borrows) a block of 1M IDs from a coordinator (a DB row or ZooKeeper), then encodes locally No coordination per request, no collisions — preferred Key generation service Random unused keys are generated in advance and handed out in batches Codes are hard to guess; but you run one more service Write path : 1. Validate the URL. 2. Take the next ID from this instance's local range. 3. Encode it in base62. 4. Insert it. For a custom alias, use a conditional insert, so the insert fails if the alias is already taken. 5. Return the short URL. Read path : 1. Look up the code at the edge or in Redis. 2. On a hit, return a 302 redirect. 3. On a miss, read from the store, put the result into Redis, then return 302. 4. Publish a click event in the background (asynchronously), so the user does not wait for it. Example 1. Instance A leases IDs 5,000,000–5,999,999. 2. Request 1 gets ID 5,000,000. It is encoded in base62 and padded on the left to make a 7-character code. Then it is stored. 3. Later, a redirect for that code finds it in Redis in 0.8 ms. 4. The click event goes to Kafka. ClickHouse counts it a few seconds later. When would I use it? - Link shortening. - Referral and campaign links. - QR codes for retail promotions. - In general, any service that maps "key → value", is mostly reads, and needs keys that are unique everywhere. What can go wrong? - Collisions with hashing. Two URLs can give the same truncated hash. You must detect this and retry. - Hot links. One very popular link can overload one cache shard. Fix: copy hot keys to several places, and cache at the edge. - Slow analytics. Writing analytics synchronously (while the user waits) slows down redirects. - Malicious URLs. Scan URLs when they are created, and rate-limit each user. - Expired links still in cache. Set the cache TTL (time to live) so it respects the link's expiry. Interview questions Q1. How do you generate short codes without collisions at scale? Give each instance its own pre-allocated range of IDs and encode them in base62. (Snowflake or UUIDv7 IDs, encoded, also work.) This way, no request needs to coordinate with other machines. Q2. 301 or 302? A 301 is cached by browsers. That means less load on you, but you lose analytics because repeat clicks never reach you. A 302 lets you see every click. Choose based on whether analytics matter. Q3. How do you keep redirects fast while counting clicks? Serve the redirect from the cache. Publish click events in the background to Kafka, and count them there.

Why? In simple words: A rate limiter counts how many requests each client sends and says "slow down" (HTTP 429) when they cross their limit. The hard part is keeping one shared, correct count when many servers handle the same client. Functional (what it must do): - Limit requests per client — by user, API key, IP or tenant. - Limits are set per rule, for example 100/min per tenant per endpoint. - When the limit is crossed, return 429 with a Retry-After header. - Rules can be configured. Non-functional (how well it must do it): - Add less than 2 ms of latency. - Stay correct across many gateway instances. - Have a clear, decided behaviour when the limiter itself fails: fail-open (allow requests) or fail-closed (block requests). What it tests: rate-limiting algorithms (10.5), atomic updates in a shared store, and failure handling. What is happening internally? Placement : Put the limiter at the API gateway, or as a sidecar/middleware next to each service. Cache the rules locally and refresh them from a config service. Store : Use a Redis cluster, with keys split across shards by client ID. The check must be atomic — read, check and write must happen as one step. Otherwise two servers could both read "99 used" and both allow request 100. Redis Lua scripts solve this. The whole script runs in one round trip, and nothing else runs in between. So there is no race between the read and the write. Here is a token bucket script. Think of a bucket that holds tokens. Each request takes a token. Tokens refill at a fixed rate. If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected. Alternatives: - Fixed window ( INCR key:minute + EXPIRE ): the simplest. But bursts can slip through at window edges (end of one minute + start of the next). - Sliding log ( ZADD , ZREMRANGEBYSCORE , ZCARD ): exact, but uses more memory because it stores every request time. - Sliding window counter (a weighted mix of two buckets): a good balance of accuracy and memory. How does it work? 1. A request arrives and the gateway authenticates it. 2. The gateway builds the key, for example t-42:/redemptions . 3. It runs the script with EVALSHA , using Redis server time. 4. If the result is 1, it forwards the request. 5. If the result is 0, it returns 429 with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Remaining . Example Tenant t-42 is on the GOLD plan: capacity 200, refill 100/s. It sends a burst of 300 requests in one second: - 200 pass immediately (the bucket was full). - The next ~100 pass as tokens refill. - The rest get 429 with Retry-After: 1 . When would I use it? - Public and partner APIs. - Protecting OTP and login from abuse. - Fairness between tenants. - Protecting your outbound calls to partners that give you a quota. What can go wrong? - Redis slow or down. Keep local fallback buckets. Fail open for non-critical APIs; fail closed for OTP/login. - Hot keys for very large tenants. One key gets too much traffic. Split it into N sub-keys, each with limit/N. - Multi-region limits. Use a quota per region, or sync counts between regions in the background. - Clock skew. App servers' clocks may differ. Use Redis TIME so everyone uses one clock. Interview questions Q1. How do you make the limiter atomic across instances? Keep the state in Redis and update it with a Lua script. Then read, check and write all happen in one atomic operation. Q2. What happens if Redis is down? It is a deliberate policy decision. For normal APIs, fail open and use approximate local limits. For sensitive endpoints, fail closed. Either way, raise an alert. Q3. Token bucket or sliding window? Use token bucket when you want to allow controlled bursts while keeping a smooth average rate. Use a sliding window counter for simple, accurate limits per time window.

Why? In simple words: Services say "tell this user X", and the system picks the right channel (SMS, email, push, WhatsApp), respects their preferences, and delivers it — without sending duplicates and without bulk campaigns blocking urgent OTPs. Functional (what it must do): - Send notifications by SMS, email, push and WhatsApp/in-app. - Triggered by services (order placed, points credited) and by campaigns (bulk sends). - Respect user preferences and opt-outs. - Templates with localisation (different languages). - Scheduling. - Delivery tracking. Non-functional (how well it must do it): - Transactional messages (like OTPs) arrive within seconds. - Millions of campaign messages must not delay OTPs. - No duplicates. - Switch to a backup provider if one fails ( failover ). What it tests: queue design, prioritisation, idempotency (doing the same request twice has the same effect as once) and third-party integration. What is happening internally? Estimates : 10M transactional messages/day (~120/s, peaks ~1,000/s). Plus 5M-message campaigns sent within an hour (~1,400/s). The flow in the diagram, in plain words: 1. Producer services call POST /notify . 2. The Notification API validates the request and removes duplicates using the idempotency key. It checks preferences, quiet hours and DND. Then it renders the template in the user's language. 3. It puts the message on one of two Kafka topics. notify.high is for transactional messages; notify.bulk is for campaigns. Separate topics keep the priorities apart. 4. Channel workers (one consumer group per channel) send through provider adapters. Each adapter has a circuit breaker (stops calling a failing provider for a while), a per-provider rate limit, and failover to a second provider. 5. Providers call back through delivery webhooks, and a status updater records the result. How does it work? 1. Remove duplicates using an (event, user, channel) key. Render the template. Put the message on the right priority topic. 2. Channel workers read the message and apply the provider's rate limit. They call the provider with an idempotency/reference ID, and record SENT. 3. Provider webhooks update the status to DELIVERED/FAILED/READ. Each webhook's signature is verified, and the handling is idempotent, so a repeated webhook does no harm. 4. Failures are retried with backoff (waiting longer each time). After N attempts, the message goes to a DLQ (dead-letter queue — a parking place for failed messages), and a fallback channel is tried (SMS if push fails). Example 1. A "points credited" event arrives. The template points credited hi (Hindi) is chosen. 2. Push is tried first. The device is offline for 10 minutes, so no delivery receipt comes back. 3. The system falls back to SMS, and the SMS is delivered. Meanwhile, a 5M-message Diwali campaign drains through notify.bulk . It runs at the SMS provider's limit of 1,000 msg/s. It does not delay any OTPs, because they travel on notify.high . When would I use it? - Any messaging over several channels. - Alerting. - Marketing campaigns. - In general: "spread work out to slow outside providers, with priorities". What can go wrong? - Duplicate sends on retries. Fix with idempotency keys. - Campaigns starving transactional messages. Fix with separate topics and separate worker pools. - Provider throttling. Shape the send rate and use more than one provider. - Regulatory issues. Respect opt-outs, DND and quiet hours in each user's timezone. - Template bugs sent to millions. Preview templates and roll out in stages. - Webhook storms. Too many status callbacks at once. Batch the status updates. Interview questions Q1. How do you ensure OTPs aren't delayed by a marketing campaign? Give each priority its own topics, its own consumer pools and its own provider quotas. Also shape (throttle) the rate of bulk traffic. Q2. How do you avoid sending duplicate notifications? Use an idempotency key per (event, user, channel). Store it with a TTL and a unique constraint. Also make the webhook handling idempotent. Q3. How do you track delivery? Keep a status machine for each message, updated by provider callbacks. Store it in a store built for heavy writes, with dashboards showing delivery rates per provider.

Why? In simple words: When you open the app, you see recent posts from people you follow. The main choice is when to build that list: when someone posts (push), or when you open the app (pull) — and celebrities with millions of followers need special handling. Functional (what it must do): - Users post. - Users follow others. - The home feed shows posts from the people you follow, newest first or ranked, page by page. Non-functional (how well it must do it): - The feed loads in < 200 ms. - New posts may take a few seconds to appear. This is called eventual consistency . - 300M DAU (daily active users). - Far more reads than writes. What it tests: fan-out strategies (how a post is spread to followers), caching at scale, and the celebrity problem. What is happening internally? Estimates : 300M DAU × 10 feed loads = 3B/day ≈ 35k QPS (peak ~100k). 150M posts/day ≈ 1.7k writes/s. There are two ways to build feeds: Fan-out on write (push) Fan-out on read (pull) --- --- --- How When someone posts, add the post ID to each follower's ready-made feed (a Redis list) When someone opens the feed, fetch recent posts from everyone they follow and merge them Read cost O(1) — read one list O(followees) — grows with how many people you follow Write cost O(followers) — huge for celebrities O(1) Best for Normal users Celebrities with millions of followers The architecture in plain words: 1. The post service saves the post in the Posts DB, sends media to blob storage/CDN, and publishes a PostCreated event. 2. Fan-out workers ask the social graph service for the followers. They add the post ID to each follower's feed:{userId} list in Redis (capped at ~800 IDs). 3. The feed service reads the user's list, merges in recent celebrity posts, fills in the full post details ( hydrates the IDs), ranks them, and returns one page using a cursor. How does it work? Hybrid — use both methods: - Normal authors: push their posts to followers' feeds. - Celebrities (above a follower threshold): skip fan-out. Merge their recent posts in when a follower reads the feed. - Inactive users: do not precompute their feeds. Build the feed on their next login. Example - A user with 300 followers posts. Fan-out workers do 300 LPUSH + LTRIM operations within ~1 s. - A celebrity with 20M followers posts. No fan-out happens. When their followers load the feed, it includes "recent posts from followed celebrities" — a small cached list. It is merged in by timestamp or score. When would I use it? - Activity feeds. - Notification inboxes. - "What's new" panels. - B2B feeds, such as new schemes shown to an outlet. - Any problem where one item must be shown to many people (one-to-many distribution). What can go wrong? - Celebrity fan-out storms. One post triggers millions of writes. - Feed caches too big. Cache feeds only for active users, and cap list sizes. - Deleted or privacy-changed posts still showing. Filter them out at hydration time. - Slow ranking. Precompute the features used for ranking. - Unstable pagination. New posts shift the pages. Use a cursor on (score + ID). Interview questions Q1. Push vs pull for feeds? Push makes reads cheap but makes writes expensive for popular authors. Pull is the opposite. Use a hybrid: push for most users, pull for celebrities. Q2. How do you paginate a feed that changes constantly? Use a cursor based on (score or timestamp, postId), not page offsets. Offsets break when new posts are added at the top.

Why? In simple words: Every phone keeps an open connection to a chat server. When you send a message, the server saves it, gives it a number in the conversation, and pushes it to the receiver's connection — or sends a push notification if they are offline. Functional (what it must do): - 1:1 chat and group chat (≤ 500 members). - Presence (online/last seen). - Delivery and read receipts. - Offline delivery through push notifications. - History synced across multiple devices. - Media. Non-functional (how well it must do it): - < 200 ms delivery when the receiver is online. - Messages are never lost. - Messages stay in order within each conversation. - 500M DAU. What it tests: long-lived connections, routing messages to the right server, ordering, storage at huge write volume, and delivery guarantees. What is happening internally? Estimates : 500M DAU × 40 messages = 20B messages/day ≈ 230k messages/s. At ~100 B each, that is ~2 TB/day of text. The architecture in plain words: 1. Clients connect over WebSocket (a connection that stays open both ways) to connection (gateway) servers. Each server holds ~100k–1M connections. These servers are stateful — they remember who is connected to them. 2. Each connection server records "userId → serverId" in a session registry in Redis. 3. The chat service stores messages in Cassandra. The partition key is conversation id and the clustering key (sort order) is message seq . 4. To deliver, the chat service finds the receiver's connection server in the registry and sends the message through internal pub/sub. 5. If the receiver is offline, it sends a push notification (FCM/APNs). 6. Large groups use fan-out workers on Kafka. Media is uploaded directly to blob storage using a pre-signed URL and served via CDN. Presence uses heartbeats stored in Redis with a TTL. How does it work? 1. The sender's client sends {clientMsgId, conversationId, body} over its WebSocket. 2. The chat service gives the message a per-conversation sequence number . It saves the message, then confirms (acks) to the sender — "sent" ✓. The clientMsgId makes resends idempotent: if the client sends the same message twice, it is stored once. 3. The service finds the receivers' connection servers and pushes the message. When the receiver's device acks, "delivered" ✓✓ flows back to the sender. When the receiver opens the chat, it becomes "read". 4. Offline receivers get a push notification. When they reconnect, the client asks for all messages after its last seen sequence in each conversation. Example 1. Asha sends "Order confirmed?" to the distributor group (40 members). 2. The message gets seq 1043 in the group conversation. 3. 32 online members receive it through their connection servers in ~100 ms. 4. 8 offline members get a push notification. 5. One of them reconnects an hour later. Its last seen seq was 1029, so it fetches seq 1029 and receives 14 messages, in order. When would I use it? - Chat and live support. - The conversational ordering channel of an assistant like NOVA. - Collaborative apps. - Any real-time messaging that goes both ways. What can go wrong? - Connection server fails. Clients reconnect to another server and resync using their sequence number. - Ordering across devices. Fix with a server-assigned sequence per conversation. - Hot group conversations. Use fan-out workers and rate limits. - Presence storms. Too many online/offline updates. Fetch presence lazily, only when a chat is opened. - Message loss. This happens if you ack before saving. Always save first, then ack. Interview questions Q1. How do you route a message to a user connected to a different server? Keep a session registry in Redis that maps each user to their connection server. Then send the message to that server through internal pub/sub or a direct RPC call. Q2. How do you guarantee ordering and no loss? Save the message before acking. Assign a sequence number per conversation. Make sends idempotent using client message IDs. On reconnect, resync from the last seen sequence. Q3. Why Cassandra for messages? The write volume is very high, and messages are read by conversation in time order. That fits Cassandra's partition key + clustering key model well, and Cassandra scales out by adding machines.

Why? In simple words: A cache keeps hot data in memory so reads take well under a millisecond. To hold more data than one machine can, you split keys across many machines and keep copies so a crash does not lose everything. Functional (what it must do): - get , put with a TTL (time to live), and delete . - Grow beyond one machine. - Survive node failures. Non-functional (how well it must do it): - Sub-millisecond latency. - Millions of operations per second. What it tests: in-memory data structures, eviction (removing old data when memory is full), partitioning, replication and consistency trade-offs. What is happening internally? - Single node : a hash map plus an eviction structure. This can be an LRU list ( least recently used goes first). Or it can be approximate LRU/LFU ( least frequently used ) done by sampling a few keys, as Redis does. TTLs are enforced in two ways: lazily, when a key is accessed, and by regularly checking a random sample of keys that have expiry. - Partitioning (splitting keys across nodes): consistent hashing with virtual nodes, done in the client or through a proxy. Redis Cluster instead uses 16,384 hash slots, and each node owns some of the slots. - Replication : each shard has a primary and replicas, copied asynchronously (in the background). Failover is handled by Sentinel or by cluster consensus (the nodes vote). - Memory efficiency : slab allocation in Memcached (memory pre-cut into fixed-size chunks), and compact encodings for small objects in Redis (listpacks). - Concurrency model : Redis runs commands on a single thread, so it needs no locks (newer versions add I/O threads). Memcached is multi-threaded, with striped locks (many small locks, each covering part of the data). - Persistence (optional) : snapshots (RDB) and append-only logs (AOF). How does it work? 1. For GET k , the client hashes k to get a slot. 2. The slot tells it which node owns the key. 3. That node looks up the key in memory and returns the value. If a node fails, its replica is promoted to primary. Keys written to the old primary just before the failure may be lost, because replication is asynchronous. For a cache, this is acceptable. Example - A 6-node Redis Cluster (3 primaries + 3 replicas, 32 GB each) holds 80 GB of hot data. - You add 2 primaries. Some slots move to them while the cluster keeps running (online). - One hot key — a festival scheme list read 50k times/s — is also copied into an in-process Caffeine cache on every app pod, with a 5 s TTL. So most reads never even reach Redis. When would I use it? - Caching. - Sessions. - Rate-limit counters. - Leaderboards. - Distributed locks (carefully). - Short-lived coordination state. What can go wrong? - Cache as the only copy. Never keep critical data only in the cache. - Hot keys. One very popular key overloads one node. - Cache and DB disagree.
