What if I process it from the right?" - "What would I need to store so I don't recompute this?" (→ hashing or DP) - "Can I binary-search on the answer? Is feasibility monotonic — once an answer works, do all bigger answers also work?" - After about 5 minutes of being truly stuck, ask a focused question: "I'm considering X and Y. X fails because… Would it be reasonable to think about Y?" A targeted question like this earns a hint, and you don't look lost.

t: 15.3 Coding round: what this guide adds to your DSA prep
x: Your DSA resource already covers patterns and problems, so this guide does not repeat them. What this guide adds for the coding round is Java fluency. The goal is simple: the language should never slow you down. Need in a coding round Section --- --- Pick the right collection and know its cost 2.1 (choosing), 2.4 HashMap, 2.6 TreeMap, 2.8 ArrayDeque, 2.9 PriorityQueue Sort objects by several keys without bugs 1.13 Comparable/Comparator (never a - b ) Avoid overflow and boxing traps 1.2 Integer cache, 1.3 overflow Build strings efficiently 1.5 StringBuilder Design a data structure where every operation is O(1) 10.3 LRU cache (HashMap + doubly linked list) Coding questions with a concurrency angle 4.14 bounded blocking queue, producer–consumer, odd–even printing Keep a short personal list of the pattern triggers from your DSA resource. For example: "sorted → two pointers / binary search; subarray → window / prefix sum…". Say this list out loud in step 4 of the script above.

1. Clarify. List 4–6 core use cases and write them down. Confirm what is out of scope. Ask about concurrency and persistence (saving data). 2. Entities. Nouns become classes, enums or records. Verbs become methods. 3. Relationships. Draw a quick class diagram. 4. Interfaces first. Name the design patterns at the places where behaviour can vary. 5. Code in this order: models → repositories (in-memory) → services → strategies → a main demo. Make the happy path work end to end before adding extras. 6. Walk through one scenario using the code. 7. Close with three points: - Thread safety — what is shared, and how it is protected. - Extensibility — where a new feature would plug in. - Testing approach. Justify every pattern in one sentence. That is what interview-level LLD sounds like. For example: "I used Strategy for pricing because pricing varies independently of the Ride entity, and I want to add new pricing schemes without modifying ride logic." Practise saying a line like this for each pattern, in every problem you solve. When stuck , say: "Let me write the main use case as a sequence of calls first." Write main using the API you wish you had. This often unlocks the design.

1. Functional requirements — list 3–5. Also say clearly what is out of scope. 2. Non-functional requirements — users/DAU (daily active users), QPS (queries per second), read/write ratio, latency, availability, consistency and data size. 3. Estimates — calculate out loud: QPS, storage per year, cache size. 4. API — 3–6 endpoints. 5. Data model and store choice — give a one-line reason for the choice. 6. High-level diagram — then walk one read request and one write request through it. 7. Offer deep dives : "The interesting parts are A and B — which would you like to explore?" 8. Close with bottlenecks, failure modes, a plan for 10× scale, and monitoring. When stuck , go back to the requirements. Say: "Given we need X at Y QPS, the bottleneck is Z, so…". Naming the bottleneck is always a valid next sentence.

Answer in three layers: 1. Definition — 1 sentence. 2. How it works — 2–3 sentences. 3. When or why it matters in production — 1 example from your own work. Example: " @Transactional is declarative transaction management. Spring wraps the bean in a proxy that begins a transaction before the method and commits or rolls back after — rolling back on unchecked exceptions by default. In practice the classic bug is self-invocation, where an internal call skips the proxy; I'd move the method to another bean." If you don't know the answer, say: "I haven't used that directly. My understanding is … and I'd verify by …". Never bluff with a confident wrong answer.

t: 15.7 Mock interviews: how to run them and score them
x: From Week 13, do one mock every Sunday. From Week 15, do two per week. Trade mocks with a peer — you interview them too. You learn as much from the interviewer's side. Scoring rubric (1–4 each) Dimension 1 4 --- --- --- Problem understanding Jumped into code; solved the wrong problem Clarified, gave examples, confirmed constraints Approach No brute force, no pattern Brute force → optimal, with reasons Communication Long silences Continuous, structured narration Code quality Buggy, messy Clean, modular, correct on the first run Testing None Dry run + edge cases; found own bugs Complexity Wrong or missing Correct for both time and space Weekly mock mix from Week 15 (when you can find partners): - 2 DSA - 1 LLD - 1 HLD - 1 Java/backend theory round. A peer asks 15–20 questions from Chapter 16 and asks two follow-ups on each. Don't wait until you feel "100% ready". Mocks are how you get ready. Timed DSA simulation (45 min, Java only, no autocomplete): 1. 5 min — understand the problem. 2. 5 min — brute force. 3. 10 min — optimise. 4. 20 min — code. 5. 5 min — test and state the complexity. Practise in a plain editor: LeetCode's editor with autocomplete off, or a blank doc. The failure notebook After every mock and every real interview , write one entry for each mistake. Do it within the hour, while it is fresh. Review the notebook every Sunday. Look at the "why I made it" column. The causes that keep coming back are your real weak spots. Fix those causes — not just the individual questions. Interview mode (Weeks 13–16): the loop Don't follow the path course → course → course → "now I'll start interviewing" . That approach wastes months. Instead, start applying from Week 13. Apply to practice companies first. Then your early real interviews feed this loop. Re-attempt every failed mock problem 3 days later.

An OA usually has 2–3 problems in 60–90 minutes. It runs on HackerRank, Codility or HackerEarth, with hidden tests. - Read all the problems first. Solve the easiest one first. - When input comes through stdin, use fast I/O: BufferedReader + StringTokenizer , not Scanner . - Watch for int overflow and edge cases. Hidden tests target exactly these. - Partial credit counts. Submit a brute force that passes some tests first, then optimise. - Keep a personal Java template file with imports, a fast reader and common helpers.

t: 15.9 The day before and the day of
x: Day before : - No new topics. - Review your flashcards, your story bank and your pattern triggers. - Prepare your setup: camera, mic, charged laptop, quiet room, water, paper and pen. - Sleep 7–8 hours. Day of : - 1 hour before: solve 2 easy problems out loud to warm up. - 10 minutes before: read your "tell me about yourself" answer and your 3 questions to ask. - During the round: restate the problem, write things down, think out loud. - Between rounds: don't replay the last round in your head. Reset with a short walk and some water. After each round : within the hour, write down the questions and how you did. Patterns across companies tell you what to fix.

1. Tick off the week's tasks in the plan (Chapter 0). 2. Pick 3 random sections from the week. Re-explain each one without notes — all seven steps, out loud. 3. Answer 10 random Q&A cards out loud. 4. Update the failure notebook and schedule your re-attempts. 5. Check your gates (the pass/fail checkpoints in the plan). If a gate fails, repeat the weak part next week instead of moving on. 6. Plan next week's sections from the plan in Chapter 0.

Question Answer --- --- JDK vs JRE vs JVM? JVM (Java Virtual Machine) runs bytecode; JRE (runtime) = JVM + libraries; JDK (dev kit) = JRE + dev tools (javac, jcmd…). [1.1] Is Java pass-by-value? Always. For objects, the reference is copied, not the object. [1.6] Why is String immutable? So it can be pooled and shared, kept secure, cache its hashCode, and be thread-safe. [1.4] == vs equals ? == compares references (or primitive values); equals compares logical content. [1.12] equals/hashCode contract? Equal objects must have equal hash codes; equal hash codes do not mean equal objects. [1.12] Integer cache range? −128 to 127, when using Integer.valueOf (and autoboxing). [1.2] StringBuilder vs StringBuffer? Same methods; StringBuffer is synchronized, so slower. Use StringBuilder. [1.5] Interface vs abstract class? Interface: a contract for many unrelated classes, no state. Abstract class: shared state and code for related classes. [1.10] Overloading vs overriding? Overloading: chosen at compile time by parameters. Overriding: chosen at runtime by the actual object type. [1.9] Can static methods be overridden? No, they are hidden; the call depends on the reference type, not the object. [1.9] final on variable/method/class? Variable: assign once / method: can't override / class: can't subclass. [1.7] Checked vs unchecked exceptions? Checked: must declare or handle. Unchecked: RuntimeException subclasses, no need. [1.15] Does finally always run? Yes, except on System.exit or a JVM crash. Never return from finally. [1.15] try-with-resources? Closes AutoCloseable resources automatically, in reverse order; extra exceptions are kept as "suppressed". [1.15] Type erasure consequences? Generic types vanish at runtime, so: no primitives as type args, no new T() , no generic arrays, no instanceof on parameterised types. [1.16] PECS? Producer extends , consumer super : read from ? extends T , write to ? super T . [1.16] How to make a class immutable? Final class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copies of mutable fields. [1.14] Comparable vs Comparator? Comparable: natural order inside the class. Comparator: outside order you can combine. [1.13] Why not a - b in comparators? It can overflow and give the wrong sign; use Integer.compare . [1.13] Shallow vs deep copy? Shallow shares nested objects; deep copies them too. Prefer copy constructors over clone. [1.14]

Question Answer --- --- HashMap default capacity and load factor? 16 and 0.75, so it resizes at 12 entries. [2.4] When does a HashMap bucket treeify? When a chain reaches 8 and the table has ≥ 64 slots; turns back into a list at 6. [2.4] Why power-of-two capacity? Index is a fast (n-1) & hash , and on resize each entry stays or moves by exactly n (one bit decides). [2.4] HashMap worst-case lookup in Java 8+? O(log n), because big buckets become trees. [2.4] Null keys in HashMap / ConcurrentHashMap / TreeMap? One allowed / none / none (it needs to compare keys). [2.4, 4.9] ArrayList growth? Grows 1.5× by copying into a bigger array (Arrays.copyOf). [2.2] ArrayList vs LinkedList? ArrayList: fast index access and CPU-cache friendly. LinkedList: O(1) insert only at a node you already hold. Pick ArrayList almost always. [2.2, 2.3] What backs HashSet? A HashMap whose values are a dummy object. [2.7] TreeMap complexity and structure? A red-black (self-balancing) tree, O(log n), with NavigableMap methods like floorKey/ceilingKey. [2.6] LinkedHashMap access order? new LinkedHashMap< (cap, 0.75f, true) + override removeEldestEntry → an LRU (least recently used) cache. [2.5] Stack/queue class to use? ArrayDeque. [2.8] Is PriorityQueue iteration sorted? No; only the head is guaranteed to be the minimum. [2.9] Fail-fast vs fail-safe iterators? Fail-fast throws CME (ConcurrentModificationException) if the collection changes; fail-safe iterates a snapshot or weakly consistent view. [2.10] Remove while iterating? Use iterator.remove() or removeIf . [2.10] Arrays.asList gotcha? Fixed size (no add/remove); with an int[] you get List<int[] . [2.11] unmodifiableList vs List.copyOf? A read-only view of the original vs an independent immutable copy. [2.11] Sort algorithms used? Primitives: dual-pivot quicksort; objects: TimSort (stable — equal items keep their order). [2.11]

Question Answer --- --- Functional interface? Exactly one abstract method; a lambda can be used for it. [3.1] Function vs Supplier vs Consumer vs Predicate? T→R, ()→T, T→void, T→boolean. [3.1] Intermediate vs terminal ops? Intermediate: lazy, return a stream. Terminal: actually run the pipeline. [3.2] map vs flatMap? One-to-one vs one-to-many, flattened into one stream. [3.2] Reuse a stream? No — you get IllegalStateException. [3.2] Parallel streams risk? They use the shared common ForkJoinPool, so blocking calls starve it; overhead is not worth it for small data. [3.4] toMap duplicate keys? IllegalStateException, unless you pass a merge function. [3.3] groupingBy with counting? groupingBy(f, Collectors.counting()) → Map<K, Long . [3.3] orElse vs orElseGet? orElse always builds the default (eager); orElseGet builds it only if needed (lazy). [3.5] Where not to use Optional? Fields, method parameters, collections. [3.5] Record features? Final class, immutable fields, auto-generated accessors/equals/hashCode/toString, compact constructor for checks. [3.7] Sealed classes? Limit which classes can extend it with permits ; switches can then cover all cases. [3.8] Switch expression yield ? Returns a value from a block { } arm of a switch expression. [3.9] Virtual threads? Cheap threads scheduled by the JVM that step off the OS thread during blocking I/O; for I/O-bound concurrency. [4.12] Pinning? A virtual thread can't step off its OS thread (inside synchronized or native code) in Java 21. [4.12] Instant vs LocalDateTime? A point in time in UTC vs a date-time with no time zone. [3.6]

Question Answer --- --- start() vs run()? start() runs the code on a new thread; run() runs it on the current thread. [4.1] sleep vs wait? sleep keeps its locks; wait releases the monitor and needs notify to wake. [4.5] Why wait in a loop? Threads can wake up for no reason (spurious wakeups), and the condition may have changed. [4.5] volatile guarantees? Visibility + ordering, but not atomicity ( count++ is still unsafe). [4.6] happens-before examples? Unlock→next lock, volatile write→read, Thread.start, Thread.join, submitting to an executor. [4.6] Why volatile in DCL singleton? In DCL (double-checked locking), it stops other threads seeing a half-built object. [4.6] ReentrantLock over synchronized? tryLock with timeout, can be interrupted, fairness option, multiple Conditions. [4.7] CAS and ABA? CAS = atomic compare-and-swap. ABA (value changes A→B→A unnoticed) is fixed with stamped references. [4.8] LongAdder vs AtomicLong? LongAdder spreads updates over many cells → faster when many threads update; reading the sum is slower. [4.8] ThreadPoolExecutor admission order? Core threads first → then queue → then extra threads up to max → then reject. [4.3] Problem with newFixedThreadPool? Its queue has no limit → memory blows up under load. [4.3] Rejection policies? Abort, CallerRuns, Discard, DiscardOldest. [4.3] Pool size I/O-bound? cores × (1 + wait time / compute time). [4.3] CHM in Java 8? ConcurrentHashMap: CAS on empty bins, synchronized on the bin's head node, lock-free reads, threads help with resizing. [4.9] containsKey-then-put race fix? Use one atomic call: putIfAbsent / computeIfAbsent / merge / compute. [4.9] CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier vs Semaphore? Wait for N events (one-shot) / N threads wait for each other (reusable) / limit how many run at once. [4.10] thenApply vs thenCompose vs thenCombine? Map the value / flatMap another async call / zip two futures together. [4.11] CompletableFuture default executor problem? It uses the shared common pool — pass your own executor for I/O. [4.11] Deadlock conditions and prevention? Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait; prevent with fixed lock order or tryLock. [4.13] How to detect deadlock in prod? Take a thread dump; look for "Found one Java-level deadlock". [4.13] ThreadLocal risk? Values leak into the next request on a pooled thread; always call remove(). [4.15]

Question Answer --- --- Heap generations? Young (Eden, S0, S1 survivor spaces) and Old. [5.3] PermGen replaced by? Metaspace (in native memory) in Java 8. [5.2] GC roots? Starting points for GC: thread stacks, static fields, JNI (native code) references, active threads. [5.4] Default GC since Java 9? G1. [5.5] G1 vs ZGC? G1: heap split into regions, aims for a pause-time target. ZGC: compacts while the app runs, pauses under 1 ms. [5.5] StackOverflowError cause? Recursion that goes too deep. [5.2] Memory leak causes in Java? Static caches, listeners never removed, ThreadLocals, inner classes holding the outer object, unclosed resources, keys changed after insert. [5.7] Tools for high CPU? top -H → convert thread ID to hex → find that nid in a thread dump; or JFR (Java Flight Recorder) / async-profiler. [5.8] Tools for OOM? For OutOfMemoryError: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError + MAT (Memory Analyzer) dominator tree; compare heap histograms over time. [5.9] Class loader delegation? A loader asks its parent first; order is bootstrap → platform → app. [5.1] JIT tiers? Interpreter → C1 (quick compile) → C2 (optimised compile), with deoptimisation if assumptions break. [5.10] Container heap sizing? -XX:MaxRAMPercentage≈75 (heap = about 75% of the container's memory). [5.11]

Question Answer --- --- @SpringBootApplication = ? @Configuration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan. [6.9] Why constructor injection? Final fields, clear dependencies, easy to test, circular dependencies fail at start-up. [6.2] @Component vs @Bean? @Component: a class found by scanning. @Bean: a factory method inside a @Configuration class. [6.3] Bean scopes? singleton, prototype, request, session, application. [6.5] Prototype in singleton fix? Get a fresh one each time via ObjectProvider / @Lookup / a scoped proxy. [6.5] Bean lifecycle order? Construct → inject → Aware callbacks → BPP (BeanPostProcessor) before → @PostConstruct → BPP after (proxy made here) → @PreDestroy. [6.6] How does auto-configuration work? Starters bring conditional config classes; they step back if you define the bean yourself. [6.9] Self-invocation problem? Calling a method from the same class skips the proxy → no @Transactional/@Async/@Cacheable. [6.7] JDK proxy vs CGLIB? JDK proxy: based on an interface. CGLIB: makes a subclass (Boot's default). [6.7] Property precedence top? Command-line args environment variables profile files application.yml. [6.8] Filter vs Interceptor? Filter: Servlet level, before Spring. Interceptor: Spring MVC level, knows which handler runs. [7.5] Global error handling? @RestControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler → return a ProblemDetail. [7.4] N+1 fixes? Fetch join, @EntityGraph, batch fetch size, DTO (plain data object) projection. [7.10] LazyInitializationException? A lazy field is read after the session closed; load it inside the transaction; turn off OSIV (Open Session In View). [7.11] Dirty checking? Changes to managed entities are UPDATEd automatically at flush. [7.9] Default fetch types? ToOne is EAGER, ToMany is LAZY — make ToOne LAZY too. [7.8] @Transactional default rollback? Only on unchecked exceptions and Errors, not checked exceptions. [7.12] REQUIRED vs REQUIRES NEW vs NESTED? Join existing or create one / always a separate new one / a savepoint inside the current one. [7.13] Isolation levels? Read Uncommitted, Read Committed (Postgres default), Repeatable Read (MySQL default), Serializable. [7.14] Optimistic vs pessimistic locking? Optimistic: @Version column + retry on conflict. Pessimistic: SELECT FOR UPDATE locks the row. [7.15] Prevent overdraw atomically? UPDATE ... SET bal = bal - p WHERE id=? AND bal = p and check the updated row count. [7.15] IDENTITY vs SEQUENCE ids? IDENTITY turns off Hibernate batch inserts; SEQUENCE allows them. [7.16] ddl-auto in prod? Set to validate, and change schema with Flyway/Liquibase migrations. [7.16] JWT validation checks? Signature, exp (expiry), iss (issuer), aud (audience). [8.2] When CSRF needed? For cookie-based browser sessions; not for APIs using bearer tokens. [8.1] @WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest? Only the web layer vs the full application context. [8.4] Why Testcontainers? Tests run against a real DB/Kafka in Docker, so behaviour matches production. [8.4] Kafka consumer idempotency? Safe to process twice: store processed event IDs (unique key) in the same transaction as the effect. [8.5] Cache-aside write rule? Update the DB first, then evict (delete) the cache key. [8.6] Circuit breaker states? Closed → Open → Half-open. [8.7] Scheduled job once per cluster? ShedLock / Quartz in cluster mode / a Kubernetes CronJob. [8.8]

Question Answer --- --- SOLID? Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion. [9.3–9.7] Composition over inheritance — why? Less tight coupling, can change behaviour at runtime, no fragile base class. [9.1] Strategy vs State? Strategy: the client picks the algorithm. State: the object moves itself between states. [9.17, 9.19] Decorator vs Proxy vs Adapter? Add behaviour / control access / convert one interface into another. [9.12–9.14] Factory vs Builder? Factory decides which class to create; Builder builds one complex object step by step. [9.9, 9.10] Best singleton in Java? An enum, or the holder-class idiom. [9.8] Pattern for undo? Command (+ Memento to save state). [9.20] Pattern for rule trees? Composite + Specification (+ Strategy for payouts). [10.12] Parking lot concurrency? Atomically take a spot from a thread-safe free-spot structure, one per spot type. [10.2] LRU in O(1)? HashMap + doubly linked list with dummy head/tail (sentinel) nodes. [10.3] Seat double-booking prevention? Lock per show / conditional DB update / Redis SET NX (set only if absent) with TTL. [10.10] Splitwise simplify? Work out net balances, then greedily match the biggest debtor and creditor using two heaps. [10.9] LLD interview order? Requirements → entities → relationships → interfaces/patterns → code → walk through a scenario → extensions. [9.25]

Question Answer --- --- 1M requests/day ≈ ? QPS About 12 QPS (queries per second), since a day ≈ 10⁵ seconds. [11.2] 99.9% vs 99.99% downtime/year? About 8.8 hours vs about 53 minutes. [11.3] L4 vs L7 load balancer? L4 routes on TCP/IP info only; L7 understands HTTP (paths, headers). [11.4] Cache stampede fixes? Let only one request reload (single-flight or lock), add random jitter to TTLs, serve stale data while refreshing. [11.5] Cache penetration fix?
